y.B: Tripling and halving do not cancel out: the new rug is 18 by 2, so 36 square feet against 24.
y.D: Half as large keeps the width being halved and loses the length being tripled. Three times one side and half the other multiplies the area by 3 × 1/2 = 1 1/2, so 24 square feet becomes 36.

qr.q: The mean of five numbers is 14. A sixth number is added, and the mean of all six numbers is 15. What is the sixth number?
qr.e: The five numbers total 5×14=70 and all six total 6×15=90, so the added number is 90−70=20.

y.A: 30 would push the total to 100 and the mean to about 16 2/3, which is too high. Six numbers must total 90 and five of them total 70, so the sixth is 90 − 70 = 20.
y.C: 15 is the new mean, not the new number. All six total 6 × 15 = 90 and the first five total 70, so the sixth is 20.
y.D: 16 is 15 + 1, adding one for the one-point rise. The rise has to cover all six numbers, so the sixth is 90 − 70 = 20.

qr.q: In a triangle, two of the angles are equal and the third angle is 30° larger than each of them. What is the measure of the largest angle?
qr.e: If each equal angle is x, then x+x+(x+30)=180, so 3x=150 and x=50; the largest angle is 50+30=80°.

y.C: 50 is 80 − 30, the size of each of the two equal angles. The largest angle is 30° bigger than those: 50 + 30 = 80°.
y.A: 70 would make the two equal angles 40 each, and 40 + 40 + 70 is 150 rather than 180.
y.D: 60 would make the equal angles 30 each, totalling 120.

qr.q: Which of these numbers is divisible by 5?
qr.e: A whole number is divisible by 5 when its last digit is 0 or 5, and 75 ends in 5 while the others end in 2, 8, and 4.

y.B: 64 ends in 4, so 5 leaves a remainder: 64 ÷ 5 is 12 with 4 over. Multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5, and here that is 75.
y.C: 58 ends in 8, and a number divides by 5 only when it ends in 0 or 5 — 55 and 60 sit either side of it. Here that number is 75.
y.D: 42 ends in 2, so 5 does not divide it — 40 and 45 are the multiples of 5 nearest to it. The one ending in 5 is 75.

qr.q: A rope is 4 feet long. How many inches long is the rope? (1 foot = 12 inches)
qr.e: Each foot is 12 inches, so 4 feet is 4 × 12 = 48 inches.

y.A: 24 is 12 × 2, two feet of rope. There are four: 4 × 12 = 48.
y.B: 16 is 4 + 12. Each foot holds 12 inches, so the feet multiply: 4 × 12 = 48.
y.C: 44 is 48 − 4, four inches short. Four feet is 4 × 12 = 48.

qr.q: A printer prints 42 pages in 6 minutes at a steady rate. How many pages does it print in 15 minutes?
qr.e: The rate is 42÷6=7 pages per minute, so in 15 minutes it prints 7×15=105 pages.

y.B: 90 is 6 × 15, the two times multiplied. Find the rate first: 42 ÷ 6 = 7 a minute, so 7 × 15 = 105.
y.C: 63 is 105 − 42. The printer does 7 pages a minute, so 15 minutes is 7 × 15 = 105.
y.D: 84 is 42 × 2, which is 12 minutes’ worth. Fifteen minutes is 7 × 15 = 105.

qr.q: The numbers in a pattern are 45, 40, 35, 30, ... . What is the next number in the pattern?
qr.e: Each number is 5 less than the one before it, so the next number is 30 − 5 = 25.

y.A: 26 is 30 − 4, taking 4 off instead of 5. Each step down is 5, so the next number is 25.
y.B: 24 is 30 − 6, one too far. The pattern drops by 5 each time: 30 − 5 = 25.
y.C: 20 is 30 − 10, two steps at once. One step gives 25, and 20 is the number after that.

qr.q: A jacket priced at $80 is marked down 25%. At the register, another $5 is taken off. What is the final price?
qr.e: 25% of $80 is $20, so the marked-down price is $60, and $60−$5=$55.

y.D: 60 is 55 + 5, the price after the 25% comes off but before the $5 at the register. That last $5 still has to go: $60 − $5 = $55.
y.A: 65 takes off $15 in all; 25% of $80 is $20, and the extra $5 makes $25.
y.C: 50 takes $30 off; the markdown is $20 and the register takes $5, which is $25.

qr.q: A team records its goals each week: Week 1 has 4 goals, Week 2 has 7 goals, Week 3 has 5 goals, and Week 4 has 6 goals. How many goals did the team score in the four weeks altogether?
qr.e: Adding the four weeks gives 4 + 7 + 5 + 6 = 22 goals.

y.A: 23 is 22 + 1, one goal too many. The four weeks are 4 + 7 + 5 + 6 = 22.
y.B: 21 is 22 − 1, one short. Adding the four weeks gives 22.
y.C: 26 is 4 + 22, the first week counted twice. The total is 22.

qr.q: Ten cards numbered 1 through 10 are placed face down and one is drawn at random. What is the probability that the card drawn shows a prime number?
qr.e: The primes from 1 to 10 are 2, 3, 5, and 7 — four of the ten cards — so the probability is 4/10=2/5.

y.B: 3/5 counts the six cards that are not prime — 1, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10 — instead of the four that are. The primes are 2, 3, 5 and 7, so the chance is 4/10 = 2/5.
y.C: 1/2 is the chance of an odd card, and 1 and 9 are odd without being prime. The primes are 2, 3, 5 and 7: 4 out of 10.
y.D: 3/10 counts 3, 5 and 7 but leaves out 2, which is prime as well. Four cards out of ten is 2/5.

qr.q: Which fraction is between 1/3 and 1/2?
qr.e: In twelfths, 1/3=4/12 and 1/2=6/12, and 5/12 falls between them; 1/4 is smaller and 3/5 and 2/3 are larger than 1/2.

y.A: 1/4 is smaller than 1/3, because quarters are smaller pieces than thirds. In twelfths it is 3/12, below 4/12, and the one in between is 5/12.
y.B: 2/3 is bigger than 1/2 — two of three pieces is more than half. Between 4/12 and 6/12 sits 5/12.
y.C: 3/5 is more than half, since half of 5 is 2 and a half and the top is 3. The one in between is 5/12.

qr.q: Priya has 5/8 of a yard of ribbon but needs 2/3 of a yard. How much more ribbon does she need?
qr.e: Using 24ths, 2/3=16/24 and 5/8=15/24, so she needs 16/24−15/24=1/24 of a yard.

y.B: 1/12 comes from trying to use twelfths, but eighths do not fit into twelfths. Twenty-fourths fit both: 2/3 = 16/24 and 5/8 = 15/24, so the gap is 1/24.
y.C: 3/5 is the tops and the bottoms worked apart — 5 − 2 = 3 and 8 − 3 = 5. Fractions have to share a bottom number first: 16/24 − 15/24 = 1/24.
y.D: 1/8 is a whole extra eighth, which would carry her past two thirds — 6/8 is more than 2/3. The gap is smaller than that: 16/24 − 15/24 = 1/24.

qr.q: A rectangular sheet of paper is 10 cm by 6 cm. A 3 cm by 4 cm rectangle is cut away from one corner. What is the area of the piece that is left?
qr.e: The whole sheet is 10×6=60 square cm and the piece removed is 3×4=12, so 60−12=48 square cm remain.

y.A: 60 is 10 × 6, the area of the whole sheet before the corner was cut away. The piece taken out comes off: 60 − 12 = 48 square cm.
y.B: 72 adds the cut-away piece instead of removing it; 60 − 12 = 48.
y.D: 44 takes away 16 rather than 12, and the piece cut out is 3 × 4.

qr.q: Three vertices of a rectangle are (1, 5), (9, 5), and (9, 2). What are the coordinates of the fourth vertex?
qr.e: The fourth vertex shares the x-value 1 with (1, 5) and the y-value 2 with (9, 2), giving (1, 2).

y.B: (2, 1) is the right pair written the wrong way round. The across number comes first, so the corner is (1, 2).
y.C: (5, 2) borrows the 5 from (1, 5), but that 5 is a height, not an across number. The new corner sits straight below (1, 5), so it keeps the 1: (1, 2).
y.D: (1, 9) picks up the 9 from (9, 2), but 9 is that corner's across number, not its height. The new corner is level with (9, 2), so it takes the 2: (1, 2).

qr.q: A stadium sold 4,180 tickets on Friday, 3,905 on Saturday, and 2,870 on Sunday. Which is the best estimate of the total number of tickets sold?
qr.e: Rounding gives 4,200+3,900+2,900=11,000, and the exact total, 10,955, is much closer to 11,000 than to 10,000.

y.A: 12,000 is 5,000 + 4,000 + 3,000, every number pushed up to the next whole thousand instead of to the nearer one. 4,180 is nearer 4,000 and 3,905 is nearer 4,000, so the three come to 4,000 + 4,000 + 3,000 = 11,000.
y.B: 10,000 is 10,955 with the 955 dropped rather than rounded. More than half a thousand is left over, so the total rounds up to 11,000.
y.D: 9,000 is 4,000 + 3,000 + 2,000, every number chopped down to its first digit. Rounded to the nearest thousand they are 4,000, 4,000 and 3,000, which come to 11,000.

qr.q: Three pencils and two erasers cost $1.30 in all. One pencil costs $0.30. What does one eraser cost?
qr.e: The pencils cost 3×$0.30=$0.90, leaving $1.30−$0.90=$0.40 for two erasers, so one eraser is $0.20.

y.A: 0.15 is 0.30 ÷ 2, half the price of one pencil. The halving belongs to what is left after the pencils: $1.30 − $0.90 = $0.40, and $0.40 ÷ 2 = $0.20.
y.D: 0.40 is 0.20 × 2, what the two erasers cost together. One eraser is half of that: $0.40 ÷ 2 = $0.20.
y.C: 0.25 would make two erasers $0.50, and only $0.40 is left after the three pencils.

qr.q: A student's five test scores have a mean of 82. If the lowest score, 62, is dropped, what is the mean of the four remaining scores?
qr.e: The five scores total 5×82=410; without the 62 the total is 348, and 348÷4=87.

y.A: 82 is the mean she started with, as if dropping a score left the average where it was. Losing a low score lifts it: the four that are left total 348, and 348 ÷ 4 = 87.
y.B: 85 is 340 ÷ 4, which needs the four scores to total 340. Take 62 off 410 and the total is 348, and 348 ÷ 4 = 87.
y.D: 92 is 82 + 10, a guess at how far the mean jumps. The 62 was 20 below the mean, and those 20 points spread over the four left: 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so 82 + 5 = 87.

qr.q: In a class, the ratio of students who walk to school to students who ride is 2:5. There are 21 more riders than walkers. How many students are in the class?
qr.e: The difference is 5−2=3 parts, so one part is 21÷3=7 students; the class has 2+5=7 parts, or 7×7=49 students.

y.A: 21 shares the 21 extra riders among all 7 parts instead of among the 3 parts the gap is worth, and 21 ÷ 7 = 3 followed by 7 × 3 lands back on the 21 it started from. The gap is 5 − 2 = 3 parts, so one part is 21 ÷ 3 = 7 and the class is 7 × 7 = 49.
y.C: 35 is 5 × 7, the riders on their own. The 2 × 7 = 14 walkers belong in the class too: 35 + 14 = 49.
y.D: 63 is 21 × 3, the extra riders multiplied by the three spare parts instead of shared among them. One part is 21 ÷ 3 = 7, and seven parts make 49.

qr.q: A mystery number is made by multiplying 2 × 3 × 3 × 5. Which of these numbers is a factor of the mystery number?
qr.e: The mystery number is 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 90, and a factor of it can only be built from those primes, using each one no more often than it appears on the card: 3 × 5 = 15 works, and 90 ÷ 15 = 6. Break each choice into primes first and check every one of them is on the card before you agree it divides.

y.A: 4 is 2 × 2, and the card has only one 2 to give, so 4 cannot be built from it. 15 is 3 × 5, and both of those are on the card.
y.B: 7 is a prime that does not appear on the card at all, so it cannot divide the number. The primes there to build a factor from are 2, 3, 3 and 5, and 3 × 5 = 15.
y.C: 25 is 5 × 5, but the card holds only one 5, so 25 cannot be made from it. 15 uses the 3 once and the 5 once: 3 × 5 = 15.

qr.q: In a quiz game, five rounds have a range of 26 points, and the lowest round score is 58. In a sixth round the score is 95. What is the range of all six scores?
qr.e: The first five rounds run from 58 up to 58 + 26 = 84. The 95 is above 84, so it becomes the highest while 58 stays the lowest, and the range is 95 − 58 = 37. When a value joins a set, only the two ends matter — check whether the new value lands outside them.

y.A: 26 is the range of the first five rounds, left exactly as it was. The 95 is higher than the old highest score of 84, so the range stretches to 95 − 58 = 37.
y.C: 11 is 95 − 84, the new score measured from the old highest score instead of from the lowest. Range always runs from lowest to highest: 95 − 58 = 37.
y.D: 153 is 95 + 58, the two scores added instead of one taken from the other. The range is the gap between the ends: 95 − 58 = 37.

qr.q: What is the smallest whole number greater than 50 that leaves a remainder of 4 when it is divided by 7?
qr.e: Every number that leaves 4 when divided by 7 is a multiple of 7 with 4 added on, and the multiple just below the target is 7 × 7 = 49, so the number is 49 + 4 = 53. Find the nearest multiple of the divisor first, add the remainder on, then check the answer really is above the limit the question set.

y.B: 54 is 50 + 4, the remainder added to the 50 instead of to a multiple of 7. The multiple of 7 just below is 49, and 49 + 4 = 53.
y.C: 56 is 7 × 8, the first multiple of 7 past 50, and a multiple of 7 leaves a remainder of 0. Adding 4 to the multiple below gives 49 + 4 = 53.
y.D: 46 is 42 + 4, so it does leave a remainder of 4 — but it is smaller than 50. The next number that leaves 4 is 49 + 4 = 53.

qr.q: On a plan of a playground, 1 cm stands for 5 m. The playground is drawn as a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm. What is the real area of the playground?
qr.e: Each centimeter stands for 5 m, so the real playground is 6 × 5 = 30 m by 4 × 5 = 20 m, and its area is 30 × 20 = 600 m². Turn both sides into real lengths first, then multiply — never scale an area straight off the plan.

y.A: 24 is 6 × 4, the area of the rectangle on the plan rather than the real playground. Each centimeter stands for 5 m, so the real sides are 30 m and 20 m, and 30 × 20 = 600 m².
y.B: 120 is 24 × 5, the plan's area multiplied by 5 just once. Both sides have to grow: 6 × 5 = 30 m and 4 × 5 = 20 m, so 30 × 20 = 600 m².
y.D: 50 is 30 + 20, the two real sides added instead of multiplied. Area comes from multiplying them: 30 × 20 = 600 m².

qr.q: A pattern on a wall is symmetrical about a vertical mirror line. One dot in the pattern sits 5 cm to the left of that line. Where is its matching dot?
c: 10 cm to the right of the line
5 cm to the right of the line
qr.e: A mirror line puts every point the same distance out on the other side, so a dot 5 cm to the left has its partner 5 cm to the right. Measure to the mirror line, never across to the other dot.

y.A: 10 is 5 × 2, the whole gap from one dot across to the other rather than the distance from the mirror. The mirror puts the matching dot the same 5 cm out on the other side.
y.B: 5 cm above the first dot keeps the right distance but moves in the wrong direction. A vertical mirror swaps left for right, so the matching dot sits 5 cm to the right of the line.
y.D: On the line itself is where a dot sits when it is its own reflection, 0 cm from the mirror. This dot is 5 cm out, so its partner is 5 cm out on the other side.

qr.q: A box is made twice as long and half as tall. Its width does not change. Its volume is now:
qr.e: Doubling the length multiplies the volume by 2 and halving the height multiplies it by 1/2, and 2 × 1/2 = 1, so the box holds what it always did. When two measurements change, multiply the changes together instead of looking at only one of them.

y.A: Twice as much counts the doubled length and forgets that the height was halved. Doubling and halving undo each other, so the box holds exactly what it held before.
y.B: Half as much counts the halved height and forgets that the length was doubled. One change undoes the other: 2 × 1/2 = 1, so the volume is unchanged.
y.C: Four times as much is what doubling two of the measurements would do. Here one measurement was doubled and another was halved, so the volume stays exactly where it was.

qr.q: Seven boxes at a market stall hold an average of 9 lemons each. How many lemons are there altogether?
qr.e: An average of 9 lemons in each of 7 boxes means the boxes hold 9 × 7 = 63 lemons in all. Going from an average back to a total is a multiplication — the average times how many things there are.

y.B: 16 lemons is 9 + 7, the two numbers added instead of multiplied. Each of the seven boxes holds 9 on average: 9 × 7 = 63.
y.C: 54 lemons is 9 × 6, one of the seven boxes left out. All seven count: 9 × 7 = 63.
y.D: 56 lemons is 7 × 8, seven eights recited instead of seven nines. Each of the seven boxes holds 9: 9 × 7 = 63.

qr.q: The largest of three consecutive whole numbers is 16. What is the sum of the next three consecutive whole numbers?
qr.e: Counting back from 16 gives 14, 15 and 16, so the next three are 17, 18 and 19, and 17 + 18 + 19 = 54. Every number in the second run is 3 more than its partner in the first, so a quicker route is the first total plus three lots of 3: 45 + 9 = 54.

y.A: 45 is 14 + 15 + 16, the first three numbers added instead of the three that come after them. Those three are 17, 18 and 19, which total 54.
y.C: 48 is 45 + 3, the step of 3 added a single time. Each of the next three numbers is 3 more than the number three places back, so the total rises by three lots of 3: 45 + 9 = 54.
y.D: 51 is 16 + 17 + 18, the next run started at 16 — but 16 is already one of the first three. The next three are 17, 18 and 19, which total 54.

qr.q: A wall display has 3⁴ blue tiles and 4³ red tiles. How many more blue tiles are there than red?
qr.e: 3⁴ is four threes multiplied — 3 × 3 = 9, 9 × 3 = 27, 27 × 3 = 81 — and 4³ is three fours, 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, so there are 81 − 64 = 17 more blue tiles. When the same two digits turn up swapped like this, work each power out on its own before comparing them; they are not the same number.

y.B: 145 is 81 + 64, the two lots of tiles added instead of compared. 3⁴ = 81 and 4³ = 64, so 81 − 64 = 17.
y.C: 33 is 81 − 48, with the red tiles worked out as 4 × 4 × 3. Three fours multiplied is 64, so 81 − 64 = 17.
y.D: 37 is 64 − 27, with the blue tiles worked out as 3 × 3 × 3, one three short. Four threes multiplied is 81, so 81 − 64 = 17.

qr.q: At the school fair a ride ticket costs $3 and a raffle strip costs $4. The cost in dollars of t ride tickets and 2 raffle strips is 3t + 8. What is the cost when t = 9?
qr.e: The letter t counts the ride tickets, so 9 tickets cost 3 × 9 = 27 dollars, and the two raffle strips are the 8 that has already been worked out: 27 + 8 = $35. Finish the part carrying the letter before adding the part that stands on its own — that part is added once, however many tickets there are.

y.A: $99 is 11 × 9, the 3 and the 8 added together before the multiplying. Only the tickets multiply: 3 × 9 = 27, and 27 + 8 = 35.
y.C: $72 is 8 × 9, the 8 multiplied by the tickets instead of the 3. The 3 is the number beside the letter: 3 × 9 = 27, and 27 + 8 = 35.
y.D: $20 is 3 + 9 + 8, every number added and none of them multiplied. A number written beside a letter means multiply: 3 × 9 = 27, and 27 + 8 = 35.

qr.q: A bag of apples weighs 38 ounces. What is that weight in pounds and ounces? (1 pound = 16 ounces)
qr.e: Sixteen ounces make a pound, so 38 ounces holds two whole pounds — 2 × 16 = 32 — with 38 − 32 = 6 ounces left over: 2 pounds 6 ounces. Coming back from one unit to two, take out as many whole big units as will fit and whatever cannot make another one is what is left over.

y.A: 3 pounds 8 ounces is the 38 read as though ten ounces made a pound. A pound is 16 ounces, and 16 + 16 = 32 with 6 over, so it is 2 pounds 6 ounces.
y.B: 3 pounds 2 ounces is 38 split up twelve at a time, which is feet and inches, not pounds and ounces. Sixteen ounces make a pound: 2 × 16 = 32, and 38 − 32 = 6, so 2 pounds 6 ounces.
y.C: 6 pounds 2 ounces is the answer back to front, with the 6 spare ounces written as the pounds. 38 ounces makes 2 whole pounds and 6 ounces over: 2 pounds 6 ounces.

qr.q: Tickets to a school concert cost $6 each. One family buys 4 tickets. Another family buys 3 tickets and a $10 programme. Which family pays more, and by how much?
qr.e: The first family pays 4 × 6 = 24 dollars and the second pays 3 × 6 + 10 = 28 dollars, so the second family pays 28 − 24 = 4 dollars more. Work each side out in full before comparing them — a missing item is far easier to spot in a total than in a sentence.

y.A: The first family, by $6, is 24 − 18, the programme left out of the second family's bill. With it, that family pays 18 + 10 = 28, which is 4 more than 24.
y.B: The second family, by $10, names the programme's price as the whole gap. The first family's extra ticket covers 6 of that, so the gap is 28 − 24 = 4.
y.D: The first family, by $4, has the right gap but the wrong family. The first family pays 4 × 6 = 24 and the second pays 3 × 6 + 10 = 28, so it is the second family that pays 4 more.

qr.q: Five cards show 14, 20, 14, 17 and 20. One more card is added so that the list has a single mode, and that mode is 20. What number is on the card that is added?
qr.e: 20 and 14 each appear twice, so one extra 20 makes 20 appear three times and leaves 14 on two, giving a single mode of 20. When a question asks you to create a mode, count the tallies as they stand and see which value needs only one more.

y.A: 14 would give three 14s against two 20s, making 14 the mode instead of 20. Another 20 gives three 20s to two 14s, so 20 becomes the single mode.
y.B: 17 gives 14, 20 and 17 two cards each, so nothing leads and the list has no single mode. Another 20 puts it ahead on three, making 20 the only mode.
y.C: 34 is 14 + 20, the two repeated numbers added together. What the list needs is one more of the number that should lead, which is 20.

qr.q: There are 38 cookies packed into bags of 5. After all the full bags are made, how many cookies are left over?
qr.e: Seven full bags use 7 × 5 = 35 cookies, and 38 − 35 = 3 cookies are left over.

y.C: 2 is 5 − 3, how many more cookies it would take to fill one more bag. The question asks what is left over: seven full bags use 35, and 38 − 35 = 3.
y.A: 7 is the number of full bags, not the cookies left over.
y.B: 4 is one more than the remainder; 7 × 5 = 35, and 38 − 35 = 3.

qr.q: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices, and 3 of the slices are eaten. What fraction of the pizza is left?
qr.e: Three of the 8 slices are gone, so 8 − 3 = 5 slices remain, which is 5/8 of the pizza.

y.B: 1/2 would mean 4 slices still there. Three were eaten, not four, so 8 − 3 = 5 are left: 5/8.
y.C: 3/5 sets the 3 eaten against the 5 left. A fraction of the pizza counts all 8 slices underneath, and 5 remain: 5/8.
y.D: 3/8 is the part that was eaten. The question asks for what is left: 8 − 3 = 5 slices, so 5/8.

qr.q: Dana has $20 and wants to buy items priced $6.85, $4.20, and $7.95. Which statement is true?
c: She can buy all three and have $1.00 left
She can buy all three with exactly $0 left
She can buy all three and have $2.00 left

y.A: $1.00 short would mean the three came to $21.00. They come to $19.00: $6.85 and $7.95 make $14.80, and $4.20 more makes $19.00, so a dollar is left over.
y.C: $0 left is what rounding every price up to the next dollar gives: $7 + $5 + $8 = $20. The real prices total $19.00, so $1.00 stays in her pocket.
y.D: $2.00 is what the cents come to on their own — 85 + 20 + 95 = 200 cents — not what is left. The bill is $19.00, so the change from $20 is $1.00.

qr.q: Which is the best estimate of 4,982 ÷ 51?
qr.e: Rounding gives 5,000÷50=100, and the exact quotient is a little under 98, so 100 is the closest estimate.

y.A: 500 is 5,000 with one zero crossed off to match the zero in 50, and the dividing by the 5 then never done. Finish it: 500 ÷ 5 = 100, and 50 × 100 = 5,000.
y.B: 10 is 5,000 ÷ 500, one zero too many on the number she is dividing by. 51 is about 50, and 5,000 ÷ 50 = 100.
y.C: 1,000 is 5,000 ÷ 5, as if she were dividing by 5 rather than by about 50. Fifty goes into 5,000 a hundred times.

qr.q: Four friends have a mean score of 20 in a game. A fifth friend joins with a score of 25. What is the mean score of all five friends?
qr.e: The four friends total 4×20=80, so all five total 105, and 105÷5=21.

y.A: 20 is the mean before the fifth friend arrived. The new 25 is above 20, so the mean creeps up: 80 + 25 = 105, and 105 ÷ 5 = 21.
y.B: 22 is close to halfway between 20 and 25, as if the new score weighed as much as the other four together. It is one score of five: 80 + 25 = 105, and 105 ÷ 5 = 21.
y.C: 25 is the new friend's own score, not the mean of everybody. All five together total 105, and 105 ÷ 5 = 21.

qr.q: How many 1-centimeter cubes are needed to fill a box that is 5 cm long, 3 cm wide, and 2 cm tall?
qr.e: Each layer holds 5 × 3 = 15 cubes and the box is 2 layers tall, so 15 × 2 = 30 cubes fill it.

y.A: 60 is 30 × 2, the box counted twice. 5 × 3 × 2 = 30.
y.C: 15 is 5 × 3, one layer. The box is 2 layers tall, so 15 × 2 = 30.
y.D: 10 is 5 × 2, the length and the height. The width is needed too: 5 × 3 × 2 = 30.

qr.q: On a scale drawing, 3 cm represents 12 meters. A hallway is actually 30 meters long. How long is that hallway on the drawing?
qr.e: Since 3 cm stands for 12 m, 1 cm stands for 4 m, so 30 m needs 30÷4=7.5 cm.

y.A: 9 is 3 × 3. One centimeter stands for 4 m, so 30 m needs 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5 cm.
y.B: 10 is 30 ÷ 3, dividing by the centimeters instead of the meters. Each centimeter is 4 m: 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5.
y.D: 2.5 is 30 ÷ 12, using the 12 on its own. Three centimeters stand for 12 m, so one stands for 4 m.

qr.q: Car A travels 150 miles on 5 gallons of gas. Car B travels 210 miles on 7 gallons. Which car goes farther on one gallon?
c: Car A, at 35 miles per gallon
Car B, at 30 miles per gallon
Car B, because it traveled more miles
Neither — both travel 30 miles per gallon
qr.e: 150÷5=30 and 210÷7=30, so the two cars have exactly the same rate of 30 miles per gallon.

y.A: Car A, at 35 miles per gallon — 35 is 5 × 7, the two gallon amounts multiplied together. A rate comes from dividing: 150 ÷ 5 = 30, and Car B gives 210 ÷ 7 = 30 as well.
y.B: Car B, at 30 miles per gallon — 30 is 210 ÷ 7, which is right for Car B. Car A works out at the same rate, 150 ÷ 5 = 30, so neither car goes farther.
y.C: More miles is not the same as more miles per gallon — Car B used more fuel too, and 210 ÷ 7 is the same 30 as 150 ÷ 5.

qr.q: A spinner has 20 equal sections, and each section is either green or white. The probability of landing on green is 2/5. How many of the sections are white?
qr.e: Two fifths of the 20 sections is 8 green sections, so the other 20 − 8 = 12 sections are white.

y.A: 15 is 20 − 5, taking off the 5 from the fraction rather than the green sections. Two fifths of 20 is 8, so white is 12.
y.B: 10 is 20 ÷ 2, half the spinner. Two fifths of 20 is 8 green, leaving 12 white.
y.D: 8 is the green sections. The question asks for the white ones: 20 − 8 = 12.

qr.q: A square and a rectangle have the same perimeter. The rectangle measures 12 cm by 4 cm. What is the area of the square?
qr.e: The rectangle's perimeter is 2(12+4)=32 cm, so the square has side 32÷4=8 cm and area 8×8=64 square cm.

y.A: 48 is 12 × 4, the rectangle’s area. The question asks for the square’s.
y.B: 32 is the perimeter the two shapes share, not an area. The square’s side is 32 ÷ 4 = 8.
y.D: 16 is 12 + 4. The square’s side is 32 ÷ 4 = 8, so its area is 8 × 8 = 64.

qr.q: The $60 price of a game is raised by 10%, and the new price is later lowered by 10%. What is the final price?
qr.e: The price rises to $66, and 10% of $66 is $6.60, so the final price is $66−$6.60=$59.40 — less than the original because the second 10% is taken from a larger number.

y.B: $59.00 is $66 − $7, with the 10% rounded up to a whole dollar. Ten percent of $66 is $6.60, and $66 − $6.60 = $59.40.
y.C: $66.00 is the price after the 10% rise, with the 10% drop that comes next never taken off. Ten percent of $66 is $6.60, so the final price is $66 − $6.60 = $59.40.
y.D: $60.00 is what you get if the 10% up and the 10% down cancel out. They do not: the rise is $6.00 on $60, but the drop is $6.60 on $66, leaving $59.40.

qr.q: Elena spent 2/5 of her money on a book, then spent 1/3 of what was left on a snack. She has $12 left. How much money did she start with?
qr.e: After the book, 3/5 remains; spending 1/3 of that leaves 2/3 × 3/5 = 2/5 of the start, so 2/5 of the money is $12 and the whole is $30.

y.A: 24 is 12 × 2. What she has left is two fifths of the start, so one fifth is 6 and the start was 30.
y.B: 20 is 5 × 4. Twelve dollars is two fifths of the start, so a fifth is 6 and the start was 30.
y.D: 36 is 12 × 3. Two fifths is what is left, so a fifth is 6 and she began with 30.

qr.q: Which of these numbers is the greatest?
qr.e: Written as decimals, 3/5=0.6 and 2/3 is about 0.667, so 0.7 is greater than all the others, including 0.68.

y.A: 3/5 is 0.6 — six tenths, which is a tenth short of 0.7. Lining all four up as decimals settles it: 0.6, 0.68, about 0.67 and 0.7.
y.B: 0.68 has more digits than 0.7, but more digits does not mean more. Line them up as 0.68 and 0.70 and the 0.7 is two hundredths bigger.
y.C: 2/3 works out at about 0.67, which beats 3/5 but is still under 0.7. Dividing 2 by 3 gives 0.666..., a shade short of seven tenths.

qr.q: In a survey, 35 out of 50 students chose soccer. What percent of the students chose soccer?
qr.e: 35/50 = 70/100, so 70% of the students chose soccer.

y.A: 35 is the number of students who chose soccer, a count out of 50 rather than a percentage. Percent means out of 100: doubling both numbers turns 35 out of 50 into 70 out of 100.
y.B: 75% would be 37.5 students out of 50, and 35 chose soccer.
y.D: 65% would be 32.5 out of 50.

qr.q: Which of these numbers is NOT divisible by 6?
qr.e: A number divisible by 6 must be even and have a digit sum divisible by 3; 358 is even but 3+5+8=16 is not a multiple of 3, while 132, 246, and 414 pass both tests.

y.A: 414 is even and 4 + 1 + 4 = 9 is a multiple of 3, so 6 does go in: 6 × 69 = 414. The one it misses is 358 — 3 + 5 + 8 = 16, which 3 does not divide.
y.B: 246 is even and 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 is a multiple of 3, so 6 goes in exactly: 6 × 41 = 246. The one it misses is 358 — 3 + 5 + 8 = 16, which 3 does not divide.
y.C: 132 is even and 1 + 3 + 2 = 6 is a multiple of 3, so 6 divides it: 6 × 22 = 132. The one that fails is 358, because 3 + 5 + 8 = 16 is not a multiple of 3.

qr.q: A list of numbers is 3, 7, 3, 9, and 5. What is the mode of the list?
qr.e: The mode is the value that appears most often, and 3 appears twice while each of the others appears once.

y.A: 9 is the largest number in the list, not the one that turns up most often. The mode counts repeats: 3 appears twice and every other number once.
y.B: 7 appears once, while 3 appears twice.
y.C: 5 also appears just once.

qr.q: What is the median of 4, 9, 11, 15, 6, and 20?
qr.e: In order the values are 4, 6, 9, 11, 15, 20; with six values the median is the mean of the middle two, (9+11)÷2=10.

y.A: 11 is the fourth value once they are in order. With six values the median sits between the third and fourth, 9 and 11.
y.B: 9 is the third value in order. Six values have no single middle, so take 9 and 11 and halve: 10.
y.D: 13 is 4 + 9, two of the values added. In order they run 4, 6, 9, 11, 15, 20, and the middle two make 10.

qr.q: A number pattern counts by 3s: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... . What is the 6th number in the pattern?
qr.e: Counting on by 3s gives 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, so the 6th number in the pattern is 18.

y.A: 24 is the 8th number, two steps too far. The 6th is 18.
y.C: 21 is the 7th number, one step too far. The 6th is 18.
y.D: 15 is the 5th number, one step short. The 6th is 18.

qr.q: How many cubes with edges of 2 cm fit exactly inside a box that is 8 cm by 6 cm by 4 cm?
qr.e: Along the edges the cubes fit 4 by 3 by 2, so 4×3×2=24 cubes fill the box.

y.B: 12 is 6 × 2. Count cubes along every edge: 4, 3 and 2, so 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.
y.C: 96 is 24 × 4, four times as many as fit.
y.D: 48 is 8 × 6, two sides in centimeters. The cubes are 2 cm, so the edges hold 4, 3 and 2 of them.

qr.q: Which of these numbers is a factor of 15?
qr.e: 15 = 3 × 5, so 5 divides 15 with nothing left over, while 2, 4, and 6 do not.

y.A: 4 lands either side of 15 rather than on it: 4 × 3 = 12 and 4 × 4 = 16. The factors of 15 are 1, 3, 5 and 15.
y.B: 6 is 1 + 5, the digits of 15 added, which does not make a factor. 6 × 2 = 12 and 6 × 3 = 18, and 15 is neither.
y.D: 2 divides even numbers, and 15 is odd, so 15 ÷ 2 leaves half a piece over. 15 = 3 × 5, so 5 is the factor here.

qr.q: Two angles are complementary, and one of them is twice as large as the other. What is the measure of the larger angle?
qr.e: Complementary angles total 90°, so x+2x=90 gives x=30° and the larger angle is 2×30=60°.

y.B: 120 is the larger angle if the two add to 180° instead of 90°. Complementary means they make a right angle: 30 + 60 = 90.
y.C: 30 is the smaller of the two angles. The larger is twice it: 2 × 30 = 60°.
y.D: 45 is 90 ÷ 2, the right angle split evenly. Here one angle is twice the other, so 90° splits into 30° and 60°.

qr.q: Which is greater, 3 × 3 × 3 or 5 × 5, and by how much?

y.A: They are close but not equal: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 and 5 × 5 = 25, which leaves 2 between them.
y.C: 3 × 3 × 3, by 3 counts 25, 26, 27 and calls that three steps, but the number you start from is not a step. 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 and 5 × 5 = 25, so the three 3s are ahead by 27 − 25 = 2.
y.D: 5 × 5 comes to 25 while three 3s make 27, so the 2 goes the other way — the 3s are ahead.

qr.q: A jar holds 15 buttons: 6 are blue, 4 are white, and 5 are black. One button is taken out without looking. What is the probability that it is black?
qr.e: There are 15 buttons in all and 5 of them are black, so the probability is 5/15, which is the same as 1/3.

y.A: 4/15 counts the white buttons instead of the black ones. Five of the 15 are black, and 5/15 is the same as 1/3.
y.B: 1/5 is 5/15 tidied up with two different numbers — 5 ÷ 5 on the top but 15 ÷ 3 underneath. Divide both by 5 and 5/15 becomes 1/3.
y.D: 2/5 is 6/15, the chance of a blue button. Black has 5 of the 15, which is 1/3.

qr.q: Five boxes each hold the same number of books. When 3 more books are added to the collection, there are 43 books in all. How many books are in each box?
qr.e: If each box holds b books, then 5b+3=43, so 5b=40 and b=8.

y.A: 9 is what 43 ÷ 5 rounds to with the 3 extra books still in the pile. They were added afterwards, so take them off first: 43 − 3 = 40, and 40 ÷ 5 = 8.
y.B: 10 is 50 ÷ 5, the answer if there were 50 books in all. There are 43, and the 3 added ones come off first: 40 ÷ 5 = 8.
y.D: 7 is one short — five boxes of 7 plus the 3 extra make 38, not 43. One more book in each box gets there: 5 × 8 + 3 = 43.

qr.q: The length of a rectangle is 3 times its width. If the perimeter is 48 cm, what is the width?
qr.e: With width w the length is 3w, so the perimeter is 2(3w+w)=8w=48, giving w=6 cm (and length 18 cm).

y.A: 8 is 48 ÷ 6. The perimeter here is eight widths, so the width is 48 ÷ 8 = 6.
y.C: 12 is 6 × 2, two widths. The width itself is 6.
y.D: 18 is 3 × 6, the length, not the width.

qr.q: Notebooks cost $2.95 each. Maya has $20 and no coupon. What is the greatest number of notebooks she can buy?
qr.e: Rounding $2.95 up to $3 gives about 6 notebooks; checking, 6 cost $17.70 and 7 would cost $20.65, which is more than $20.

y.A: 8 is 20 ÷ 2.50, as if a notebook cost $2.50. At $2.95 each, 8 would cost $23.60, well past her $20.
y.B: 7 is what 20 ÷ 2.95 rounds up to, but she cannot buy part of a notebook and 7 whole ones cost $20.65. Six cost $17.70, which she can afford.
y.D: 5 is 20 ÷ 4, as if a notebook cost $4. They are $2.95, so a sixth one still fits: 6 × $2.95 = $17.70.

qr.q: A rectangular pool measures 10 m by 6 m. A walkway 2 m wide is built all the way around it. What is the area of the walkway alone?
qr.e: The pool plus walkway measures 14 m by 10 m, or 140 square meters, and the pool covers 60, so the walkway is 140−60=80 square meters.

y.C: 60 is 10 × 6, the area of the pool itself. The walkway is the ring around it: the pool and walkway together are 14 m by 10 m, so 140 − 60 = 80 square meters.
y.B: 140 is the whole area including the pool, and the pool's 60 comes off.
y.D: 32 is not 140 − 60, which comes to 80.

qr.q: What is the smallest number greater than 100 that is a multiple of both 4 and 15?
qr.e: A number both 4 and 15 divide is a multiple of 4 × 15 = 60, because 4 and 15 share no factor bigger than 1. The multiples of 60 are 60, 120, 180, and the first one past 100 is 120. With two conditions, list the common multiples first and then check which one clears the extra condition.

y.B: 60 is 4 × 15, the smallest number both 4 and 15 divide — but the question wants one greater than 100. The next common multiple is 60 × 2 = 120.
y.C: 105 is 15 × 7, the first multiple of 15 past 100, but 4 does not divide it. The number has to be a multiple of both, and that is 120.
y.D: 104 is 4 × 26, the first multiple of 4 past 100, but 15 does not divide it. The first number past 100 that both divide is 120.

qr.q: A list of four numbers is 18, 25, 31 and 22. One more number is added and the range does not change. Which of these numbers could the new one be?
qr.e: The range is 31 − 18 = 13, and it only changes if the new number falls outside 18 and 31. Of these four, only 27 lands between them, so both ends stay where they are and the range is still 13. When a value joins a list, ask one question only: does it beat either end?

y.A: 10 is below 18, the lowest number already in the list, so it would become the new lowest and stretch the range to 31 − 10 = 21. Only a number between the two ends leaves the range alone.
y.C: 33 is above 31, the highest number already in the list, so the top end moves and the range grows to 33 − 18 = 15. Only a number from 18 up to 31 keeps the range unchanged.
y.D: 13 is the range itself, not one of the numbers. It is below 18, so adding it would stretch the range to 31 − 13 = 18. A number between the two ends, such as 27, leaves it alone.

qr.q: A photograph is 4 inches wide and 6 inches tall. It is enlarged to 12 inches wide, keeping the same shape. How tall is the enlarged photograph?
qr.e: The width goes from 4 inches to 12 inches, which is 12 ÷ 4 = 3 times as wide, so the height is 6 × 3 = 18 inches. Find the number the sides are multiplied by first, then use it on the side you want.

y.A: 14 is 6 + 8, the same 8 inches added to the height as were added to the width. An enlargement multiplies instead: the width grew 12 ÷ 4 = 3 times, so the height is 6 × 3 = 18 inches.
y.C: 24 is 6 × 4, the height multiplied by the old width. The number to multiply by is 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so the height becomes 6 × 3 = 18 inches.
y.D: 9 is 6 + 3, the 3 added to the height instead of multiplied by it. Three times as wide means three times as tall: 6 × 3 = 18 inches.

qr.q: A door mat is a rectangle 90 cm long and 60 cm wide. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
qr.e: A rectangle whose sides are not all equal matches along the fold down its middle and the fold across its middle, so it has 2 lines of symmetry. The diagonals only work when all four sides are the same length, which is what makes a square's answer 4 and a rectangle's 2.

y.B: 4 is the number a square has, counting both diagonals as folds. Fold this mat along a diagonal and a long side lands on a short one, so only 2 folds match.
y.C: 1 counts the fold down the middle and stops there. The mat also folds across the middle the other way, so there are 2 lines.
y.D: 0 would mean no fold matches. Folding the mat end to end brings the two halves exactly together, so it has 2 lines.

qr.q: A box holds exactly 36 one-centimetre cubes. A second box is twice as long, twice as wide and twice as tall. How many of the same cubes does it hold?
qr.e: Doubling the length, the width and the height each multiplies the number of cubes by 2, so the second box holds 36 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 288 cubes. A box grows in three directions at once, so one doubling counts three times over.

y.A: 72 is 36 × 2, one doubling counted and the other two forgotten. All three measurements double, so the box holds 36 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 288 cubes.
y.C: 144 is 36 × 4, two of the three doublings counted. The third one counts as well: 36 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 288 cubes.
y.D: 108 is 36 × 3, the three doublings turned into a single multiplication by 3. Each doubling multiplies on its own: 36 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 288 cubes.

qr.q: A bus route ran 6 trips on Monday carrying an average of 24 riders on each trip, and 4 trips on Tuesday carrying an average of 34 riders on each trip. What was the average number of riders per trip over the two days?
qr.e: Monday's 6 trips carried 6 × 24 = 144 riders and Tuesday's 4 trips carried 4 × 34 = 136, which is 280 riders across 10 trips, so 280 ÷ 10 = 28 riders per trip. Two averages cannot simply be averaged when the groups are different sizes — turn each one back into a total, add the totals, and divide once at the end.

y.B: 29 riders is 58 ÷ 2, the two averages averaged as though each day had the same number of trips. Monday carried 6 × 24 = 144 riders and Tuesday 4 × 34 = 136, so 280 ÷ 10 = 28.
y.C: 58 riders is 24 + 34, the two averages added instead of the riders counted. Each day's riders come first: 144 + 136 = 280, and 280 ÷ 10 = 28.
y.D: 280 riders is everyone who rode over the two days, before they are shared among the trips. There were 10 trips in all: 280 ÷ 10 = 28.

qr.q: A hall is set out with 2⁴ rows of chairs and 5² chairs in each row. How many chairs are there altogether?
qr.e: 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 rows and 5² = 5 × 5 = 25 chairs in each row, so the hall holds 16 × 25 = 400 chairs. Turn each power into an ordinary number first, and what is left is a plain multiplication.

y.B: 200 is 8 × 25, with the rows worked out as 2 × 4 instead of four twos multiplied. 2⁴ = 16, so 16 × 25 = 400.
y.C: 160 is 16 × 10, with the chairs in a row worked out as 5 × 2. Squaring gives 5 × 5 = 25, so 16 × 25 = 400.
y.D: 41 is 16 + 25, the rows added to the chairs in a row instead of multiplied. Every row holds 25 chairs: 16 × 25 = 400.

qr.q: A tray holds 14 tomatoes. A market stall has t full trays and 5 loose tomatoes. Which expression gives the total number of tomatoes?
qr.e: Each tray brings 14 tomatoes, so t trays bring 14t, and the 5 loose ones are added once: 14t+5. Ask which part repeats and which part happens only once — the repeating part is the one that gets the letter.

y.A: 14+5t is one tray plus five tomatoes for every tray, the two numbers swapped round. It is the trays that repeat: 14t+5.
y.B: 14t-5 takes the five loose tomatoes away instead of adding them on. They are extra tomatoes: 14t+5.
y.C: 19t is 14 + 5 multiplied by every tray, which puts five loose tomatoes into each one. There are only five altogether: 14t+5.

qr.q: A garden path is made from 6 stone slabs laid end to end, each 80 centimeters long. How long is the path in meters?
qr.e: The six slabs come to 6 × 80 = 480 centimeters, and 480 ÷ 100 = 4.8 meters. Two-step measuring is safest done in the small unit all the way through and changed to the big unit at the very end — and a quick check helps: six slabs a little under a meter each should come out near five meters.

y.A: 480 meters is the path measured in centimeters with the word meters put after it. 480 centimeters is 480 ÷ 100 = 4.8 meters.
y.B: 48 meters is 6 × 8, the zero dropped from the 80. Six slabs of 80 come to 480 centimeters, which is 4.8 meters.
y.D: 0.48 meters is 480 ÷ 1,000, shorter than a single slab. There are 100 centimeters in a meter: 480 ÷ 100 = 4.8 meters.

qr.q: A garden show charges $3 for an adult and $2 for a child. A group of 4 adults and 7 children go in together. What does the group pay altogether?
qr.e: The adults pay 4 × 3 = 12 dollars and the children pay 7 × 2 = 14 dollars, so the group pays 12 + 14 = 26 dollars. Price each group on its own first — a single multiplication can never cover two different prices.

y.A: 22 is 11 × 2, all eleven visitors charged the child's price. The adults pay 4 × 3 = 12 and the children pay 7 × 2 = 14, so the total is 12 + 14 = 26.
y.C: 33 is 11 × 3, everyone charged the adult's price. Only the 4 adults pay 3 each: 4 × 3 = 12, and 7 × 2 = 14 for the children, giving 12 + 14 = 26.
y.D: 29 is 4 × 2 + 7 × 3, the two prices swapped round. Adults pay the larger one, so it is 4 × 3 = 12 and 7 × 2 = 14, and 12 + 14 = 26.

qr.q: A garden flag is made three times as long and three times as wide. How much cloth does the new flag need?
qr.e: Tripling the length multiplies the cloth by 3 and tripling the width multiplies it by 3 again, so the new flag needs 3 × 3 = 9 times as much. Count how many measurements changed, then multiply the changes together.

y.A: 3 times as much counts only one of the two triplings. The length is tripled and so is the width, so the cloth grows 3 × 3 = 9 times.
y.C: 6 times as much comes from adding the two triplings as 3 + 3 = 6. They multiply instead: 3 × 3 = 9 times as much cloth.
y.D: 27 times as much is 3 × 3 × 3, a tripling counted three times over. A flat piece of cloth has only a length and a width: 3 × 3 = 9.

qr.q: A sign painter cuts capital letters from card and folds each one to test it. Which letter matches both when it is folded down the middle and when it is folded straight across?
qr.e: The letter H matches when it is folded down the middle and again when it is folded straight across, so it has both lines of symmetry. Test the two folds one at a time and keep only the letter that survives both.

y.A: The letter T matches when it is folded down the middle, but folded straight across the crossbar at the top has nothing to meet at the bottom. The letter H matches both ways.
y.B: The letter E matches when it is folded across, the top arm landing on the bottom arm, but its upright spine sits on the left only, so the fold down the middle fails. The letter H matches both ways.
y.D: The letter M matches when it is folded down the middle, but folded straight across the points along the bottom have nothing to meet above them. Only the letter H matches both ways.

ma.e: Add by place value to get 4,150.

y.A: 3,150 is the sum with the carried thousand left behind. The 400 and the 750 make 1,150, so that thousand joins the others: 2,400 + 1,750 = 4,150.
y.B: 4,050 is a hundred short. The 400 and the 750 make 1,150, and it is easy to carry the thousand and leave the extra hundred behind: put it back and 2,400 + 1,750 = 4,150.
y.D: 4,250 is a hundred too many, one carry counted twice. The 400 and the 750 make 1,150, so 2,400 + 1,750 = 4,150.

ma.q: What is 315 ÷ 7?

y.C: 47 keeps the 7 you were dividing by in the ones place. Seven fives make 35, so the last digit is a 5: 315 ÷ 7 = 45.
y.A: 39 is too small: 7 × 39 = 273, which is 42 short of 315.
y.D: 51 overshoots: 7 × 51 = 357.

ma.q: Of 36 theater seats, two thirds are filled. How many seats are filled?

y.C: 18 is 36 ÷ 2, half the seats rather than two thirds of them. Split the 36 into three first: 36 ÷ 3 = 12, then 12 × 2 = 24.
y.A: 20 is not two thirds of 36; a third of 36 is 12, so two thirds is 24.
y.B: 27 comes from taking 3/4 of 36 rather than 2/3.

ma.q: Three quarters of a gallon fills how many one-eighth-gallon jars?
ma.e: 3/4 = 6/8, so there are six eighths.

y.A: 4 is the 4 from "three quarters" — the number of parts a gallon splits into, not a number of jars. Three quarters is the same as 6/8, so it fills 6 jars.
y.C: 8 is how many eighth-gallon jars a whole gallon fills. Only three quarters of a gallon is being poured, and 3/4 is 6/8, so it fills 6 jars.
y.D: 3 is the 3 from "three quarters", the number of quarter-gallons. Each quarter fills two of the eighth-gallon jars, so 3 × 2 = 6 jars.

ma.q: What is 6.4 × 0.5?
ma.e: Multiplying by 0.5 means taking half.

y.A: 12.8 is 6.4 ÷ 0.5, the 6.4 divided by the half rather than multiplied by it. Multiplying by 0.5 takes half, and half of the 6.4 comes to 3.2.
y.B: 0.32 is a tenth of the answer; half of 6.4 is 3.2.
y.D: 32 is ten times too big — multiplying by 0.5 makes a number smaller, not larger.

ma.q: An $8.75 fare is reduced by a $3.90 coupon. What is the new fare?

y.A: 4.75 is 8.75 − 4, the coupon rounded up to a whole $4. That takes off 10 cents too much, so add them back: 4.75 + 0.10 = 4.85.
y.B: 5.15 takes the cents the other way round, 90 − 75 = 15, because 75 looked too small to take 90 from. Borrow a whole dollar from the 8 instead: 8.75 − 3.90 = 4.85.
y.C: 5.85 keeps all 8 dollars after a dollar has been borrowed from them. After the borrow there are 7 dollars: 7 − 3 = 4, so the fare is $4.85.

ma.q: Thirty percent of 90 campers choose chess. How many campers choose chess?

y.A: 9 is 90 ÷ 10, one tenth of the campers with the other two tenths never added on. Thirty percent means three tenths: 9 × 3 = 27.
y.B: 63 is 90 − 27, the campers who did not choose chess rather than the ones who did. Three tenths chose it: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, then 9 × 3 = 27.
y.D: 60 is 90 − 30, the thirty taken off the ninety rather than used as a percentage. Thirty percent means three tenths: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, then 9 × 3 = 27.

ma.q: What is 40% of 70?

y.B: 30 is 70 − 40, the forty taken off the seventy rather than used as a percentage. Forty percent means four tenths: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, then 7 × 4 = 28.
y.C: 42 is 70 − 28, the part left behind rather than the part asked for. Forty percent means four tenths: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, then 7 × 4 = 28.
y.D: 7 is 70 ÷ 10, one tenth found and the other three tenths never added on. Four tenths means 7 × 4 = 28.

ma.q: What is 7 + 3 × 9?
ma.e: Multiply first, then add, to get 34.

y.A: 37 is 34 + 3, with the 3 counted once on its own and again in the 3 × 9. The 3 is only there to multiply: 3 × 9 = 27, then 27 + 7 = 34.
y.C: 90 is 10 × 9, from adding the 7 and the 3 first. Multiplying comes first: 3 × 9 = 27, then 27 + 7 = 34.
y.D: 25 is 34 − 9, one nine short — only two of the three nines added on. There are three: 3 × 9 = 27, then 27 + 7 = 34.

ma.q: What is 5/6 - 1/3?
ma.e: 1/3 = 2/6; the difference is 3/6 = 1/2.

y.B: 2/3 is 4/6, from taking 5 − 1 on the tops while the bottoms were still different. Make them match first: 1/3 is 2/6, so 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2.
y.C: 1/3 is what is left when 1/3 is changed to 3/6 instead of 2/6 — the 3 is the bottom you are changing, not the new top. Two sixths make a third, so 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2.
y.D: 4/3 comes from working the tops and the bottoms separately, 5 − 1 = 4 and 6 − 3 = 3. Only the tops get subtracted, once the bottoms match: 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, or 1/2.

ma.e: Add by place value to get 6,350.

y.B: 6,450 puts a 4 in the hundreds, but that column is 7 + 5 + 1 = 13, so a 3 goes there and the total is 6,350.
y.C: 6,250 leaves out the hundred carried over from the tens, where 7 + 8 = 15, so the hundreds come to 12 instead of 13. With the carry, 3,770 + 2,580 = 6,350.
y.D: 6,360 puts a 6 in the tens, but 7 + 8 = 15, so a 5 goes in the tens and a hundred carries over: 3,770 + 2,580 = 6,350.

ma.q: What is 750 ÷ 10?

y.A: 7.5 is 750 ÷ 100, the point moved two places instead of one. Dividing by 10 moves each digit one place to the right: 10 × 75 = 750, so 750 ÷ 10 = 75.
y.B: 70 is 700 ÷ 10, with the 50 of the 750 never shared out. Those 50 make five more tens, because 50 ÷ 10 = 5, so 750 ÷ 10 = 75.
y.C: 740 is 750 − 10, the 10 taken away rather than shared out. Sharing 750 into 10 equal parts gives 750 ÷ 10 = 75.

ma.q: What is 3/8 + 1/4?
ma.e: 1/4 = 2/8, so the sum is 5/8.

y.A: 4/12 comes from adding the tops and the bottoms, 3 + 1 = 4 and 8 + 4 = 12. The bottoms are made to match instead: 1/4 is 2/8, so 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8.
y.B: 1/2 is 4/8, from adding 3 + 1 on the tops and keeping the 8 underneath. Once 1/4 becomes 2/8 it is 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8.
y.C: 7/8 is 3/8 + 4/8, with the 4 from 1/4 copied up as the new top. Two eighths make a quarter, so 1/4 is 2/8: 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8.

ma.q: An 8.75 m ribbon loses 3.9 m of trim. What length remains?

y.B: 4.75 is 8.75 − 4, the trim rounded up to a whole 4 m. That takes off 10 cm too much, so add them back: 4.75 + 0.10 = 4.85.
y.C: 5.15 takes the hundredths the other way round, 90 − 75 = 15, because 75 looked too small to take 90 from. Borrow from the 8 instead: 8.75 − 3.90 = 4.85.
y.D: 5.85 keeps all 8 whole meters after one of them has been borrowed. After the borrow there are 7: 7 − 3 = 4, so 4.85 m remains.

ma.q: Thirty percent of 90 badges are blue. How many badges are blue?

y.A: 63 is 90 − 27, the badges that are not blue rather than the blue ones. Three tenths are blue: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, then 9 × 3 = 27.
y.C: 9 is 90 ÷ 10, one tenth of the badges with the other two tenths never added on. Thirty percent means three tenths: 9 × 3 = 27.
y.D: 60 is 90 − 30, the thirty taken off the ninety rather than used as a percentage. Thirty percent means three tenths: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, then 9 × 3 = 27.

ma.e: Add by place value to get 7,450.

y.A: 7,350 leaves out the hundred carried over from the tens, where 5 + 9 + 1 = 15, so the hundreds come to 13 instead of 14. With the carry, 4,455 + 2,995 = 7,450.
y.C: 7,460 rounds 2,995 up to 3,000 and then adds the extra five on instead of taking it back off. 4,455 + 3,000 = 7,455, and 7,455 − 5 = 7,450.
y.D: 7,550 puts a 5 in the hundreds, but that column is 4 + 9 + 1 = 14, so a 4 goes there and the total is 7,450.

ma.q: What is 720 ÷ 8?

y.A: 9 is 72 ÷ 8, the 720 read as 72 and its zero left out of the answer. Put the zero back: 8 × 90 = 720, so 720 ÷ 8 = 90.
y.B: 72 is 720 with a zero crossed off, which shares it into 10 rather than into 8 — that shortcut only works when the dividing is by 10. Eight nines make 72, so eight nineties make 720: 720 ÷ 8 = 90.
y.C: 80 is 720 ÷ 9, the fact remembered the wrong way round — 72 ÷ 9 = 8 in place of 72 ÷ 8 = 9. Here the 8 is the one doing the sharing: 8 × 90 = 720, so 720 ÷ 8 = 90.

ma.q: What is 6 + 4 × 8?
ma.e: Multiply first, then add, to get 38.

y.A: 80 is 10 × 8, from adding the 6 and the 4 first. Multiplying comes first: 4 × 8 = 32, then 32 + 6 = 38.
y.B: 42 is 38 + 4, with the 4 counted once on its own and again in the 4 × 8. The 4 is only there to multiply: 4 × 8 = 32, then 32 + 6 = 38.
y.D: 30 is 38 − 8, one eight short — only three of the four eights added on. There are four: 4 × 8 = 32, then 32 + 6 = 38.

ma.q: A 36-card deck has two thirds picture cards. How many picture cards are there?

y.D: 18 is 36 ÷ 2, half the deck rather than two thirds of it. Split the 36 into three first: 36 ÷ 3 = 12, then 12 × 2 = 24.
y.A: 20 is not two thirds of 36; a third of 36 is 12, so two thirds is 24.
y.B: 27 comes from taking 3/4 of 36 rather than 2/3.

ma.q: What is 7.2 ÷ 0.6?
ma.e: Multiply both numbers by 10: 72 ÷ 6 = 12.

y.B: 1.2 is 7.2 ÷ 6, dividing by 6 instead of by 0.6. Make both numbers ten times bigger first: 72 ÷ 6 = 12.
y.C: 10 would mean 0.6 × 10 = 6, not 7.2.
y.D: 120 is ten times too big; 72 ÷ 6 = 12.

ma.q: What is 20% of 80?

y.D: 60 is 80 − 20, the twenty taken off the eighty rather than used as a percentage. Twenty percent means two tenths: 80 ÷ 10 = 8, then 8 × 2 = 16.
y.A: 12 is 15% of 80; 20% is a fifth, which is 16.
y.C: 21 is over a quarter of 80, and a fifth is 16.

ma.q: What is 630 ÷ 6?

y.A: 15 is 105 with the 0 in the middle left out. Six will not go into the 3, and that step puts a 0 in the answer rather than nothing at all: 6 × 105 = 630.
y.B: 100 is 600 ÷ 6, with the 30 of the 630 never shared out. The 30 gives another 5, because 6 × 5 = 30, so 630 ÷ 6 = 105.
y.C: 315 is 630 ÷ 2, halved and then not shared any further. Dividing by 6 is halving and then sharing into 3: 315 ÷ 3 = 105.

ma.e: Add by place value to get 8,990.

y.A: 9,000 is 5,400 + 3,600, both numbers rounded to the nearest hundred. Added exactly, 5,414 + 3,576 = 8,990.
y.D: 8,890 puts an 8 in the hundreds, but that column is 4 + 5 = 9, so the total is 8,990.
y.B: 9,090 carries a thousand that is not there; the hundreds make 4 + 5 = 9 with no carry, so the thousands are 5 + 3 = 8.

ma.q: Three quarters of a yard makes how many one-eighth-yard strips?
ma.e: 3/4 = 6/8, so there are six eighths.

y.B: 3 is the 3 from "three quarters", the number of quarter-yards. Each quarter makes two eighth-yard strips, so 3 × 2 = 6.
y.C: 4 is the 4 from "three quarters" — the number of parts a yard splits into, not a number of strips. Three quarters is the same as 6/8, so it makes 6 strips.
y.D: 8 is how many eighth-yard strips a whole yard makes. Only three quarters of a yard is used, and 3/4 is 6/8, so it makes 6 strips.

ma.q: A garden is 6 m by 3 m. What fencing length goes around it?
ma.e: Perimeter = 2(6+3) = 18 m.

y.A: 9 is 6 + 3 — one long side and one short one. The fence goes round all four.
y.B: 12 is 6 + 6, the two long sides, with the short ones missing.
y.D: 15 is 6 + 6 + 3 — one short side left out.

ma.q: A triangular flag has base 10 cm and height 6 cm. What is its area?

y.B: 60 is 10 × 6, the base times the height — the whole rectangle around the triangle. The triangle fills half of it: 60 ÷ 2 = 30.
y.D: 16 is 10 + 6, the base and the height added rather than multiplied. Multiply them and take half: 10 × 6 = 60, then 60 ÷ 2 = 30.
y.C: 38 is not half of 10 × 6; 10 × 6 = 60, and half of that is 30.

ma.q: A roof triangle has angles 45° and 60°. What is its third angle?
ma.e: Triangle angles total 180°: the third angle is 75°.

y.B: 120 is 180 − 60, with the 45° angle never taken off. Both known angles come off the 180: 180 − 45 − 60 = 75.
y.C: 105 is 45 + 60, the two known angles added together instead of taken away from 180. The three angles make 180, so 180 − 105 = 75.
y.D: 135 is 180 − 45, with the 60° angle never taken off. Both known angles come off the 180: 180 − 45 − 60 = 75.

ma.q: A square patio has side length 10 units. What is its area?

y.A: 110 is 100 + 10 — the area with one more side added on the end. The area is just 10 × 10.
y.B: 40 is 10 × 4, the perimeter: the distance all the way round the patio, not the space inside it.
y.C: 20 is 10 × 2, two sides. Area covers the whole patio, so it is 10 × 10.

ma.q: A banner is 10 cm by 3 cm. What is its perimeter?
ma.e: Perimeter = 2(10+3) = 26 cm.

y.A: 13 is 10 + 3, only two of the four sides.
y.B: 30 is 10 × 3, the area. Area is the space inside the banner; perimeter is the distance round its edge.
y.D: 23 is 10 + 10 + 3 — one short side left out.

ma.q: A triangular flag has base 10 cm and height 8 cm. What is its area?

y.A: 80 is 10 × 8, the whole rectangle the triangle sits in. A triangle fills half of it, so halve it: 40.
y.B: 18 is 10 + 8. Area multiplies the base and the height, it never adds them.
y.D: 48 is 40 + 8, the area with the height added on again. Once you have half of 10 × 8 you are done.

ma.q: A sail triangle has angles 65° and 55°. What is its third angle?
ma.e: Triangle angles total 180°: the third angle is 60°.

y.A: 115 is 180 − 65, with the 55° angle never taken off. Both known angles come off the 180: 180 − 65 − 55 = 60.
y.C: 120 is 65 + 55, the two known angles added together instead of taken away from 180. The three angles make 180, so 180 − 120 = 60.
y.D: 125 is 180 − 55, with the 65° angle never taken off. Both known angles come off the 180: 180 − 65 − 55 = 60.

ma.q: A square mosaic has side length 7 units. What is its area?
ma.e: Area = 7² = 49.

y.A: 28 is 7 × 4, the perimeter — the distance round all four sides, not the space inside.
y.C: 14 is 7 × 2, two sides. Area covers the whole square: 7 × 7.
y.D: 56 is 49 + 7, the area with one more side added on. 7 × 7 = 49 is all of it.

ma.q: A pen is 8 cm by 3 cm. What is its perimeter?
ma.e: Perimeter = 2(8+3) = 22 cm.

y.B: 19 is 8 + 8 + 3 — one short side is missing.
y.C: 24 is 8 × 3, the area. That is the ground the pen covers, not the fence around it.
y.D: 11 is 8 + 3, one long side and one short one.

ma.q: A triangular sign has base 10 cm and height 4 cm. What is its area?

y.A: 14 is 10 + 4, the base and the height added rather than multiplied. Multiply them and take half: 10 × 4 = 40, then 40 ÷ 2 = 20.
y.B: 40 is 10 × 4, the base times the height — the whole rectangle around the triangle. The triangle fills half of it: 40 ÷ 2 = 20.
y.C: 28 doubles 10 + 4, which is a perimeter-style total; the area is 1/2 × 10 × 4 = 20.

ma.q: A roof triangle has angles 45° and 75°. What is its third angle?
ma.e: Triangle angles total 180°: the third angle is 60°.

y.A: 105 is 180 − 75, with the 45° angle never taken off. Both known angles come off the 180: 180 − 45 − 75 = 60.
y.C: 135 is 180 − 45, with the 75° angle never taken off. Both known angles come off the 180: 180 − 45 − 75 = 60.
y.D: 120 is 45 + 75, the two known angles added together instead of taken away from 180. The three angles make 180, so 180 − 120 = 60.

ma.q: A square game board has side length 4 units. What is its area?
ma.e: Area = 4² = 16.

y.A: 20 is 16 + 4, the area with a side added on the end. The area is just 4 × 4.
y.B: 12 is 16 − 4. Nothing is taken off an area: 4 × 4 = 16.
y.C: 8 is 4 × 2, two sides. A square has four, and its area is 4 × 4.

ma.q: A $100 item is 75% off. What is its sale price?

y.A: 75 is three quarters of the $100, which is the money that comes off — not the price paid. The sale price is what is left: 100 − 75 = 25.
y.B: 175 is 100 + 75, the discount added on instead of taken off. A sale makes the price smaller: 100 − 75 = 25.
y.C: 12.50 is 100 ÷ 8, one halving too many — 100 halves to 50, then to 25, then to 12.50. A quarter of the price is left, not an eighth: 100 − 75 = 25.

ma.q: What is 5.5÷0.1?
ma.e: Dividing by 0.1 makes the number ten times as large: 55.

y.A: 0.55 is 5.5 × 0.1, the tenth multiplied in rather than divided into. Dividing asks how many tenths are in 5.5, and there are 55 of them.
y.B: 5.5 is 5.5 ÷ 1, the 0.1 read as a whole 1. A tenth goes in ten times as often as a 1 does: 5.5 ÷ 0.1 = 55.
y.D: 550 is 5.5 ÷ 0.01, the point moved two places instead of one. Dividing by 0.1 makes a number ten times bigger, not a hundred times: 5.5 ÷ 0.1 = 55.

ma.q: Solve 3x+5=83.
ma.e: Subtract 5, then divide by 3: x=26.

y.B: 27 is what 83 ÷ 3 comes to with the remainder dropped — the sharing done before the 5 came off, since 3 × 27 = 81 leaves 2 over. The 5 comes off first: 83 − 5 = 78, then 78 ÷ 3 = 26.
y.C: 78 is 83 − 5, the first step on its own — that is 3x, not x. Share it out: 78 ÷ 3 = 26.
y.D: 75 is 78 − 3, the 3 taken away as well as the 5. The 3 is multiplying x, and dividing is what undoes that: 78 ÷ 3 = 26.

ma.q: Four tenths of 70 teams earn a badge. How many teams earn a badge?
ma.e: Four tenths of 70 is 28.

y.A: 7 is 70 ÷ 10, one tenth of the teams with the other three tenths never added on. Four tenths means 7 × 4 = 28.
y.B: 56 is four fifths of 70, from halving the bottom of 4/10 and leaving the top alone. Four tenths means 70 ÷ 10 = 7, then 7 × 4 = 28.
y.D: 66 is 70 − 4, the four taken off the seventy rather than used as four tenths of it. A tenth of 70 is 7, so four tenths is 7 × 4 = 28.

ma.q: A square stage has side length 9 units. What is its area?
ma.e: Area=9²=81.

y.B: 18 is 9 × 2, two sides. Area is 9 × 9.
y.C: 36 is 9 × 4, the perimeter — round the edge, not the space inside.
y.D: 90 is 81 + 9, the area with one more side added on. 9 × 9 = 81 is all of it.

ma.q: What is 160÷2?
ma.e: Half of 160 is 80.

y.B: 8 is 16 ÷ 2, with the zero of the 160 left off the answer. Sixteen tens shared between 2 is eight tens: 160 ÷ 2 = 80.
y.C: 320 is 160 × 2, the 160 doubled rather than halved. Dividing by 2 makes it smaller: 160 ÷ 2 = 80.
y.D: 40 is 160 ÷ 4, one halving too many — 160 halves to 80, and 80 halves again to 40. Only one halving was asked for: 160 ÷ 2 = 80.

ma.q: What is 25% of 88?
ma.e: One fourth of 88 is 22.

y.A: 11 is 88 ÷ 8, one eighth of the 88 rather than one quarter — one halving too many. A quarter is two halvings: 88 ÷ 2 = 44, then 44 ÷ 2 = 22.
y.B: 44 is 88 ÷ 2, the first halving done and the second one forgotten. A quarter is two halvings: 44 ÷ 2 = 22.
y.D: 63 is 88 − 25, the twenty-five taken off the eighty-eight rather than used as a percentage. A quarter of 88 is 88 ÷ 4 = 22.

ma.q: What is 7×6?

y.A: 49 is 7 × 7, seven sevens counted rather than six. Take one seven off: 49 − 7 = 42.
y.C: 84 is 7 × 12, twelve sevens rather than six — the six doubled. Halve it back: 84 ÷ 2 = 42.
y.D: 13 is 7 + 6, the two numbers added rather than multiplied. Six sevens: 7 × 6 = 42.

ma.q: What is 3/4 of 48?

y.A: 24 is 48 ÷ 2, half of the forty-eight rather than three quarters of it. Quarter it first: 48 ÷ 4 = 12, then 12 × 3 = 36.
y.D: 12 is 48 ÷ 4, one quarter of the forty-eight rather than three quarters of it. Three quarters means three of those quarters: 12 × 3 = 36.
y.C: 42 is not three quarters of 48; a quarter of 48 is 12, so three quarters is 36.

ma.q: What is 5×13?

y.A: 55 is 50 + 5, one five added on to the ten fives instead of three. Ten fives make 50 and three more make 15, so 50 + 15 = 65.
y.C: 75 is 50 + 25 — after 5 × 10 = 50, the next step multiplied by 5 again instead of by 3. Three fives make 15, so 50 + 15 = 65.
y.B: 120 is not 5 × 13, which comes to 65.

ma.q: 2.5 feet equals how many inches?

y.A: 24 is 2 × 12, the half foot never turned into inches. Half a foot is 6 inches, so 24 + 6 = 30.
y.C: 14.5 is 12 + 2.5, the twelve added on rather than multiplied by. Each foot is 12 inches: 2.5 × 12 = 30.
y.D: 25 is 2.5 × 10, counted as if a foot were ten inches. A foot is twelve inches: 2.5 × 12 = 30.

ma.q: What is 7×8?

y.B: 64 is 8 × 8, eight eights rather than seven. Take one eight away: 64 − 8 = 56.
y.A: 112 doubles the product; 7 × 8 is 56.
y.C: 22 is not 7 × 8; adding 7 and 8 gives 15, and multiplying gives 56.

ma.q: A storage box measures 6×2×2. What is its volume?

y.A: 56 is the area of the six outside faces added together — the paper to wrap the box, not the space inside it. The space inside is 6 × 2 × 2 = 24.
y.C: 14 is 6 × 2 + 2, two sides multiplied and the third one added on. All three multiply: 6 × 2 = 12, then 12 × 2 = 24.
y.D: 10 is 6 + 2 + 2, the three sides added instead of multiplied. Volume multiplies them: 6 × 2 × 2 = 24.

ma.q: A poster is 3 feet long. How many inches is that?
ma.e: 3 × 12 = 36 inches.

y.D: 9 is 3 × 3, the three feet tripled rather than turned into inches. A foot is 12 inches, so 3 × 12 = 36.
y.A: 30 is 3 × 10; a foot holds 12 inches, not 10.
y.C: 15 is 3 + 12, adding the feet to the inches instead of multiplying.

ma.q: What is the mean of daily readings 54, 58, and 62?
ma.e: The sum is 174; divide by 3 to get 58.

y.A: 56 is the middle of 54 and 58 on their own, with the 62 left out. All three readings count: 54 + 58 + 62 = 174, and 174 ÷ 3 = 58.
y.B: 60 is the middle of 58 and 62, with the 54 left out. Add all three, then share: 174 ÷ 3 = 58.
y.D: 174 is the three readings added up — the total, not the mean. Share it between the three days: 174 ÷ 3 = 58.

ma.q: What is the median of 53,56,59,62,66?
ma.e: The ordered middle value is 59.

y.B: 13 is 66 − 53, the biggest take away the smallest — the spread of the numbers, not the middle one. With five numbers in order, the middle is the third: 59.
y.C: 62 is the fourth number in order, one step past the middle. With five numbers, the middle is the third one: 59.
y.D: 56 is the second number in order, one step short of the middle. With five numbers, the middle is the third one: 59.

ma.q: Which value is the mode of 56,59,59,61,64?
ma.e: 59 occurs most often.

y.B: 56 is the smallest number in the list, and it appears only once. The mode is the one that turns up most often: 59 is there twice.
y.C: 61 appears just once, the same as 56 and 64. Only 59 is repeated, so 59 is the mode.
y.D: 64 is the biggest number here, not the most common one. 59 is the one written twice.

ma.q: An aquarium measures 6×3×4. What is its volume?

y.A: 22 is 6 × 3 + 4, two sides multiplied and the third one added on. All three multiply: 6 × 3 = 18, then 18 × 4 = 72.
y.C: 13 is 6 + 3 + 4, the three sides added instead of multiplied. Volume multiplies them: 6 × 3 × 4 = 72.
y.D: 108 is the six outside faces added together — the skin of the box, not what fits inside it. Inside is 6 × 3 × 4 = 72.

ma.q: An 8-foot rope is how many inches long?
ma.e: 8 × 12 = 96 inches.

y.A: 80 is 8 × 10, as if a foot held ten inches. A foot holds 12, so 8 × 12 = 96.
y.B: 20 is 8 + 12, the two numbers added instead of multiplied. Each of the 8 feet is 12 inches long: 8 × 12 = 96.
y.C: 24 is 8 × 3, three counted for each foot — but 3 is the feet in a yard. Inches go 12 to a foot: 8 × 12 = 96.

ma.q: What is the mean of readings 59,63,67?
ma.e: The sum is 189; divide by 3 to get 63.

y.A: 61 is the middle of 59 and 63 on their own, with the 67 left out. All three readings go in: 59 + 63 + 67 = 189, and 189 ÷ 3 = 63.
y.B: 189 is the three readings added up — the total, not the mean. Share it between the three: 189 ÷ 3 = 63.
y.D: 65 is the middle of 63 and 67, with the 59 left out. Add all three first: 189 ÷ 3 = 63.

ma.q: What is the median of 58,61,64,67,71?
ma.e: The ordered middle value is 64.

y.A: 13 is 71 − 58, the biggest take away the smallest — the spread of the numbers, not the middle one. In order, the middle of five is the third: 64.
y.B: 67 is the fourth number in order, one step past the middle. With five numbers, the middle is the third one: 64.
y.D: 61 is the second number in order, one step short of the middle. With five numbers, the middle is the third one: 64.

ma.q: Which value is the mode of 61,64,64,66,69?
ma.e: 64 occurs most often.

y.A: 66 appears just once, the same as 61 and 69. The mode is the repeated one, and 64 is there twice.
y.B: 69 is the biggest number in the list, not the most common one. 64 is the one written twice.
y.C: 61 is the smallest number here, and it appears only once. 64 appears twice, so 64 is the mode.

ma.q: A bag holds 4 red and 6 blue marbles. What is P(red)?
ma.e: There are 10 marbles and 4 are red: 4/10.

y.A: 4/6 sets the reds against the blues. A chance is out of every marble in the bag, and there are 10 of them: 4/10.
y.B: 1/10 is the chance of one particular marble out of the ten. Any of the 4 reds would do, so it is 4/10.
y.C: 6/10 is the blue share — 6 blue out of 10 marbles. The reds are the other 4: 4/10.

ma.q: A crate measures 7×5×4. What is its volume?

y.B: 39 is 7 × 5 + 4, multiplying two edges and then adding the third instead of multiplying all three.
y.C: 166 is the surface area, 2 × (35 + 20 + 28) — the paper needed to cover the crate rather than the space inside it.
y.D: 16 is 7 + 5 + 4, the three edges added. Volume multiplies them: 7 × 5 = 35, then 35 × 4 = 140.

ma.q: A block measures 3×2×2. What is its volume?

y.A: 7 is 3 + 2 + 2, the three sides added instead of multiplied. Volume multiplies them: 3 × 2 × 2 = 12.
y.B: 8 is 3 × 2 + 2, two sides multiplied and the third one added on. All three multiply: 3 × 2 = 6, then 6 × 2 = 12.
y.C: 32 is the six outside faces added together — the skin of the block, not the space inside it. Inside is 3 × 2 × 2 = 12.

ma.q: An 8-foot banner is how many inches long?
ma.e: 8 × 12 = 96 inches.

y.A: 24 is 8 × 3, three counted for each foot — but 3 is the feet in a yard. Inches go 12 to a foot: 8 × 12 = 96.
y.C: 80 is 8 × 10, as if a foot held ten inches. It holds 12, so 8 × 12 = 96.
y.D: 20 is 8 + 12, the two numbers added instead of multiplied. Each of the 8 feet is 12 inches long: 8 × 12 = 96.

ma.q: Which value is the mode of 66,69,69,71,74?
ma.e: 69 occurs most often.

y.A: 66 is the smallest number in the list, and it turns up only once. 69 turns up twice, so 69 is the mode.
y.B: 71 appears just once, the same as 66 and 74. Only 69 is repeated.
y.C: 74 is the biggest number here, not the most common one. 69 is the one written twice.

ma.q: What is the mean of 67,71,75?
ma.e: The sum is 213; divide by 3 to get 71.

y.A: 69 is the middle of 67 and 71 on their own, with the 75 left out. All three count: 67 + 71 + 75 = 213, and 213 ÷ 3 = 71.
y.B: 213 is the three numbers added up — the total, not the mean. Share it between the three: 213 ÷ 3 = 71.
y.C: 73 is the middle of 71 and 75, with the 67 left out. Add all three first: 213 ÷ 3 = 71.

ma.q: What is the median of 66,69,72,75,79?
ma.e: The ordered middle value is 72.

y.A: 69 is the second number in order, one step short of the middle. With five numbers, the middle is the third one: 72.
y.B: 75 is the fourth number in order, one step past the middle. With five numbers, the middle is the third one: 72.
y.D: 13 is 79 − 66, the biggest take away the smallest — the spread of the numbers, not the middle one. In order, the middle of five is the third: 72.

ma.q: A bag holds 3 red and 3 blue marbles. What is P(red)?
ma.e: There are 6 marbles and 3 are red: 3/6.

y.A: 6/3 is the fraction upside down, all six marbles set over the three reds. A chance counts the reds out of every marble: 3/6.
y.B: 1/6 is the chance of one particular marble out of the six. Any of the 3 reds counts, so it is 3/6.
y.D: 3/3 sets the reds against the blues, and it would mean red every time. A chance is out of all 6 marbles: 3/6.

ma.q: A box measures 4×4×2. What is its volume?

y.A: 18 is 4 × 4 + 2, two sides multiplied and the third one added on. All three multiply: 4 × 4 = 16, then 16 × 2 = 32.
y.C: 10 is 4 + 4 + 2, the three sides added instead of multiplied. Volume multiplies them: 4 × 4 × 2 = 32.
y.D: 64 is 4 × 4 × 4, the third side counted as 4 when it is only 2. Use the sides as they are: 4 × 4 × 2 = 32.

ma.q: A 7-foot curtain is how many inches long?
ma.e: 7 × 12 = 84 inches.

y.B: 70 is 7 × 10, as if a foot held ten inches. It holds 12, so 7 × 12 = 84.
y.C: 19 is 7 + 12, the two numbers added instead of multiplied. Each of the 7 feet is 12 inches long: 7 × 12 = 84.
y.D: 21 is 7 × 3, three counted for each foot — but 3 is the feet in a yard. Inches go 12 to a foot: 7 × 12 = 84.

ma.q: Which value is the mode of 72,75,75,77,80?
ma.e: 75 occurs most often.

y.A: 72 is the smallest number in the list, and it shows up only once. 75 shows up twice, so 75 is the mode.
y.B: 80 is the biggest number here, not the most common one. 75 is the one written twice.
y.D: 77 appears just once, the same as 72 and 80. Only 75 is repeated.

ma.q: What is the mean of 73,77,81?
ma.e: The sum is 231; divide by 3 to get 77.

y.B: 75 is the middle of 73 and 77 on their own, with the 81 left out. All three count: 73 + 77 + 81 = 231, and 231 ÷ 3 = 77.
y.C: 79 is the middle of 77 and 81, with the 73 left out. Add all three first: 231 ÷ 3 = 77.
y.D: 231 is the three numbers added up — the total, not the mean. Share it between the three: 231 ÷ 3 = 77.

ma.q: What is the median of 72,75,78,81,85?
ma.e: The ordered middle value is 78.

y.A: 81 is the fourth number in order, one step past the middle. With five numbers, the middle is the third one: 78.
y.C: 13 is 85 − 72, the biggest take away the smallest — that is the spread, not the middle. The middle of five in order is the third: 78.
y.D: 75 is the second number in order, one step short of the middle. With five numbers, the middle is the third one: 78.

ma.q: A bag holds 5 red and 4 blue marbles. What is P(red)?
ma.e: There are 9 marbles and 5 are red: 5/9.

y.B: 4/9 is the blue share — 4 blue out of the 9 marbles. The reds are the other 5: 5/9.
y.C: 1/9 is the chance of one particular marble out of the nine. Any of the 5 reds counts, so it is 5/9.
y.D: 5/4 sets the reds against the blues. A chance is out of every marble, and there are 9 altogether: 5/9.

ma.q: A sheet of paper is 9 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
ma.e: Perimeter is the whole way round: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 cm.

y.A: 13 is 9 + 4 — that is only two of the four sides.
y.C: 36 is 9 × 4, which is the area. Area is the space inside the paper; perimeter is the walk around its edge.
y.D: 18 is 9 + 9, the two long sides, with both short ones left out.

ma.q: A rug is 7 feet long and 3 feet wide. A ribbon is sewn all the way around its edge. How long is the ribbon?
ma.e: "All the way around" is the perimeter: 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 feet.

y.A: 10 is 7 + 3 — one long side and one short one. The ribbon goes round all four.
y.B: 14 is 7 + 7, the two long sides only.
y.C: 21 is 7 × 3, the area — how much floor the rug covers, not how far it is round the edge.

ma.q: A square tile has sides of 6 inches. What is its perimeter?
ma.e: Four equal sides: 6 × 4 = 24 inches.

y.B: 12 is two sides. A square has four.
y.C: 18 is three sides — one is still missing.
y.D: 36 is 6 × 6, the area of the tile, not the distance round it.

ma.q: A rectangular garden has an area of 24 square metres. It is 4 metres wide. How long is it?
ma.e: Area = length × width, so length = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 m.

y.A: 5 is one short. Count the fours: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 — that is six of them.
y.B: 12 is half of 24. Halving only gives the answer when the other side is 2.
y.D: 20 is 24 − 4. The two sides were multiplied to make the area, so divide to get one back.

ma.q: A card has an area of 18 square centimetres and is 3 centimetres wide. How tall is it?

y.A: 5 is one short: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 is six threes.
y.B: 9 is half of 18 — right only if the card were 2 cm wide.
y.C: 15 is 18 − 3. Area comes from multiplying, so divide to undo it.

ma.q: A doormat covers 8 square feet. It is 4 feet long. How wide is it?
ma.e: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 feet.

y.A: 1 is one short: 4, then 4 again, makes 8 — two fours fit, not one.
y.C: 4 is 8 − 4. Undo a multiplication by dividing, not subtracting.
y.D: 32 is 8 × 4, which multiplies the area again instead of splitting it.

ma.q: A rectangular photo has a perimeter of 18 inches. It is 6 inches long. How wide is it?
ma.e: Two lengths take 12, leaving 18 − 12 = 6 for the two widths, so each width is 6 ÷ 2 = 3 inches.

y.A: 6 is what is left once both lengths are taken off — but that 6 is TWO widths. Halve it.
y.B: 12 is 18 − 6, which takes off one length when the photo has two.
y.D: 9 is half the perimeter, which is one length plus one width. The 6 still has to come off.

ma.q: A flowerbed is edged with 22 metres of brick. The bed is 7 metres long. How wide is it?
ma.e: Two lengths take 14, leaving 22 − 14 = 8 for the two widths, so each width is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 m.

y.B: 8 is both widths together. One width is half of it.
y.C: 11 is half of 22 — one length plus one width. The 7 still has to come off.
y.D: 15 is 22 − 7, taking off one length when the brick runs along two.

ma.q: If 3x + 7 = 19, what is x?
ma.e: Subtract 7, then divide by 3: x = 4.

y.D: 16 is 19 − 3, the total with the 3 taken off instead of the 7. The 7 comes off first: 19 − 7 = 12, then 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
y.A: 3 does not check: 3 × 3 + 7 = 16, not 19.

ma.q: Which bus route number is divisible by both 2 and 3?
ma.e: 24 is even and its digit sum is 6, so it is divisible by 6.

y.A: 164 is even, but its digits add to 1 + 6 + 4 = 11, which is not in the 3 times table. The digits of 24 add to 6, and 6 is a multiple of 3.
y.B: 166 is even, but its digits add to 1 + 6 + 6 = 13, so 3 will not divide it. The digits of 24 add to 6, and 6 is a multiple of 3.
y.C: 170 is even, but its digits add to 1 + 7 + 0 = 8, so it is not a multiple of 3. The digits of 24 add to 6, and 6 is a multiple of 3.

ma.q: A game starts with 8 base points and adds 5 packs of 10 points. What is the total?
ma.e: Multiply first, then add, to get 58.

y.A: 48 is 58 − 10, the total with ten taken off it — one pack of points short. All five packs count: 5 × 10 = 50, then 50 + 8 = 58.
y.C: 63 is 58 + 5, the total with the 5 counted a second time. The 5 is the number of packs, not points of its own: 5 × 10 = 50, then 50 + 8 = 58.
y.B: 130 adds the 8 first and then multiplies, (8 + 5) × 10; the five packs are multiplied before the base points go on.

ma.q: Three quarters of a cup makes how many one-eighth-cup samples?
ma.e: 3/4 = 6/8, so there are six eighths.

y.A: 3 is the 3 from three quarters, the top number read straight off. Turn 3/4 into eighths first: 3/4 = 6/8, which is six samples.
y.C: 4 is the 4 from three quarters, the bottom number read straight off. It is the size of the pieces, not how many: 3/4 = 6/8, so six samples.
y.D: 8 is how many eighths fit in a whole cup. Only three quarters of a cup is being shared out, and 3/4 = 6/8, so six.

ma.q: A 6.4-meter ribbon is cut in half. How long is each piece?
ma.e: Cutting in half means multiply by 0.5: 3.2 meters.

y.D: 12.8 is 6.4 × 2, the ribbon doubled rather than halved. Cutting in half means 6.4 ÷ 2 = 3.2 meters for each piece.
