y.C: 24 is a multiple of 12 but not of 9, which goes 9, 18, 27, 36.

MA.q: If y/6 = 11, what is y?
MA.e: Multiply both sides by 6: y = 11 × 6 = 66.

y.A: 77 is 11 × 7, not 11 × 6; the 6 under the y is what has to be undone.
y.B: 17 is 11 + 6, adding the 6 instead of multiplying by it.
y.D: 55 is 11 × 5. Multiplying both sides by 6 gives 66.

MA.q: Solve 5x − 8 = 37.
MA.e: Add 8 to get 5x = 45, then divide by 5: x = 9.

y.A: 11 does not check: 5 × 11 − 8 = 47, not 37.
y.C: 7 does not check either: 5 × 7 − 8 = 27, ten short of 37.
y.D: 5.8 comes from subtracting the 8 instead of adding it, 29 ÷ 5; moving the − 8 across makes 5x = 45.

MA.q: What is 2a^2 + 3 when a = 4?

y.A: 11 is 2 × 4 + 3, multiplying before squaring; the exponent belongs to the a alone.
y.B: 67 squares the 2a together, (2 × 4)² + 3 = 64 + 3; only the a is squared.
y.C: 19 comes from taking 4² as 8 — doubling instead of squaring. 4² is 16, so 2 × 16 + 3 = 35.

MA.q: What is the reflection of (−5, 2) across the x-axis?
MA.e: Reflection across the x-axis keeps x and changes the sign of y.

y.B: (5, −2) flips both signs; reflecting across the x-axis leaves x at −5 and changes only the y.
y.C: (−2, 5) swaps the two coordinates; a reflection across the x-axis keeps x where it is.
y.D: (5, 2) changes the sign of x and leaves y alone, which is a reflection across the y-axis.

MA.q: A rectangle is 13 meters long and 7 meters wide. What is its area?
MA.e: Area = length × width = 13 × 7 = 91 square meters.

y.A: 40 is 2 × (13 + 7), the perimeter; area multiplies the two sides together.
y.C: 182 is 13 × 7 × 2, the area counted twice.
y.D: 78 is 13 × 6; the width is 7 meters, so it is 13 × 7.

MA.q: A triangle has base 15 cm and height 8 cm. What is its area?
MA.e: Area = 1/2 × 15 × 8 = 60 square centimeters.

y.B: 120 is 15 × 8, the whole rectangle around the triangle; a triangle is half of it.
y.C: 23 is 15 + 8, adding the base and height instead of multiplying and halving.
y.D: 46 is 2 × (15 + 8), a perimeter; area needs 1/2 × 15 × 8.

MA.q: The perimeter of a square photo frame is 56 cm. What is the length of one side?
MA.e: A square has four equal sides, so each side is 56 ÷ 4 = 14 cm.

y.A: 28 is 56 ÷ 2, which counts only two sides; a square has four.
y.C: 16 divides the 40 and then appends the leftover 6 (10 + 6); the whole 56 goes into the division, giving 14.
y.D: 52 subtracts 4 instead of dividing by 4.

MA.q: What is the volume of a rectangular prism measuring 9 cm by 5 cm by 4 cm?
MA.e: Volume = 9 × 5 × 4 = 180 cubic centimeters.

y.B: 200 is not 9 × 5 × 4; multiplying the three out gives 180.
y.C: 160 is 8 × 5 × 4, with the 9 taken as 8.
y.D: 90 is half the volume — 9 × 5 = 45 and then 45 × 2 rather than 45 × 4.

MA.q: A triangle has angles of 37° and 68°. What is the third angle?
MA.e: Triangle angles total 180°; 180 − 37 − 68 = 75°.

y.B: 85 is ten over; the two known angles add to 105, not 95.
y.C: 70 subtracts 110 from 180; 37 + 68 is 105, which leaves 75.

MA.q: How many centimeters are in 2.35 meters?
MA.e: One meter is 100 centimeters, so 2.35 × 100 = 235.

y.A: 23.5 multiplies by 10; a meter holds 100 centimeters.
y.B: 2,350 multiplies by 1,000, which turns meters into millimeters.
y.D: 0.0235 divides by 100 instead of multiplying; centimeters are smaller than meters, so the number gets bigger.

MA.q: How much time passes from 9:38 a.m. to 11:05 a.m.?
MA.e: From 9:38 to 10:38 is 1 hour, then to 11:05 is 27 minutes.

y.B: 1 hour 33 minutes subtracts the minutes the wrong way round, 38 − 5; borrowing an hour gives 65 − 38 = 27.
y.C: 1 hour 17 minutes falls ten short; 10:38 to 11:05 is 27 minutes.
y.D: 2 hours 27 minutes counts an extra hour; 9:38 to 11:05 passes 10:38 only once.

MA.q: What is the mean of 14, 19, 21, and 26?
MA.e: The total is 80, and 80 ÷ 4 = 20.

y.A: 19 is one of the four numbers, not their average; they total 80, and 80 ÷ 4 = 20.
y.C: 18 would need a total of 72; 14 + 19 + 21 + 26 is 80.
y.D: 21 is one of the four numbers again, and 21 × 4 = 84, more than the 80 they total.

MA.q: A fair spinner has 10 equal sections numbered 1 through 10. What is the probability of landing on a multiple of 3?
MA.e: The multiples of 3 are 3, 6, and 9, so 3 of 10 outcomes are favorable.

y.A: 1/2 is 5/10, which counts five favorable numbers; the multiples of 3 up to 10 are 3, 6 and 9.
y.B: 1/5 is 2/10, counting only two multiples of 3; there are three.
y.D: 2/5 is 4/10, which counts a fourth multiple of 3; the next one after 9 is 12, past the spinner.

MA.q: What is the range of 23, 31, 18, 27, and 35?
MA.e: Range = greatest − least = 35 − 18 = 17.

y.A: 53 is 35 + 18, adding the greatest and least instead of subtracting.
y.B: 12 is not the spread from 18 to 35; the range is 35 − 18 = 17.
y.D: 13 is 31 − 18, using 31 rather than the greatest value, 35.

VR.q: ANCIENT most nearly means:
VR.e: Ancient means belonging to the distant past or very old; age does not necessarily imply value.

y.B: Valuable means worth a lot. Age can raise a price, but plenty of ancient things are worthless.
y.C: Partly hidden is about being out of sight, which has nothing to do with age.
y.D: Carefully built is about workmanship, not about how long ago something was made.

VR.q: BRISK most nearly means:
VR.e: Brisk means quick and energetic, as in a brisk walk; uneven, damp, and noisy describe other qualities, not speed.

y.A: Uneven means not regular or level, whereas a brisk walk is usually steady.
y.C: Noisy means loud.
y.D: Damp means slightly wet, and a brisk wind can be perfectly dry.

VR.q: CONCEAL most nearly means:
VR.e: To conceal is to hide something from view or knowledge; protecting may involve concealment but is not equivalent.

y.A: Protect means to keep from harm. You might hide a thing in order to protect it, but hiding is the act itself.
y.C: Carry means to move something from place to place.
y.D: Discover means to find — the opposite of concealing.

VR.q: DROWSY most nearly means:
VR.e: Drowsy means sleepy or ready to fall asleep; weakness is not required.

y.A: Worried means anxious, which usually keeps a person awake.
y.B: Weak means lacking strength; you can be wide awake and weak.
y.D: Lonely means without company.

VR.q: ENORMOUS most nearly means:
VR.e: Enormous means extremely large or huge; an enormous object need not be heavy.

y.A: Distant means far away, which is about position rather than size.
y.B: Heavy means weighing a lot, and a huge balloon is light.
y.C: Empty means containing nothing; an enormous room can be empty or full.

VR.q: FORTUNATE most nearly means:
VR.e: Fortunate means favored by good luck; wealth or preparation can help but are not the meaning.

y.B: Prepared means ready in advance — nearly the opposite, since luck is what arrives without planning.
y.C: Wealthy means having a lot of money. A person can be fortunate in health and have none.
y.D: Grateful means thankful, which is how a fortunate person might feel rather than what the word means.

VR.q: GENEROUS most nearly means:
VR.e: A generous person willingly gives or shares; the other positive traits are not synonyms.

y.A: Famous means widely known.
y.B: Patient means willing to wait.
y.C: Successful means having achieved something, which says nothing about sharing it.

VR.q: COURAGEOUS most nearly means:
VR.e: Courageous means brave or fearless, willing to face danger; strength is physical, and wild and foolish describe poor judgment rather than courage.

y.A: Foolish means unwise. Courage weighs the danger; foolishness ignores it.
y.B: Wild means uncontrolled.
y.C: Strong means physically powerful, but courage is about facing fear and a weak person can have plenty.

VR.q: IDLE most nearly means:
VR.e: Idle means not active or not in use; the other choices describe unrelated conditions.

y.A: Complete means finished, with nothing missing.
y.C: Cheerful means in good spirits; a person can be busy and cheerful at once.
y.D: Balanced means evenly arranged.

VR.q: LOYAL most nearly means:
VR.e: Loyal means faithful and dependable in support; obedience may occur without loyalty.

y.A: Truthful means honest in what you say. A loyal friend can still tell you an uncomfortable truth.
y.C: Brave means facing danger.
y.D: Obedient means doing as you are told; loyalty is about standing by someone, not about following orders.

VR.q: MURKY most nearly means:
VR.e: Murky water or an unclear idea is cloudy and difficult to see through; depth and temperature are unrelated.

y.B: Cold is about temperature, and murky water can be warm.
y.C: Shallow means not deep, and shallow water is often the clearest there is.
y.D: Still means not moving, and still water usually settles clear.

VR.q: NEGLECT most nearly means:
VR.e: To neglect is to fail to give proper care or attention, closest to ignore; damage may result but is not the action itself, and misplace concerns losing objects, not withholding attention.

y.A: Dislike is a feeling; you can neglect something you love.
y.B: Misplace means to lose track of where a thing is, which is an accident rather than a failure to attend to it.
y.D: Damage means to harm. Neglect can lead to damage, but the word names the not-caring, not the harm.

VR.q: OBVIOUS most nearly means:
VR.e: Obvious means easy to see or understand, or clear; an obvious statement can still be unimportant or incorrect.

y.A: Unusual means rare, and something obvious is often perfectly ordinary.
y.B: Important means mattering a lot, which is separate from being easy to see.
y.D: Correct means right, and an obvious answer can be wrong.

VR.q: PATIENT most nearly means:
VR.e: A patient person can wait or endure difficulty calmly, which is closest to tolerant.

y.A: Healthy means well. The other sense of the word, someone under a doctor's care, is a noun and not what this question asks for.
y.C: Slow is about speed; a patient person can work quickly and still wait well.
y.D: Quiet means making little sound.

VR.q: QUIET most nearly means:
VR.e: Quiet most directly means making little or no sound, closest to silent.

y.B: Empty means containing nothing. An empty room is often quiet, but the two words are not the same.
y.C: Secret means kept hidden, and you can keep a secret out loud.
y.D: Careful means taking care.

VR.q: SLENDER most nearly means:
VR.e: Slender means thin or slim in build; tall, elegant, and pale describe other qualities a slender thing need not have.

y.B: Elegant means graceful or stylish. Slender things often look elegant, but the word describes the shape.
y.C: Pale is about color.
y.D: Tall is about height, and something can be slender and short.

VR.q: WEARY most nearly means:
VR.e: Weary means very tired; disappointment or injury may cause weariness but are not synonyms.

y.A: Injured means hurt; you can be worn out without being harmed.
y.B: Cautious means careful of danger.
y.C: Disappointed means let down, which is a feeling about an outcome rather than a lack of energy.

VR.q: The librarian spoke ____ so the students at nearby tables could continue reading.
VR.e: Protecting nearby readers from interruption requires speaking softly; speed and pride do not control volume.

y.B: Firmly is about how decided she sounded, not about how much noise reached the nearby tables.
y.C: Rapidly is about speed, and fast speech can still be loud.
y.D: Proudly describes her feelings, which the readers at the next table would not notice.

VR.q: The puzzle appeared simple, but its final step was surprisingly ____.
VR.e: But signals a contrast with simple, making complex the logical completion.

y.A: Familiar would not be surprising, and the sentence turns on a surprise.
y.B: Brief means short, and shortness is not the opposite of simple.
y.D: Colorful describes appearance, not difficulty.

VR.q: A portable radio is one that can be easily ____ from place to place.
VR.e: Portable means able to be carried or moved easily; the sentence provides a direct definition.

y.A: Purchased means bought, which any radio can be.
y.B: Repaired means mended.
y.C: Heard is what a radio is for whether it travels or not; this sentence is about moving it.

VR.q: Since the evidence was incomplete, the judge refused to reach a ____ conclusion.
VR.e: Incomplete evidence prevents a definite, certain conclusion; the other adjectives do not express certainty.

y.A: A judge would not refuse to be fair; what incomplete evidence prevents is being sure.
y.C: Lengthy means long, and length is not what evidence settles.
y.D: Public means open to everyone, which is about where a conclusion is announced.

VR.q: Kai checked every measurement twice, showing that he was ____.
VR.e: Rechecking every measurement demonstrates thoroughness; nervousness is possible but not required by the evidence.

y.B: Curious means wanting to know things; measuring the same thing twice is about care, not curiosity.
y.C: Skillful means good at something, which checking twice neither shows nor needs.
y.D: Nervous is possible, but the sentence says the double-checking shows how he works.

VR.q: The audience's applause was so ____ that it could be heard outside the theater.
VR.e: Being heard outside provides an intensity clue; thunderous means extremely loud.

y.B: Brief is about how long the applause lasted, not how loud it was.
y.C: Sudden is about when it started.
y.D: Polite applause is quiet, which is the opposite of carrying outside the theatre.

VR.q: The class created a chart to ____ the results of its survey.
VR.e: A chart can summarize and display collected results; prediction concerns results not yet collected.

y.A: Predict means to say what will happen, and the survey has already been done.
y.B: Question means to ask about, and the asking is finished.
y.C: Erase means to rub out, which is not what a chart does to results.

VR.q: The medicine did not cure the cold, but it did ____ the soreness in Mina's throat.
VR.e: Relieve means reduce discomfort, fitting what medicine can do even without curing the illness.

y.A: Replace means to put something else in its place.
y.C: Measure means to find the size of, and measuring a sore throat would not help it.
y.D: Explain means to make clear; the sentence contrasts curing with something done to the soreness.

VR.q: The witness gave a ____ account, including the time, place, and exact words spoken.
VR.e: Listing time, place, and exact words is evidence of a detailed account.

y.A: Doubtful means uncertain, and this account is full of specifics.
y.B: Private means not shared, but the account was given.
y.D: Dramatic is about how exciting it was, not about how much it included.

VR.q: After the long morning hike, the campers were so ____ that they ate every sandwich in the basket.
VR.e: A long hike explains why the campers were hungry enough to eat every sandwich; muddy, lost, and thirsty do not explain the eating.

y.A: Thirsty would be met by drinking, not by eating every sandwich in the basket.
y.B: Lost does not explain the eating.
y.D: Muddy describes how they looked after the hike.

VR.q: The editor asked Rosa to ____ the article before it was printed.
VR.e: An editor logically asks for revisions before publication; the other actions do not improve the article.

y.B: Fold is something done to paper, not to what an article says.
y.C: Announce means to make public, which the printing already does.
y.D: Recite means to say aloud from memory.

VR.q: Although the coach pointed out every mistake, Ellis gave a ____ reply and thanked her for the advice.
VR.e: Accepting correction and thanking the coach shows a mature reply; boastful and stern clash with the thanks, and careless does not describe a considered response.

y.A: Careless would not go with thanking her for the advice.
y.B: Stern means severe, which is how the coach spoke rather than how Ellis answered.
y.D: Boastful means bragging, and a list of one's own mistakes gives nothing to brag about.

VR.q: The two routes are ____; each takes exactly forty minutes.
VR.e: Equal travel times make the routes equivalent for this comparison; directness or distance is not established.

y.A: Nearby means close to here, not equal to one another.
y.B: Direct means without detours, and two routes can both take forty minutes with one of them winding.
y.D: Crowded is about traffic, which the sentence never raises.

VR.q: While the first speaker wandered from topic to topic, the second was ____.
VR.e: While signals contrast; concise means brief and focused, opposing wandering.

y.A: Louder is about volume, and the contrast is with wandering from topic to topic.
y.B: Amusing is about being funny.
y.C: Confident is about manner, and the first speaker may have wandered confidently.

VR.q: The park added signs to ____ visitors from feeding the wild animals.
VR.e: Signs can discourage, or persuade people not to do, the prohibited action.

y.A: You remind someone of something, not from it; the from here needs a verb that stops an action.
y.C: Permit would allow the feeding that the signs exist to stop, and it does not take from either.
y.D: Protect does take from, but it would mean shielding the visitors themselves; the feeding is what the signs are about.

VR.q: A single cloudy night was not enough to ____ the astronomer's month-long study.
VR.e: The sentence emphasizes that one setback could not ruin a much longer study.

y.A: Repeating a month-long study is not something a single night does.
y.B: Describe means to put into words, which a cloudy night cannot do.
y.C: Begin would make the night helpful, and the sentence says it was not enough to do harm.

VR.q: The mayor promised to ____ the complaint rather than dismiss it without investigation.
VR.e: To address a complaint is to deal with it; the contrast with dismiss confirms that meaning.

y.A: Repeat means to say again, which is not the opposite of dismissing a complaint.
y.C: Announce means to make public, and the complaint has already been made.
y.D: Collect means to gather, and the mayor already has it.

QR.q: What number comes next in 2, 5, 10, 13, 26, 29, ...?
QR.e: The rule alternates +3 and ×2; after 29, multiply by 2 to get 58.

y.A: 56 is not 29 × 2; the sequence alternates + 3 and × 2, and doubling 29 gives 58.
y.C: 55 is 26 + 29, adding two terms together; the rule doubles the last one.
y.D: 32 is 29 + 3, repeating the + 3; the two rules take turns, and × 2 is next.

QR.q: Nine notebooks cost $22.50. At the same rate, what do fourteen notebooks cost?
QR.e: One notebook costs $22.50 ÷ 9 = $2.50; fourteen cost $35.00.

y.B: 31.50 would make one notebook $2.25; $22.50 ÷ 9 is $2.50.
y.C: 36.50 is $1.50 over; fourteen at $2.50 each come to $35.00.

QR.q: The ratio of maple trees to pine trees is 4:7. If there are 66 trees, how many are maple?
QR.e: Eleven parts total make 66, so each part is 6; maple trees = 4 × 6 = 24.

y.A: 48 is 8 × 6, twice the maple share; maple is 4 parts.
y.B: 18 would make each part 4.5 and the wood 49.5 trees; 66 ÷ 11 = 6, so maple is 4 × 6 = 24.
y.C: 42 is 7 × 6, the pine share.

QR.q: A jar is 3/5 full. One third of the liquid is poured out. What fraction of the jar remains filled?
QR.e: One third of 3/5 is 1/5 poured out; 3/5 − 1/5 = 2/5 remains.

y.A: 4/5 is more than the jar held to begin with, and pouring cannot raise the level.
y.C: 1/5 is the amount poured out, not the amount left.
y.D: 3/10 halves the 3/5 instead of taking a third of it; a third of 3/5 is 1/5.

QR.q: A plant grows from 40 cm to 50 cm. What is the percent increase?
QR.e: The increase is 10 cm, and 10/40 = 0.25 = 25%.

y.A: 10% is the rise in centimeters read as a percent; 10 out of 40 is 25%.
y.B: 40% is the starting height, not a percentage of it.
y.C: 20% divides the 10 rise by the new 50; percent increase measures against the starting 40.

QR.q: A bag holds 2 red and 3 blue marbles. What is the probability of drawing two red marbles without replacement?
QR.e: The probability is 2/5 × 1/4 = 2/20 = 1/10.

y.A: 1/5 is double the answer; once a red is taken only 1 of the 4 left is red, so 2/5 × 1/4 = 1/10.
y.B: 2/5 is the chance of the first marble being red, before the second draw happens at all.
y.D: 1/4 is the chance of the second being red given the first was; both draws have to happen.

QR.q: Three times a number minus 4 equals 29. What is the number?
QR.e: Add 4 to get 33, then divide by 3 to get 11.

y.A: 9 does not check: 3 × 9 − 4 = 23, not 29.
y.B: 25/3 comes from subtracting the 4 instead of adding it; moving the − 4 across makes 3n = 33.

QR.q: The mean of five numbers is 16. Four numbers are 9, 13, 17, and 20. What is the fifth?
QR.e: The total must be 5 × 16 = 80; known values total 59, so the fifth is 21.

y.B: 20 leaves the five totalling 79; a mean of 16 needs 5 × 16 = 80.
y.C: 19 leaves a total of 78, two short of 80.
y.D: 80 is the total the five numbers must reach, not the missing one.

QR.q: Every edge of a cube is doubled. How does its volume change?
QR.e: Volume scales in three dimensions: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

y.A: 4 times is what happens to the area of each face; volume uses all three edges.
y.B: Doubling the edge doubles each of three directions, and they multiply: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
y.C: 6 times comes from 2 + 2 + 2; the three doubled directions multiply rather than add.

QR.q: Which is the best estimate of 2,987 ÷ 61?
QR.e: Use compatible numbers: 3,000 ÷ 60 = 50.

y.A: 500 is ten times too big; 60 × 50 = 3,000, which is about 2,987.
y.B: 5 is ten times too small — 61 × 5 is only about 300.
y.D: 40 would make the product about 2,440; 60 × 50 = 3,000 is far closer to 2,987.

QR.q: Points A(−2, 4) and B(5, 4) are how many units apart?
QR.e: The y-coordinates match, and the horizontal distance is 5 − (−2) = 7.

y.A: 9 is more than the gap; from −2 up to 0 is 2 units and on to 5 is 5 more.
y.B: 3 is 5 − 2, dropping the minus sign on the −2.
y.C: 11 is wider than the whole gap; both points share a y of 4, so the distance is 5 − (−2) = 7.

QR.q: A red book is left of a blue book. A green book is right of the blue book. Which order must occur from left to right?
QR.e: Red must be left of blue, and green must be right of blue, forcing red-blue-green.

y.A: This puts blue to the left of red, and red has to be left of blue.
y.C: This reverses the whole chain: green belongs to blue's right, not its left.
y.D: Green sits left of blue here, but green has to be on blue's right.

QR.q: Which fraction is closest to 3/4?
QR.e: 11/15 ≈ 0.733, only about 0.017 from 0.75; the others are farther.

y.B: 7/10 is 0.7, about 0.05 from 0.75; 11/15 is about 0.017 away.
y.C: 5/8 is 0.625, an eighth below 3/4.
y.D: 9/14 is about 0.643, further from 0.75 than 11/15 is.

QR.q: Boat A travels 48 miles in 3 hours. Boat B travels 70 miles in 5 hours. How much faster is Boat A?
QR.e: Boat A travels 16 mph and Boat B 14 mph, so Boat A is 2 mph faster.

y.A: 4 is not the gap between the rates; Boat A does 48 ÷ 3 = 16 and Boat B 70 ÷ 5 = 14.
y.B: 16 is Boat A's own rate, not how much faster it is.
y.C: 14 is Boat B's rate.

QR.q: What is the next number in 6, 10, 19, 35, 60, ...?
QR.e: The increases are 4, 9, 16, and 25 (2², 3², 4², 5²); next add 6² = 36 to get 96.

y.A: 91 is 60 + 31; the increases are the squares 4, 9, 16, 25, so the next one is 36.
y.C: 85 is 60 + 25, repeating the last increase instead of moving on to 6².
y.D: 90 is 60 + 30; the increases are square numbers, and after 5² comes 6² = 36.

QR.q: A code uses one of 4 letters followed by one of 5 digits. How many codes are possible?
QR.e: Each of 4 letters pairs with each of 5 digits: 4 × 5 = 20.

y.A: 9 is 4 + 5, adding the two lists; pairing multiplies them.
y.B: 16 is 4 × 4; there are 5 digits, not 4.
y.D: 25 is 5 × 5; there are 4 letters.

QR.q: Four workers pack 240 kits in 3 hours at equal steady rates. How many kits can six workers pack in 5 hours?
QR.e: Each worker packs 240 ÷ 4 ÷ 3 = 20 kits per hour; 6 × 5 × 20 = 600.

y.B: 720 is 6 × 5 × 24; each worker packs 240 ÷ 4 ÷ 3 = 20 kits an hour, not 24.
y.C: 900 is more than 6 × 5 × 20, which comes to 600.
y.D: 480 is 240 × 2, doubling the original batch; the workers and the hours both change.

QR.q: Which number has exactly three positive factors?
QR.e: 49 = 7² has factors 1, 7, and 49; the other numbers have more than three.

y.B: 27 has four factors — 1, 3, 9 and 27.
y.C: 18 has six factors: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18.
y.D: 30 has eight factors: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15 and 30.

QR.q: A fair number cube is rolled 120 times. About how many rolls should be greater than 4?
QR.e: Outcomes 5 and 6 are 2/6 = 1/3 of rolls; 1/3 × 120 = 40.

y.A: 20 counts one face out of six; 5 and 6 are both greater than 4, which makes 2 of 6.
y.C: 60 is half the rolls, but only two of the six faces are above 4.
y.D: 80 is two thirds of the rolls — the share that comes out 4 or less.

QR.q: A cube has edge length 3 cm. What is its total surface area?
QR.e: Each face has area 3² = 9, and six faces total 6 × 9 = 54 cm².

y.A: 27 is 3 × 3 × 3, the volume of the cube rather than its surface.
y.B: 18 is 2 × 9, two faces; a cube has six.
y.D: 81 is 9 × 9; each face is 9 square centimeters and there are six of them.

QR.q: A mixture has lemon juice and water in a 3:8 ratio. If it contains 24 cups of water, how many cups of lemon juice are there?
QR.e: Eight parts equal 24, so one part is 3; lemon juice is 3 parts = 9 cups.

y.A: 12 is half of 24; the ratio is 3 to 8, not 1 to 2.
y.B: 6 would make one part 2 and the water 16 cups, not 24.
y.D: 8 is one of the ratio numbers, not a count of cups.

QR.q: An elevator moves from floor −3 to floor 8. How many floors does it move?
QR.e: From −3 to 0 is 3 floors and from 0 to 8 is 8 more, totaling 11.

y.B: 8 counts only the floors above ground; the lift starts three below it.
y.C: 24 is 3 × 8, multiplying the two floor numbers instead of adding the distances.
y.D: 5 is 8 − 3, taking the two numbers the wrong way round; the trip crosses zero, so the distances add.

QR.q: Of 28 students, 17 study French, 14 study Spanish, and 6 study both. How many study neither?
QR.e: At least one = 17 + 14 − 6 = 25; neither = 28 − 25 = 3.

y.A: 9 subtracts the overlap twice, 17 + 14 − 6 − 6, before taking the result from 28.
y.B: 11 is 17 − 6, the French-only group, not those studying neither.
y.C: 0 would need all 28 to study a language, and 17 + 14 − 6 = 25.

QR.q: If every glip is a tor and no tor is a mip, which statement must be true?
QR.e: Since all glips are tors and no tor is a mip, no glip can be a mip.

y.A: The chain runs from glips to tors and says nothing about what mips are.
y.C: Nothing rules mips out of existence; they are only kept apart from tors.
y.D: Every glip is a tor and no tor is a mip, so no glip can be a mip.

QR.q: A $100 jacket is discounted 20%, then the sale price is discounted 10%. What is the final price?
QR.e: After 20% off, price is $80; 10% of $80 is $8, leaving $72.

y.A: 70 takes 30% off in one go; the second 10% comes off $80, not off $100.
y.B: 90 applies only the 10%; the 20% comes first.
y.D: 80 is the price after the first discount, with the second still to come.

QR.q: Which expression is equivalent to 4(2x − 3) + 5?
QR.e: Distribute and combine constants: 8x − 12 + 5 = 8x − 7.

y.A: 6x + 2 comes from adding the 4 and the 2 rather than multiplying them; 4 × 2x is 8x.
y.C: 8x + 2 distributes correctly but adds the 3 instead of subtracting it; −12 + 5 = −7.
y.D: 8x − 12 distributes and then forgets the + 5; −12 + 5 = −7.

QR.q: The data are 3, 6, 7, 12, 20. If 40 is added, what is the new median?
QR.e: With six ordered values, median is the mean of the third and fourth: (7 + 12)/2 = 9.5.

y.A: 7 is the third of six values; with an even count the middle two are averaged.
y.B: 12 is the fourth value; it pairs with 7, and their average is 9.5.
y.C: 14 is neither middle value; (7 + 12) ÷ 2 = 9.5.

QR.q: A model tower is 18 cm tall at a scale of 1 cm to 4 m. How tall is the real tower?
QR.e: Each centimeter represents 4 meters, so 18 × 4 = 72 meters.

y.B: 90 is 18 × 5; the scale is 4 meters to the centimeter.
y.C: 54 is 18 × 3, a meter short on every centimeter.
y.D: 22 is 18 + 4, adding the scale instead of multiplying by it.

QR.q: After spending 2/7 of her money, Jo has $45 left. How much did she have at first?
QR.e: The $45 remaining is 5/7 of the original; original = 45 × 7/5 = 63.

y.A: 60 would leave five sevenths as about $42.86, not $45.
y.C: 56 would leave five sevenths as exactly $40.
y.D: 54 would leave five sevenths as about $38.57.

QR.q: What is the remainder when 2,345 is divided by 12?
QR.e: 12 × 195 = 2,340, leaving a remainder of 5.

y.A: 11 is more than the remainder; 12 × 195 = 2,340, and 2,345 − 2,340 = 5.
y.C: 1 is four short of the remainder, which is 5.
y.D: 7 is two over the remainder.

QR.q: Set A is 4, 8, 8, 9, 11. Set B is 2, 7, 8, 10, 14. How much greater is Set B's range?
QR.e: Range A = 11 − 4 = 7; range B = 14 − 2 = 12; difference = 5.

y.B: 12 is Set B's own range, 14 − 2; the question asks how much greater it is than Set A's.
y.C: 3 is not the difference between the ranges; Set A's is 7 and Set B's is 12.
y.D: 7 is Set A's range, 11 − 4.

QR.q: A quadrilateral has angles 92°, 105°, and 78°. What is the fourth angle?
QR.e: Quadrilateral angles total 360°; known angles total 275°, leaving 85°.

y.B: 95 is ten over; the three known angles total 275.
y.C: 75 subtracts 285 from 360 rather than 275.

QR.q: Lee finishes 1/3 of a project Monday and 2/5 Tuesday. What fraction remains?
QR.e: Completed = 5/15 + 6/15 = 11/15; remaining = 4/15.

y.A: 2/15 is two fifteenths short; 1/3 is 5/15 and 2/5 is 6/15, so 11/15 is done.
y.C: 7/15 treats 2/5 as 3/15; over fifteenths it is 6/15.
y.D: 8/15 treats 2/5 as 2/15; it is 6/15.

QR.q: After a 25% discount, a lamp costs $54. What was its original price?
QR.e: The sale price is 75% of the original; $54 ÷ 0.75 = $72.

y.B: 67.50 adds 25% to the $54; the sale price is 75% of the original, so it is $54 ÷ 0.75.
y.C: 79 is not $54 ÷ 0.75, which comes to $72.
y.D: 81 would leave a sale price of $60.75 after 25% off.

QR.q: Which whole number multiplied by itself gives a product closest to 130?
QR.e: 11 × 11 = 121 is only 9 away from 130, while 12 × 12 = 144 is 14 away.

y.A: 12 picks the first square past 130 — 12 × 12 = 144 — without comparing distances: 144 is 14 away and 121 only 9.
y.B: 10 rounds 130 down to the friendly 100 = 10 × 10, but 121 is far closer to 130 than 100 is.
y.D: 13 comes from 130 ÷ 10; the question wants a number times itself, and 13 × 13 = 169 overshoots.

QR.q: A train travels 54 miles per hour for 2 hours 20 minutes. How far does it travel?
QR.e: 2 hours 20 minutes = 2 1/3 hours; 54 × 2 1/3 = 126 miles.

y.A: 118 is not 54 × 2 1/3; two hours give 108 miles and the extra third gives 18 more.
y.B: 108 is two hours' travel; the extra 20 minutes add 18 miles.
y.D: 144 comes from reading 20 minutes as two thirds of an hour; it is one third, so 54 × 7/3 = 126.

QR.q: A meal includes one of 3 entrées and one of 4 sides. One side is unavailable with one entrée. How many allowed pairs remain?
QR.e: Normally 3 × 4 = 12 pairs; removing one unavailable pair leaves 11.

y.B: 7 is 3 + 4, adding the two lists; pairing multiplies them.
y.C: 8 removes four pairs; only one combination is unavailable.
y.D: 10 removes two pairs, and just one is ruled out, leaving 11.

QR.q: A rectangular field is 24 m by 15 m. A runner completes 2 1/2 laps around it. How far does the runner travel?
QR.e: One lap is perimeter 2(24 + 15) = 78 m; 2.5 × 78 = 195 m.

y.A: 156 is two laps; the runner does two and a half.
y.B: 390 is 5 × 78, five laps rather than two and a half.
y.C: 97.5 is 2.5 × 39, using 24 + 15 as a lap; a lap goes round all four sides, 2 × 39 = 78.

RC.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “A Seed Bank on Ice”?
c: How farmers choose which mountain fields to sow
How a seed vault preserves backup crop diversity
Why crop seeds sprout best when frozen in ice
Why regional collections are no longer needed
RC.e: The passage explains duplicate storage, testing, renewal, and future recovery.

y.A: No farmer chooses a field here; the vault stores duplicate samples of seed.
y.C: Cold and dry storage keeps seeds alive, but germination falls over time and fresh seed has to be grown. Freezing does not make them sprout better.
y.D: The passage says in its second sentence that the vault does not replace ordinary seed collections.

RC.q: Why are seeds periodically tested?
c: To sell the oldest packets to farmers
To see whether they can still sprout
To sort the packets by color and size
To keep the vault warm through winter
RC.e: Germination tests directly check whether seeds remain viable.

y.A: Nothing is sold. The samples are duplicates held in case a regional collection is lost.
y.C: Sorting is never mentioned; the test is whether the seed still sprouts.
y.D: The vault is kept cold and dry, which is the opposite of warm.

RC.q: Why store duplicates?
c: A surviving copy can replace a destroyed collection.
Two seeds of the same crop always sprout faster than one.
Farms are no longer able to store their own seeds.
The mountain vault must look full to its visitors.
RC.e: A backup is useful when the original regional collection is lost.

y.B: A duplicate is insurance, not speed, and nothing suggests two seeds sprout faster than one.
y.C: The vault stores copies alongside ordinary collections rather than instead of them.
y.D: How full the vault looks to visitors is never raised.

RC.q: Why compare the vault to a library?
c: Both hold only paper records and printed books.
Both preserve collections for future use.
Both are always built deep underground in rock.
Both lend out their items to daily visitors.
RC.e: The analogy emphasizes organized preservation and later access.

y.A: The passage calls these books living, which is the point of the comparison: they are seeds, not paper.
y.C: A mountain vault is described, but the likeness is about preserving, not about where either one sits.
y.D: Nothing is lent out; the seeds are held in case they are ever needed.

RC.q: “Varieties” most nearly means:
RC.e: Crop varieties are distinct types of a crop.

y.A: Seasons are times of year, and what could be lost here is kinds of crop.
y.B: The containers are the packets; it is what is inside them that might be restored.
y.D: Disease, war and disaster are the accidents. This word names what they might destroy.

RC.q: How does Theo change?
c: He copies Ada's plain kite exactly and never decorates again.
He gives up kite flying and takes up another hobby instead.
He decides the weak wind ruined both of the day's flights.
He begins judging a kite by how it flies, not how it looks.
RC.e: Theo stops blaming the wind and plans to test before decorating.

y.A: He keeps one small ribbon and plans to decorate his next kite — after testing it.
y.B: He flies the same kite again as soon as the tail is on.
y.C: The wind was the same for both, and Ada's kite climbed; that is why he stopped blaming it.

RC.q: What did Theo tie onto his kite?
c: A tail of folded paper bows
A heavier frame made of thin wood
A second spool of heavy string
A new row of shiny foil stars
RC.e: The passage states he tied on a tail of folded paper bows; the foil stars were removed, not added.

y.B: No frame is mentioned, and what he adds is light rather than heavy.
y.C: String never comes up. A tail is what keeps the nose up.
y.D: He pulls the stars off rather than adding more.

RC.q: Why did Theo keep one small ribbon on the handle?
c: Its weight there could not affect the flight.
It helped him steer the kite's nose upward.
Ada asked him to keep one ribbon for luck.
He forgot the ribbon was still tied there.
RC.e: On the handle the ribbon's weight “meant nothing to the sky”; the other choices invent forgetfulness, a request, or steering.

y.B: The tail keeps the nose up. The ribbon on the handle is not on the kite at all.
y.C: Ada asks him nothing; he watches her kite and works it out himself.
y.D: The passage says he kept it, which is a choice rather than an oversight.

RC.q: Which lesson is best supported?
c: The wind matters far more than a kite's own design.
Watching another flier is a waste of good practice time.
How well something works can matter more than looks.
Decorations always ruin a project, so avoid them.
RC.e: The plain kite outflies the decorated one in the same wind. Putting it all down to the wind is too absolute, and the passage contradicts both the idea that watching another flier wastes practice time and the claim that decorations always ruin a project.

y.A: The wind was identical for both kites, which is exactly what ruled it out as the cause.
y.B: Watching Ada is how he found the answer.
y.D: He keeps a ribbon where its weight does not matter and plans to decorate his next kite after testing it.

RC.q: “Steadily” most nearly means:
RC.e: Ada's kite climbs in an even, controlled way; the other words do not describe its motion.

y.B: Wobbling and diving is what Theo's kite did; Ada's did the opposite.
y.C: Noise is never described, and the word here is about how the kite moved.
y.D: Sudden movement is the reverse of steady; the climb was even.

RC.q: Which summary best captures “A Bridge for Animals”?
c: How cameras are used to photograph forest wildlife
How a habitat-like overpass helped animals cross safely
How deer decide which forest plants they will eat
Why towns should ban highways that cross forests
RC.e: Design, placement, and increasing animal use form the central idea.

y.A: The cameras are one step in the work, used to find the routes animals already took.
y.C: The shrubs and logs are there to make the bridge feel like habitat, not as food to choose between.
y.D: The highway stays. What the passage describes is a way to let animals cross it.

RC.q: What helped choose the bridge location?
RC.e: Biologists studied existing animal routes using those clues.

y.A: Weather is never mentioned.
y.C: No vote appears; biologists studied what the animals were already doing.
y.D: The color of the road has nothing to do with where animals crossed.

RC.q: Why did use likely increase after plants matured?
c: The crossing seemed more like natural habitat.
The overpass became shorter and easier to cross.
Animals were fed on the bridge to draw them there.
The highway was closed to traffic at night.
RC.e: Mature plants and faded scent made the overpass more natural and inviting.

y.B: The bridge did not change size. The plants on it grew and the human scent faded.
y.C: No food is ever put on the bridge.
y.D: Nothing closes the road; fences guide the animals toward the crossing.

RC.q: Why mention the early photographs?
c: To show success developed over time
To compare the sizes of different deer
To criticize the engineers who built it
RC.e: Few early crossings contrast with later increased use.

y.B: The early photographs show few crossings, and the reasons given are young plants and human scent, not the cameras.
y.C: No deer are compared with one another.
y.D: The passage says the project succeeded.

RC.q: “Guided” most nearly means:
RC.e: Fences directed animals toward the overpass.

y.A: Observing is what the cameras did; the fences did something to where the animals went.
y.B: Fences do protect, but these ones steer animals toward the crossing.
y.C: Measuring is not what a fence does.

RC.q: In the example, how tall is the tower?
RC.e: The tower's shadow is 15 times the stick's, so its height is 15 meters.

y.A: 45 is not what the example gives: a one-meter stick with a two-meter shadow means each shadow is twice its object, so 30 ÷ 2 = 15.
y.B: 60 doubles the tower's shadow; the shadow is the longer of the two, so the height is half of 30.
y.D: 30 is the length of the tower's shadow, not its height.

RC.q: Why must measurements be taken at the same time?
RC.e: Changing sun angle changes shadow proportions.

y.A: Level ground is a requirement throughout, not something that changes over ten minutes.
y.B: Towers do not grow. What the passage warns about is a shadow measured ten minutes later.
y.D: The stick stays the same length; its shadow is what moves.

RC.q: What does the passage explain?
c: Why sunlight makes tall sticks lean over
How to build a tower of a given height
Why shadow methods are always inaccurate
RC.e: It gives the principle, example, and accuracy conditions.

y.B: A leaning stick is named as a problem, but nothing says sunlight causes the lean.
y.C: The method measures a tower that already stands.
y.D: The passage gives the conditions under which it does work: level ground, upright objects, the same moment.

RC.q: What could spoil the comparison?
c: A stick made of light wood
A tower of only ten meters
RC.e: The passage explicitly lists an upright object as necessary.

y.A: Nearby objects are what make the method work, since sunlight strikes them at the same angle.
y.B: The weight of the wood is never mentioned; being upright is what matters.
y.C: The method works at any height, and thirty meters is only the example.

RC.q: How is the passage organized?
c: Problem, then debate, then a public vote
Method, reason it works, then limitations
Biography of an observer, then a quotation
A claim followed only by the author's opinion
RC.e: The author explains procedure, geometry, and conditions.

y.A: There is no debate and no vote, only a method and the conditions it needs.
y.C: No observer is named and nobody is quoted.
y.D: The passage explains why the method works and where it fails, which is more than an opinion.

RC.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
c: A cave stops changing once its tunnels and rooms are cut.
Earthquakes and heavy storms dig out most limestone caves.
Stalactites are icicles of frozen water hanging from the ceiling.
Acidic water slowly dissolves limestone and builds formations.
RC.e: The passage traces acidic rainwater from dissolving cracks to building stalactites.

y.A: The passage says the opposite: even then, the water keeps working.
y.B: The first sentence rules that out — a cave is not carved by one storm or earthquake.
y.C: They are called stone icicles, built from specks of mineral, not frozen water.

RC.q: According to the passage, what makes rainwater slightly acidic?
RC.e: The passage states that rainwater collects carbon dioxide, which makes it slightly acidic.

y.A: The specks are what the water leaves behind afterwards, not what makes it acidic.
y.B: One heavy storm is what the passage says a cave is not made by.
y.D: The cracks are where the water goes; the acid comes from carbon dioxide picked up in the soil.

RC.q: Based on the passage, why does a stalactite seem unchanging to a visitor?
c: Stalactites stop growing once a cave is finished.
Cave lights are too dim to show any change.
Water no longer reaches the cave's high ceiling.
Each drop adds only a tiny speck of mineral.
RC.e: Growth by single specks over thousands of years is too slow to see. The passage contradicts both the idea that stalactites stop growing and the idea that water no longer reaches the ceiling, and it never mentions the cave lights being too dim.

y.A: The water keeps working even after the tunnels and rooms are cut.
y.B: Cave lighting is never mentioned.
y.C: Each drop falls from the ceiling, so water is still reaching it.

RC.q: Which contrast is most important to the passage?
c: Narrow tunnels versus wide, open rooms
Soft surface soil versus hard limestone
Sudden events versus slow, repeated changes
RC.e: The opening rejects sudden carving and the rest shows slow, drop-by-drop work; the other pairs are details that are not opposed.

y.A: Tunnels and rooms are both mentioned, but they are not set against each other.
y.B: Storms and earthquakes are grouped together as the sudden events the passage rules out, not contrasted with each other.
y.C: Water passes through soil on its way to the limestone, so the two are a sequence rather than a contrast.

RC.q: Which lesson is supported?
c: A place that looks finished has stopped changing for good.
Water always destroys any stone that it touches over time.
Tiny changes, repeated over time, can produce great results.
Only sudden and violent forces can reshape solid stone.
RC.e: Specks of mineral and slow widening build whole caves; the other three use absolutes the passage contradicts.

y.A: Visitors see rock that looks finished, and the passage says every tunnel is still the sum of tiny changes.
y.B: The same water also builds: each drop leaves a speck that becomes a stalactite.
y.D: Sudden force is exactly what the first sentence rules out.

MA.e: Place-value addition gives 9,215.

y.B: 9,205 is 10 short: the units make 9 + 6 = 15, so a ten carries into 2 + 8 and the tens digit is 1, not 0.
y.C: 9,225 is 10 too many. The tens column makes 2 + 8 + 1 = 11 — a 1, with one hundred carried.
y.D: 9,105 loses 110: a ten out of the units column and a hundred out of the tens.

MA.e: Regrouping across zeros gives 3,562.

y.A: 4,562 is 1,000 too many; after the regrouping the thousands column is 9 − 6 = 3, not 10 − 6.
y.B: 3,672 is 110 over. After regrouping the tens are 9 − 3 = 6 and the hundreds 9 − 4 = 5, which gives 562.
y.D: 4,438 puts 10 − 6 in the thousands and then copies 438 straight down instead of subtracting it.

y.A: 1,204 is 70 more than 63 × 18; check it as 1,260 − 126.
62 is one too few: 32 × 62 = 1,984, a whole 32 short of 2,016.
y.C: 68 overshoots: 32 × 68 = 2,176.
y.D: 58 gives 32 × 58 = 1,856, well under 2,016.

y.A: 11/20 is not a fifteenth at all; 2/5 becomes 6/15, so the sum is 7/15 + 6/15.
y.B: 3/5 is 9/15, which treats 2/5 as 2/15; it is 6/15.
y.C: 1 would need the two to make 15/15; they make 13/15, two fifteenths short.

y.A: 8/20 subtracts the numerators and adds the denominators; both fractions go over 24 first.
y.C: 2/4 is 12/24, which is not the difference: 11/12 is 22/24 and 3/8 is 9/24, leaving 13/24.
y.D: 7/12 keeps twelfths and takes 4/12 away, but 3/8 is 9/24, which is more than 4/12.

MA.e: Cancel 5/15 and 7/14 to get 1/6.

y.A: 5/6 leaves the 5 on top after cancelling; 5 divides into 15 three times, so it cancels away too.
y.B: 1/3 is double the product: 5/14 × 7/15 is 35/210, which reduces to 1/6.
y.D: 12/29 adds instead of multiplying, 5 + 7 over 14 + 15.

y.A: 3 1/4 keeps the quarter from 2 1/4; the whole becomes 9/4 first, and 9/4 × 4/3 = 3.
y.C: 1 1/2 falls short of what the division gives; 2 1/4 is 9/4, and dividing by 3/4 means multiplying by 4/3.
y.D: 2 falls short: three quarters go into 2 1/4 exactly three times, because 3 × 3/4 = 9/4.

y.B: 12.444 is 0.1 short; written as 20.030 − 7.486, the tenths come to 5 after the regrouping.
y.C: 13.544 is a whole 1 too many; the units column is 19 − 7 = 12 once a one has been borrowed.
y.D: 12.534 is 0.01 short; the hundredths after regrouping give 4, not 3.

MA.e: 275×16=4,400 with three decimal places =4.4.

y.A: 3.4 is a full 1 under; 275 × 16 = 4,400, and three decimal places make that 4.4.
y.B: 44 is the right digits with the point one place out; 4,400 with three decimals is 4.400.
y.C: 4.04 puts the digits in the wrong places; 275 × 16 = 4,400, so the answer is 4.4.

y.A: 0.63 is a tenth of the quotient; 157.5 ÷ 25 = 6.3.
y.C: 63 is ten times too big — 2.5 × 63 would be 157.5, not 15.75.

y.B: 53 is 35 + 18, adding the 18 from “18%” to the 35 that is 10% of 350; 10% is 35 and 8% is 28, so 18% is 63.
y.C: 68 is five over; 0.18 × 350 = 63.
y.D: 58 is five under; 35 for the 10% and 28 for the 8% give 63.

y.A: 5 is (6 + 24) ÷ 6, adding before dividing; the division happens first.
y.B: 8 is not 6 + 4. The brackets make 6, then 24 ÷ 6 = 4, and 6 + 4 = 10.
y.D: 14 is 6 + 24 ÷ 3, which uses only the 3 inside the brackets; 3 × 2 = 6 comes first.

y.B: 64 is 2^6, one factor of 2 too many.
y.C: 25 writes the base and the exponent side by side; 2^5 means five 2s multiplied together.
y.D: 10 is 2 × 5, multiplying the base by the exponent.

MA.q: Which is the prime factorization of 90?
MA.e: 90=2×3×3×5, all prime.

y.A: 9 × 10 does make 90, but neither 9 nor 10 is prime.
y.C: 2 × 45 stops early — 45 is 3 × 3 × 5.
y.D: 3 × 30 leaves 30 unbroken, and 30 is 2 × 3 × 5.

MA.q: Solve 4x+9=61.

y.B: 11 does not check: 4 × 11 + 9 = 53, not 61.
y.D: 17.5 comes from adding the 9 instead of subtracting it, 70 ÷ 4; taking it off first gives 4x = 52.

MA.q: 3b²−2 when b=5 equals:

y.A: 77 adds the 2 instead of subtracting it; 3 × 25 = 75, and 75 − 2 = 73.
y.C: 13 is 3 × 5 − 2, multiplying before squaring; the exponent belongs to the b alone.
y.D: 23 is 25 − 2, leaving the 3 out; b² is multiplied by 3 first.

MA.q: Which value satisfies 2n+3<13?
MA.e: 2(4)+3=11<13; others are not less.

y.A: 8 gives 2 × 8 + 3 = 19, well above 13.
y.B: 5 gives exactly 13, and the sign asks for less than 13 rather than equal to it.
y.C: 6 gives 2 × 6 + 3 = 15, above 13.

MA.q: A rectangle is 14 cm by 9 cm. Its perimeter is:

y.A: 23 is 14 + 9, one length and one width; a rectangle has two of each.
y.C: 36 is not the sum of the four sides, which is 14 + 9 + 14 + 9 = 46.
y.D: 126 is 14 × 9, the area; perimeter adds the sides rather than multiplying them.

MA.q: Bases are 8 cm and 14 cm; height is 5 cm. Area?

y.A: 50 is not half of 22 × 5; the average base is (8 + 14) ÷ 2 = 11, and 11 × 5 = 55.
y.B: 110 is (8 + 14) × 5, the whole rectangle on the average base; a trapezoid is half of it.
y.D: 44 falls 11 short; the average base is 11 and the height 5, giving 55.

MA.q: An L-shaped hallway floor is made of two rectangles: one is 9 m by 4 m and the other is 5 m by 3 m. What is the total area of the floor?
MA.e: Add the two rectangle areas: 9 × 4 = 36 and 5 × 3 = 15, so 36 + 15 = 51 m².

y.B: 21 adds the four dimensions, 9 + 4 + 5 + 3, instead of multiplying each rectangle out.
y.C: 98 multiplies the combined lengths by the combined widths, 14 × 7, which counts floor that is not there.
y.D: 36 is 9 × 4, the first rectangle only; the 5 by 3 piece adds another 15.

MA.q: Volume of a 12×4×3 prism?
MA.e: 12×4×3=144 cubic units.

y.A: 96 is 2 × 12 × 4, the top and bottom faces rather than the space between them.
y.C: 192 is 16 × 12; the three edges multiply together, 12 × 4 × 3.
y.D: 48 is 12 × 4, one face only; the height of 3 multiplies it.

MA.q: Two angles are complementary. One angle measures 27°. What is the measure of the other angle?
MA.e: Complementary angles total 90°, and 90 − 27 = 63°.

y.A: 53 is ten short: 90 − 27 is 63.
y.B: 153 is 180 − 27, which is the supplementary angle; complementary angles total 90°.
y.C: 73 is 100 − 27. Angles are complementary at 90°, not 100°.

MA.q: 3.6 kilograms equals how many grams?
MA.e: Multiply kilograms by 1,000.

y.A: 360 multiplies by 100; a kilogram holds 1,000 grams.
y.B: 36,000 multiplies by 10,000.
y.D: 36 multiplies by 10 only.

MA.q: Scale 1 inch=7 feet. A 5-inch wall represents:

y.A: 42 is 6 × 7, one inch too many.
y.B: 28 is 4 × 7, one inch short.
y.C: 12 is 5 + 7, adding the inches to the scale instead of multiplying by it.

y.B: 70 is the total of the four numbers; the mean divides that by 4.
y.C: 20 would need a total of 80, and 11 + 16 + 18 + 25 is 70.
y.D: 18 is one of the four numbers, and it would need a total of 72.

MA.e: Average middle values: (9+15)/2=12.

y.A: 11 is not the average of the two middle values; (9 + 15) ÷ 2 = 12.
y.B: 9 is the third of six values; with an even count the two middle ones are averaged.
y.C: 15 is the fourth value; it pairs with 9, and their average is 12.

MA.q: A card numbered 1–12 is chosen. Probability of a factor of 12?

y.A: 1/3 is 4/12, which misses two factors; 12 has six — 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
y.B: 5/12 counts five factors; 12 is a factor of itself, which makes six.
y.D: 2/3 is 8/12, two more than there are.

y.A: 12 is not the spread; the greatest is 51 and the least 37, so the range is 14.
y.B: 13 is one short; the least of the five is 37, not 38.
y.D: 9 is 51 − 42, using 42 rather than the least value, 37.

MA.q: Reflect (4,−7) across the y-axis.
MA.e: A y-axis reflection changes x sign only.

y.B: (−4,7) changes both signs; a reflection across the y-axis leaves y at −7.
y.C: (−7,4) swaps the two coordinates as well as changing a sign.
y.D: (4,7) changes the sign of y and leaves x alone, which is a reflection across the x-axis.

VR.q: ADEPT most nearly means:
VR.e: Adept means highly skillful; patient, famous, and cheerful describe unrelated qualities.

y.A: Famous means widely known; a person can be highly skilled and unknown.
y.B: Patient means willing to wait.
y.D: Cheerful means in good spirits.

VR.q: DOCILE most nearly means:
VR.e: Docile means calm and willing to be taught or guided, closest to obedient; restless is nearly opposite, while ancient and noisy are unrelated.

y.B: Restless means unable to settle — nearly the opposite of docile.
y.C: Noisy means loud.
y.D: Ancient means very old.

VR.q: CANDID most nearly means:
VR.e: Candid means truthful and direct; shyness, preparation, and humor do not require honesty.

y.A: Humorous means funny, and a candid remark is often anything but.
y.B: Prepared means ready in advance, whereas candour is usually unrehearsed.
y.D: Shy means uneasy with people — nearly the opposite of speaking plainly.

VR.q: DILIGENT most nearly means:
VR.e: A diligent person works carefully and persistently; the other choices describe luck, sound, or commonness.

y.A: Silent means making no sound; a diligent worker may chatter all day.
y.C: Fortunate means lucky, which is the opposite sort of explanation for getting things done.
y.D: Ordinary means usual or unremarkable.

VR.q: ELABORATE most nearly means:
VR.e: Elaborate means detailed or carefully developed; age, completion, and intent are separate traits.

y.A: Accidental means unplanned, and something elaborate takes planning.
y.C: Unfinished means not completed, whereas an elaborate thing is usually finished with care.
y.D: Ancient means very old.

VR.q: FEEBLE most nearly means:
VR.e: Feeble means lacking strength, or weak; noisy, foolish, and narrow do not express low strength.

y.A: Foolish means unwise, which is about judgment rather than strength.
y.B: Noisy means loud; a feeble voice is quiet, but the word itself means lacking strength.
y.C: Narrow is about width.

VR.q: GRACIOUS most nearly means:
VR.e: Gracious means courteous and considerate; the distractors concern understanding, wealth, or precision.

y.A: Exact means precise.
y.C: Puzzled means confused.
y.D: Wealthy means having a lot of money, and a gracious host need not be rich.

VR.q: HAZARDOUS most nearly means:
VR.e: Hazardous means dangerous or risky; something may be exciting, hidden, or unusual without being unsafe.

y.A: Exciting means thrilling, and a hazard can be dull and still be a hazard.
y.B: Hidden means out of sight; a danger in plain view is no less dangerous.
y.C: Unusual means rare, and some hazards are very common indeed.

VR.q: IMMENSE most nearly means:
VR.e: Immense means extremely large; weight, distance, and emptiness are not measures of overall size.

y.A: Distant means far away, which is about position rather than size.
y.B: Empty means containing nothing; an immense hall can be packed.
y.D: Heavy means weighing a lot, and an immense cloud weighs very little.

VR.q: LINGER most nearly means:
VR.e: To linger is to remain longer than expected; hurrying is nearly opposite, while arguing and trembling are unrelated.

y.A: Argue means to disagree in words.
y.C: Tremble means to shake.
y.D: Hurry means to move fast — the opposite of staying on.

VR.q: MUNDANE most nearly means:
VR.e: Mundane means ordinary or lacking excitement; difficulty, newness, and disorder are separate ideas.

y.A: Messy means untidy, and a mundane task can be perfectly neat.
y.B: Modern means of the present time; mundane things have always been mundane.
y.D: Difficult means hard, whereas mundane suggests the everyday.

VR.q: NOTABLE most nearly means:
VR.e: Notable means worthy of attention, or remarkable; the distractors are unrelated surface qualities.

y.B: Polite means well-mannered.
y.C: Readable means easy to read.
y.D: Secret means kept hidden — nearly the opposite of worth noticing.

VR.q: OBSCURE most nearly means:
VR.e: Obscure can mean unclear or not easily understood; cheerfulness, polish, and width do not match that sense.

y.A: Polished means smooth or refined, which is closer to clear than to unclear.
y.B: Narrow is about width.
y.C: Cheerful means in good spirits.

VR.q: PRUDENT most nearly means:
VR.e: Prudent means showing wise, careful judgment; curiosity, strength, and generosity do not necessarily involve caution.

y.A: Curious means wanting to know things, which can lead you into risk rather than away from it.
y.B: Generous means giving.
y.C: Strong means physically powerful.

VR.q: RELUCTANT most nearly means:
VR.e: Reluctant means hesitant or unwilling; being unable is different from not wanting to act.

y.B: Ready means prepared and willing, which is the opposite.
y.C: Unable means not capable; a reluctant person can do the thing and would rather not.
y.D: Confused means unable to understand.

VR.q: SPARSE most nearly means:
VR.e: Sparse means thinly scattered or not dense; texture, flatness, and color do not express low density.

y.A: Pale is about color.
y.C: Level means flat and even.
y.D: Soft is about texture, while sparse is about how thinly something is spread.

VR.q: VERIFY most nearly means:
VR.e: To verify is to confirm that something is true or accurate; arranging, announcing, or merely comparing does not establish truth.

y.B: Announce means to make public, which can be done without checking anything.
y.C: Compare means to set side by side; comparing may be part of verifying, but not the whole of it.
y.D: Arrange means to put in order.

VR.q: The gardener spread straw around the young plants to ____ the soil from drying too quickly.
VR.e: Straw can prevent rapid drying by slowing evaporation; loosening, measuring, and decorating do not fit the stated purpose.

y.B: Loosen means to make less tight, and the sentence needs a word that stops the drying.
y.C: Decorate is about appearance, not about keeping moisture in.
y.D: Measure means to find the size of, and measuring would not slow the drying.

VR.q: Although the directions seemed ____, following them produced a complicated paper sculpture.
VR.e: Although signals contrast between simple directions and a complicated result; the other choices do not create that clear contrast.

y.A: Secret does not contrast with complicated, and the directions were plainly followed.
y.B: Lengthy goes with complicated rather than against it, and Although asks for a contrast.
y.C: Careless directions would not produce a sculpture at all.

VR.q: The creek was unusually ____ after the storm, so the hikers used the bridge instead of stepping across.
VR.e: Storm water can make a creek swollen and unsafe to step across; clear, shallow, or calm water would not explain using the bridge.

y.B: Calm water would not send the hikers to the bridge.
y.C: Shallow water is what you can step across, which is exactly what they avoided.
y.D: Clear is about how the water looks, not how much of it there is.

VR.q: Because the two accounts ____ each other, the reporter checked which one was accurate.
VR.e: Accounts that contradict each other cannot both be accurate in the same way, so checking is logical; entertaining, copying, or completing one another would not create the stated uncertainty.

y.B: Accounts that completed each other would agree, leaving nothing to check.
y.C: Entertained is about being amusing.
y.D: Copied accounts would say the same thing, so neither could be the wrong one.

VR.q: The watchmaker needed a ____ tool that could lift a gear no wider than a grain of rice.
VR.e: A tiny gear requires a delicate, precise tool; weight, familiarity, and price do not show suitability for fine work.

y.A: Familiar means already known, which says nothing about handling something tiny.
y.C: Heavy is the wrong direction for lifting a gear no wider than a grain of rice.
y.D: Expensive is about price, and the sentence is about what the tool has to do.

VR.q: Nia listened to both sides of the disagreement before deciding, showing that she was ____.
VR.e: Hearing both sides before judging demonstrates fairness; inventiveness and timidity are irrelevant, and impatience conflicts with listening.

y.A: Impatient would mean cutting one side off.
y.B: Inventive is about coming up with new ideas, not about hearing both sides.
y.C: Timid means easily frightened, which does not explain reaching a decision.

VR.q: Before planting the seeds, Raul ____ the rows with small wooden stakes.
VR.e: Marking rows logically happens before planting; harvesting comes later, while watering or erasing does not establish locations.

y.A: Harvesting comes at the end, and the seeds are not yet in the ground.
y.B: Watering is done with water, not with wooden stakes.
y.D: Erased means rubbed out, and there is nothing there yet to remove.

VR.q: The principal's reminder was ____ rather than accusing; it focused on the rule, not on blaming anyone.
VR.e: A neutral reminder avoids accusation and blame; impatience, humor, and indirectness are not established by the clues.

y.A: Impatient describes a mood, and the sentence contrasts with accusing.
y.B: Indirect means not saying a thing plainly, and this reminder stated the rule plainly.
y.D: Humorous means funny, which is not the opposite of accusing.

VR.q: The old diary was ____, with several pages missing and others too faded to read.
VR.e: Missing and unreadable pages make the record incomplete; value, privacy, and binding do not address lost content.

y.A: Valuable is about worth, and what the sentence gives is missing and faded pages.
y.C: Private means not shared; a diary is private whether or not its pages survive.
y.D: Leather-bound describes the cover, not what is inside it.

VR.q: When clouds covered the sun, the temperature began to ____.
VR.e: Less direct sunlight can cause temperature to drop; the other verbs do not sensibly describe temperature in this context.

y.A: Shine is what the sun does, not something a temperature does.
y.C: Pause means to stop for a moment, and a temperature does not pause when the light is cut off.
y.D: Expand means to grow bigger in size.

VR.q: The committee invited a soil expert to ____ whether the vacant lot could support a garden.
VR.e: An expert can assess, or evaluate, the soil's suitability; celebrating, promising, and remembering do not answer the question.

y.B: Remember means to recall, and this question has not been answered before.
y.C: Celebrate would come after a decision.
y.D: Promise would commit to an answer before anyone had looked.

VR.q: The scratch was so ____ that it disappeared after one light coat of polish.
VR.e: Easy removal with one light coat shows the scratch was minor; its shape, age, or shine does not explain the result.

y.B: Recent is about when it happened; an old scratch can be just as shallow.
y.C: Crooked describes the shape of the line, not how deep it goes.
y.D: Shiny describes the polish rather than the scratch.

VR.q: The twins look nearly identical, but their interests are quite ____.
VR.e: But contrasts similar appearance with distinct, or different, interests; the other adjectives do not establish difference.

y.A: Serious does not contrast with looking identical.
y.B: Practical describes a kind of interest, not a difference between two people's.
y.C: Popular is about what others think of them.

VR.q: The ____ cook turned yesterday's rice and a few leftover vegetables into a delicious soup.
VR.e: Turning leftovers into a good meal shows a resourceful cook; gentle, forgetful, and athletic do not explain making much from little.

y.A: Forgetful would not turn yesterday's leftovers into soup.
y.C: Athletic is about the body, not about making do with what is there.
y.D: Gentle is about manner.

VR.q: The new schedule will ____ effect on Monday, when the buses begin arriving earlier.
VR.e: “Take effect” is the correct idiom for beginning to operate; the other verbs do not form the standard expression.

y.A: You make a change, but a schedule takes effect; the phrase is a fixed one.
y.B: Hold does not pair with effect in this way.
y.C: Turn does not pair with effect either.

VR.q: Compared with the rough first draft, the final poster looked ____.
VR.e: Revision makes a final product polished; the other choices do not logically contrast with a rough draft.

y.A: Ordinary does not contrast with rough.
y.B: Accidental means unplanned, and the final poster is the planned one.
y.D: Temporary is about how long a thing lasts.

VR.q: The historian included two letters from the period to ____ her claim about daily life.
VR.e: Period letters provide evidence that can support a historical claim; postponing, shortening, or disguising does not use evidence logically.

y.A: Postpone means to put off; evidence does not delay a claim.
y.B: Shorten is about length.
y.D: Disguise means to hide, and a historian includes letters to show her reasoning.

QR.q: A scooter travels 42 miles on 3 gallons of fuel. A small cart travels 65 miles on 5 gallons. How many more miles per gallon does the scooter travel?
QR.e: The rates are 14 and 13 miles per gallon, so the scooter travels 1 more; 13 and 14 are the individual rates, and 2 comes from subtracting the gallons rather than the rates.

y.A: 2 subtracts the gallons, 5 − 3, instead of the rates.
y.C: 13 is the cart's own rate, 65 ÷ 5.
y.D: 14 is the scooter's own rate, 42 ÷ 3.

QR.q: A mural crew paints 2/7 of a wall Monday and 3/14 Tuesday. What fraction of the wall remains unpainted?
QR.e: Painted = 4/14 + 3/14 = 7/14, leaving 7/14 = 1/2; the other fractions come from subtracting or stopping too early.

y.A: 1/14 subtracts 3/14 from 4/14; the two painted parts are added, then taken from the whole.
y.B: 5/14 is not the remainder; 4/14 + 3/14 = 7/14 painted, which leaves 7/14.
y.C: 8/14 leaves one fourteenth too much; the crew painted 7/14.

QR.q: A theater adds seats to four rehearsal rows in this pattern: 11, 15, 22, 32. If the increases grow by 3 each time, how many seats are in the next row?
QR.e: The increases are 4, 7, and 10, so the next is 13; 32 + 13 = 45. The other choices use a wrong next increase.

y.B: 42 is 32 + 10, repeating the last increase; each one grows by 3, so the next is 13.
y.C: 43 is 32 + 11, and the increases run 4, 7, 10, then 13.
y.D: 46 is 32 + 14, growing the increase by 4 instead of 3.

QR.q: A trail mix uses raisins and seeds in a ratio of 5:4. A 72-ounce batch contains how many ounces of seeds?
QR.e: Nine parts equal 72, so each part is 8; seeds are 4 × 8 = 32.

y.B: 36 halves the total; the 72 ounces split into nine parts, not two.
y.D: 40 is 5 × 8, the raisin share; the question asks for the seeds, which are 4 parts.
y.A: 20 would need each part to be 5 ounces, which makes the batch 45 rather than 72.

QR.q: A library shelf is 60% full when it holds 48 books. How many books fit when the shelf is completely full?
QR.e: If 48 is 60%, the whole is 48 ÷ 0.60 = 80; the distractors add a percentage or use an incorrect scale.

y.A: 72 would make 48 two thirds of the shelf rather than 60%.
y.B: 76 would put 48 at about 63%.
y.C: 78 would put 48 at about 62%.

QR.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 4 blue, 3 green, 2 yellow, and 1 red. What is the probability of not landing on blue?
QR.e: Six of ten sections are not blue, and 6/10 = 3/5; 2/5 is the blue probability, and 4/5 and 7/10 miscount the nonblue sections.

y.A: 2/5 is 4/10, the blue sections; the question asks about the other six.
y.C: 4/5 is 8/10, counting eight as not blue; there are six.
y.D: 7/10 counts seven; the four blue sections leave six of the ten.

QR.q: A club pays a $6 setup fee plus $4 per badge. Its bill is $38. How many badges did it order?
QR.e: Subtract the $6 fee to get $32, then divide by $4 for 8 badges; 6 and 7 mishandle the fee, and 11 adds it instead of undoing it.

y.A: 6 badges cost 6 + 4 × 6 = $30, not $38.
y.B: 7 badges come to $34.
y.D: 11 adds the $6 fee before dividing, 44 ÷ 4; the fee comes off first.

QR.q: Four water samples have an average volume of 26 milliliters. Three contain 21, 24, and 28 milliliters. What is the fourth volume?
QR.e: The total is 4 × 26 = 104; known volumes total 73, leaving 31. The others result from averaging only known values or subtracting incorrectly.

y.B: 25 would make the four total 98; an average of 26 needs 4 × 26 = 104.
y.C: 27 leaves a total of 100, four short of 104.
y.D: 29 leaves a total of 102.

QR.q: A warehouse packs 4,116 pencils equally into 79 cartons. About how many pencils go in each carton?
QR.e: Use 4,000 ÷ 80 = 50; 500 is a place-value error, and 40 or 60 are poorer estimates.

y.B: 500 is ten times too big; 80 × 50 = 4,000, close to 4,116.
y.C: 40 would give about 3,160, well under 4,116.
y.D: 60 would give about 4,740, overshooting it.

QR.q: A map marker at (−4, 2) moves 7 units east and 5 units north. What are its new coordinates?
QR.e: East adds 7 to x and north adds 5 to y, giving (3, 7); the distractors reverse signs, directions, or coordinate changes.

y.A: (−11, 7) moves west instead of east; east adds 7 to −4, giving 3.
y.B: (3, −3) moves south instead of north; north adds 5 to 2, giving 7.
y.D: (1, 9) uses the 5 on x and the 7 on y, swapping the two moves.

QR.q: A rectangular pen has a perimeter of 46 meters and a width of 8 meters. What is its length?

y.A: 7 is 15 − 8, how much longer the length is than the width, not the length itself.
y.B: 19 takes the width off the whole perimeter and halves what is left, (46 − 8) ÷ 2; half the perimeter is 23, and the width comes off that.
y.C: 30 subtracts the width twice, 46 − 8 − 8; halving leaves one length and one width, so only one 8 comes off.

QR.q: Mei presents before Luis. Luis presents before Tori. Which statement must be true?
QR.e: The chain Mei–Luis–Tori guarantees Mei is before Tori; the other choices reverse or contradict the order.

y.A: Tori comes after Luis, who comes after Mei, so Tori cannot be first.
y.C: Luis is before Tori, which makes Tori last rather than Luis.
y.D: Nothing in the chain allows two of them at the same time.

QR.q: Four recipes use 5/12, 7/16, 9/20, and 11/24 cup of oil. Which amount is greatest?
QR.e: The values are about .417, .438, .450, and .458; 11/24 is greatest. The distractors reflect numerator-only or denominator-only comparison.

y.A: 5/12 is about 0.417, the smallest of the four.
y.D: 9/20 is 0.45, still under 11/24.

QR.q: On a trail map, 2.5 centimeters represent 10 kilometers. How far does 7 centimeters represent?
QR.e: The scale is 4 km per cm, so 7 cm represents 28 km; 17.5 km comes from multiplying by 2.5, and 25 km and 35 km use incorrect scales.

y.B: 17.5 is 7 × 2.5, multiplying by the centimeters on the map instead of the 4 km each one stands for.
y.C: 25 would make the scale about 3.6 km per centimeter; it is 10 ÷ 2.5 = 4.
y.D: 35 is 7 × 5, and the scale is 4 km per centimeter.

QR.q: A box holds 4 silver, 7 gold, and 9 copper coins. One coin is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is silver or gold?
QR.e: There are 4 + 7 + 9 = 20 coins, and 4 + 7 = 11 of them are silver or gold, so the probability is 11/20.

y.A: 1/5 is 4/20, the silver coins alone; the draw counts silver or gold.
y.B: 7/20 is the gold coins alone; adding the 4 silver ones makes 11.
y.C: 9/20 is the copper coins — the one color the draw has to avoid.

QR.q: A museum tour offers 3 start times and 4 route choices at each time. How many time-and-route combinations are possible?
QR.e: Each of 3 times pairs with 4 routes, so 3 × 4 = 12; 7 adds the categories, and 16 and 24 overcount.

y.A: 7 is 3 + 4, adding the two lists; pairing multiplies them.
y.C: 16 is 4 × 4, and there are 3 start times.
y.D: 24 is 3 × 4 × 2, doubling pairs that have already been counted.

QR.q: A pump fills 18 liters every 4 minutes at a steady rate. How many liters does it fill in 14 minutes?
QR.e: The rate is 4.5 liters per minute; 4.5 × 14 = 63. The distractors scale only by whole 4-minute blocks or round the rate.

y.A: 54 is 3 × 18, three whole four-minute blocks — 12 minutes rather than 14.
y.B: 56 is not 4.5 × 14; the rate is 18 ÷ 4 = 4.5 liters a minute.
y.C: 60 would need a rate of about 4.3 liters a minute; it is 4.5.

QR.q: Two display lights flash every 8 seconds and every 12 seconds. If they flash together now, after how many seconds will they next flash together?
QR.e: The least common multiple of 8 and 12 is 24; 20 adds the intervals, and 48 and 96 are larger common multiples rather than the next one.

y.A: 20 is 8 + 12, adding the intervals; what is wanted is the first moment both fit.
y.B: 48 is a common multiple of 8 and 12, but 24 comes first.
y.D: 96 is 8 × 12, a common multiple and the largest here; the least is 24.

QR.q: After donating 3/8 of a collection, Sam has 45 cards left. How many cards were in the collection at first?
QR.e: The 45 cards are 5/8 of the original, so 45 × 8/5 = 72; the others treat 45 as the donated part or add incorrectly.

y.B: 60 would leave five eighths as 37.5 cards, not 45.
y.C: 75 would leave five eighths as about 47.
y.D: 120 treats the 45 as the 3/8 donated; they are the 5/8 left.

QR.q: The lap times are 31, 34, 36, 39, and 44 seconds. A sixth time of 50 seconds is added. What is the new median?
QR.e: With six values, average the third and fourth: (36 + 39)/2 = 37.5; 36 and 39 keep a single middle value, and 40 averages the wrong pair.

y.A: 36 is the median of the original five times; with six the middle two are averaged.
y.C: 39 is the fourth of the six values, and it pairs with 36 for an average of 37.5.
y.D: 40 is not the average of 36 and 39, which is 37.5.

QR.q: A rectangular banner is 6 feet by 10 feet. Its length is doubled while its width stays the same. How does its area change?
c: It becomes four times as large.
QR.e: Original area is 60 and new area is 120 square feet, so it doubles; fourfold growth would require doubling both dimensions.

y.A: 50% would be half again as much; doubling the length takes the area from 60 to 120.
y.B: Four times as large needs both dimensions doubled, and only the length changes.
y.C: 10 square feet is a side length read as an area; the area gains 60 square feet.

QR.q: At dawn the temperature was −6°C. By noon it had risen 11 degrees. What was the noon temperature?

y.B: −17 subtracts the 11 instead of adding it; the temperature rose, so it moves up from −6.
y.C: −5 is the right size with the wrong sign: rising 11 degrees from −6 passes zero and lands above it.
y.D: 17 is 6 + 11, which drops the minus on the dawn temperature.

QR.q: In a group of 32 students, 18 play an instrument, 15 sing, and 7 do both. How many do neither?
QR.e: At least one activity = 18 + 15 − 7 = 26, so neither = 32 − 26 = 6.

y.A: 4 follows a slip in the total: 18 + 15 is 33, not 35, so 33 − 7 = 26 and 32 − 26 = 6.
y.B: 7 is the number doing both, which gets subtracted once; it is not the answer.
y.D: 11 is 18 − 7, the instrument-only group, not those doing neither.

QR.q: Every zep is a lum. No lum is square. Which statement must be true?
QR.e: Since all zeps are lums and no lum is square, no zep can be square; the other choices reverse the relation or assume existence.

y.A: The chain runs from zeps to lums and says nothing about what squares are.
y.C: This needs at least one zep to exist, which nothing here promises.
y.D: Nothing rules squares out of existence; they are only kept apart from lums.

QR.q: A $80 backpack is discounted 25%, then a $6 coupon is applied. What is the final price?
QR.e: A 25% discount removes $20, leaving $60; subtracting $6 gives $54. The distractors omit or misorder a reduction.

y.B: 59 is not $60 − $6; a quarter off $80 leaves $60, and the coupon takes $6 from that.
y.C: 60 is the price after the discount, with the coupon still to come off.
y.D: 68 is not the result of either order: 25% of $80 is $20, leaving $60, and $6 more leaves $54.

QR.q: A rental cost is described by 3(2h + 5) − 4. Which expression gives the same cost?
QR.e: Distribute to get 6h + 15, then subtract 4 for 6h + 11; the others fail to distribute or combine constants correctly.

y.A: 6h + 1 is not 15 − 4; distributing gives 6h + 15, and 15 − 4 = 11.
y.B: 5h + 11 has the constant right but never multiplies the 2h by 3, and 3 × 2h = 6h.
y.C: 6h + 15 distributes correctly and then forgets the − 4.

QR.q: A closed cube-shaped gift box has edges 4 inches long. How many square inches of paper cover its six faces exactly?
QR.e: Each face is 4 × 4 = 16 square inches; six faces total 96.

y.A: 24 is 6 × 4, six edges rather than six faces; each face is 4 × 4 = 16.
y.C: 64 is 4 × 4 × 4, the volume of the box; paper covers the surface.
y.D: 128 is 16 × 8, counting eight faces; a cube has six.

QR.q: A game score follows 4, 12, 15, 45, 48, ... by alternating two operations. What is the next score?
QR.e: The rule alternates ×3, +3; after 48, multiply by 3 to get 144. 51 repeats the +3, and 96 and 192 use wrong multipliers.

y.A: 51 is 48 + 3, repeating the + 3; the rules alternate and × 3 is next.
y.B: 96 is 48 × 2, and the rule multiplies by 3.

QR.q: A chef has 3 1/2 liters of soup and fills containers holding 1/4 liter each. How many full containers can be filled?
QR.e: 3 1/2 = 14/4, so fourteen 1/4-liter containers can be filled; the distractors multiply or use only the whole-number part.

y.A: 7 counts halves rather than quarters; there are 14 quarter-liters in 3 1/2.
y.C: 12 counts the three whole liters only and leaves the extra half out.

QR.q: A teacher arranges 286 tiles in rows of 9. How many tiles are left after making as many complete rows as possible?
QR.e: 9 × 31 = 279, leaving 286 − 279 = 7; the other remainders come from nearby multiples or digit shortcuts.

y.C: 2 would need 284 to be a multiple of 9; 279 is the largest one below 286.
y.D: 8 is one over the remainder, which is 7.

QR.q: Team Red's times are 12, 15, 15, 18, 20. Team Blue's are 10, 14, 16, 19, 22. How much greater is Team Blue's range?
QR.e: Red's range is 8 and Blue's is 12, a difference of 4.

y.A: 2 compares the two fastest times, 12 and 10, rather than the ranges.
y.B: 8 is Red's range on its own; the question asks how much greater Blue's is.
y.D: 12 is Blue's range on its own, 22 − 10; Red's is 8, so the gap is 4.

QR.q: A straight path and a diagonal path meet, forming adjacent angles. One angle is 68°. What is the other angle?
QR.e: Adjacent angles on a straight line total 180°, so 180 − 68 = 112°.

y.A: 22 is 90 − 68, which treats the two angles as a right angle; a straight line is 180°.
y.B: 68 assumes the two angles are equal, which happens only when both are 90°.
y.C: 102 falls ten short: 180 − 68 = 112.

QR.q: The first box holds 30 books on 5 shelves. The second box holds 42 books on 7 shelves. Which statement is true?
c: The first box holds more per shelf.
They hold the same number per shelf.
The second box holds 2 more per shelf.
The second box holds 12 more per shelf.
QR.e: Both rates equal 6 books per shelf (30 ÷ 5 = 6 and 42 ÷ 7 = 6).

y.A: Fewer shelves does not mean more on each: 30 ÷ 5 and 42 ÷ 7 both come to 6.
y.C: 2 is the difference in the number of shelves, 7 − 5, not a difference per shelf.
y.D: 12 is the difference in the totals, 42 − 30, which is not a per-shelf figure either.

QR.q: A reservoir rises from 120 centimeters to 150 centimeters. What is the percent increase?
QR.e: The increase is 30, and 30/120 = 25%.

y.B: 20% divides the 30 rise by the new 150; percent increase is measured against the starting 120.
y.C: 30% is the rise in centimeters read as a percent; 30 out of 120 is 25%.
y.D: 80% is 120 ÷ 150, the ratio the other way up.

QR.q: A square rug has an area of 190 square feet. Its side length, in feet, is between which pair of consecutive whole numbers?
