QR.e: 13 × 13 = 169 and 14 × 14 = 196, and 169 < 190 < 196, so the side is between 13 and 14.

y.A: 9 and 10 surround the square root of 95; halving the area is not the same as taking its root.
y.B: 12 and 13 stops at 12 × 12 = 144, which is below 190 — and so is 13 × 13 = 169, so the pair starts at 13.
y.C: 14 and 15 makes 14 the lower end, but 14 × 14 = 196 is already past 190, so 14 is the upper end.

QR.q: A cyclist travels 18 miles per hour for 1 hour 40 minutes. How far does the cyclist travel?
QR.e: 1 hour 40 minutes = 5/3 hours; 18 × 5/3 = 30. 24 miles treats 40 minutes as 1/3 hour, and 27 and 36 miles misconvert the time.

y.A: 24 treats 40 minutes as a third of an hour; it is two thirds, so 18 × 5/3 = 30.
y.B: 27 is 18 × 1.5, reading 40 minutes as half an hour.
y.D: 36 is 18 × 2, a full two hours.

QR.q: A badge can use one of 5 shapes and one of 3 colors, but the star shape cannot be green. How many allowed badges are possible?
QR.e: Normally 5 × 3 = 15 combinations; removing the one forbidden star-green pair leaves 14. The others remove too many or none.

y.B: 8 is 5 + 3, adding the two lists; pairing multiplies them.
y.C: 12 removes three combinations; only one, the green star, is ruled out.
y.D: 15 is the count before the forbidden pair is taken out.

QR.q: A rectangular courtyard is 18 meters by 12 meters. A walker completes 3 laps around it. How far does the walker travel?
QR.e: One lap is 2(18 + 12) = 60 meters; three laps total 180.

y.A: 90 is 3 × 30, going round with only one long and one short side counted; a lap has two of each.
y.C: 648 is 18 × 12 × 3, the area three times over; a lap follows the edges.
y.D: 60 is one lap; the walker does three.

RC.q: Which statement best explains what the students learned from the moth survey?
c: Pond insects are always harder to photograph than meadow moths.
Students should collect wildlife data in daylight, not at night.
The brightest lamp is the most reliable way to count moths.
Discovering an unfair condition helped students improve a survey.
RC.e: The problem, the revision and the lesson are all in [¶2–¶4]. Saying pond insects are always harder to photograph makes a rule out of one detail; moving to daylight contradicts the night survey, which worked once the lamps matched; and the brightest lamp is the very condition that made the first comparison unfair.

y.A: [¶3] says several pond species were hard to see until they settled, which is one evening's observation rather than a rule about every pond insect.
y.B: The night survey worked once the lamps matched; daylight is never suggested.
y.C: The brighter lamp is what made the first comparison unfair — the problem, not the method.

RC.q: Why were the students unable to compare the first station counts fairly?
c: Some teams forgot their notebooks and lost their counts.
The teams used lamps of different brightness.
The moths were released before anyone recorded the time.
The pond station began counting an hour after the others.
RC.e: [¶2] explicitly says Lena's brighter lamp could attract moths from farther away. Lost notebooks and a late start at the pond station are never stated, and releasing the moths before the time was recorded contradicts [¶1], where the students recorded the time before releasing each moth.

y.A: The students carried notebooks and recorded the time; none is lost.
y.C: [¶1] has them record the time and then let each moth fly away, in that order.
y.D: Both stations counted on the same moonless Friday, and no late start is mentioned.

RC.q: What can be inferred about the identical lights used in the second count?
c: They made location, rather than brightness, the meaningful difference.
They guaranteed that every moth in the whole meadow was seen and counted.
They caused every station to attract exactly the same kinds of moths.
They made it unnecessary to photograph any of the visiting moths.
RC.e: Controlling brightness lets location be compared more fairly, as [¶3–¶4] imply. Seeing every moth in the whole meadow and drawing exactly the same kinds of moths at every station are guarantees the passage does not support, and making photographs unnecessary is contradicted by the survey method.

y.B: Identical lamps make the stations comparable; they cannot guarantee that nothing was missed.
y.C: The pond station drew species with narrow wings and muted colors, so the stations still differed.
y.D: Photographing each visitor is the method throughout, and nothing replaces it.

RC.q: In [¶3], “settled” most nearly means:
RC.e: The moths became visible when they landed on the sheet. Paying a debt, making a choice and becoming calm are all real meanings of settled, but none of them fits a moth arriving on a surface.

y.A: Paying a debt is a real meaning of the word, but no money is involved here.
y.B: Making a choice is another real meaning, and a moth choosing the sheet is not what the sentence describes.
y.D: Becoming calm would be about the moth's mood; what the students could not see was the moth until it was on the sheet.

RC.q: Which sequence best describes the development of the passage?
c: A list of moth species is followed by a description of each kind.
An investigation is described, a flaw noticed, the method improved.
Two students argue about the count until a teacher settles it.
A meadow and a pond are compared in each of the four seasons.
RC.e: [¶1] begins the investigation, [¶2] identifies the flaw, and [¶3–¶4] describe the revision and lesson. The other structures are not present.

y.A: Only two kinds of moth are described at all, and then only in passing.
y.C: Nobody argues and no teacher appears; Lena notices the problem and the team fixes it.
y.D: The two counts happen a week apart, not across four seasons.

RC.q: Which choice best summarizes the discovery beneath Bellweather's steps?
c: Why nineteenth-century buildings often had weak stone foundations
How surveyors searched for buried treasure beneath old town halls
How a town identified and preserved an old survey marker
Why Bellweather replaced its town hall with a history museum
RC.e: The identification in [¶1–¶2] and the preservation in [¶3–¶4] are what the passage covers. Weak stone foundations never come up, [¶4] says the stone revealed no buried treasure, and the town hall is never replaced.

y.A: Foundations come up only because a new one had to be poured, and nothing says they were weak.
y.B: [¶4] says the stone revealed no buried treasure.
y.D: The town hall stays, with a glass panel built into its new landing.

RC.q: According to [¶2], why did surveyors place durable markers?
c: To give later mapmakers fixed starting points
To mark where public buildings should be constructed
To decorate the open spaces around the town
To warn people about tunnels running under the town
RC.e: [¶2] directly states that later mapmakers could begin from fixed points. Siting public buildings and warning about tunnels are not given as purposes—and [¶4] denies any tunnel—while decorating the open spaces repeats the residents' mistaken assumption in [¶1].

y.B: The town hall was built around the marker decades later, which is the reverse of the marker showing where to build.
y.C: Decoration is what most residents assumed it was, and Imani suspected otherwise.
y.D: [¶4] says there was no forgotten tunnel.

RC.q: Why would moving the stone reduce its value as a survey record?
c: Its carved 1882 date would become harder to read.
The new glass panel would no longer fit the landing.
The town hall would lose its front entrance and steps.
Its exact position was the information it preserved.
RC.e: [¶2–¶3] show that the marker's carefully measured location made it useful; moving it would destroy that evidence. The carved date, the glass panel and the front steps are all about appearance or construction, not surveying.

y.A: Moving the stone would not touch the carving; what would be lost is where it stood.
y.B: The panel was designed after the decision to leave the stone, so it is the solution rather than the reason.
y.C: A new landing was built either way, so the entrance was never at risk.

RC.q: In [¶4], “quieter” suggests that the stone's importance was:
c: secret from all of the town's residents
related to the silence of the building
less useful than the workers believed
RC.e: [¶4] contrasts the marker with treasure and tunnels, so “quieter” means less dramatic but still meaningful.

y.A: Most residents assumed it was decoration, which is a wrong guess rather than a secret.
y.C: No sound is described anywhere; the word is set against treasure and tunnels.
y.D: [¶4] calls it a useful reference point that the town chose to keep.

RC.q: The author's attitude toward the town's solution is best described as:
RC.e: [¶3–¶4] presents the glass panel as preserving both practical and historical value. Doubtful and impatient conflict with that praise, and no humor supports amused.

y.A: The last paragraph says the town preserved both a reference point and a piece of its story, which is praise.
y.B: Nothing in the passage is played for humour.
y.C: The solution took an archivist, an engineer and a crew, and the passage describes that patiently.

RC.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
c: A brief conversation helps Mara see her nervousness and begin preparing.
Mara decides that drawing pictures is easier than writing stories.
A long train delay keeps Mara from reaching the festival on time.
A stranger on the train persuades Mara to give away her story.
RC.e: [¶2–¶4] shows the sketcher's comment helping Mara shift from avoidance to rehearsal. Nothing else on the list happens: she does not choose drawing over writing, the train is not delayed, and no stranger takes her story.

y.B: Mara says nothing about preferring drawing, and by the end she is reading her own paragraph aloud.
y.C: The train reaches the festival town, and no delay is mentioned.
y.D: The story stays in her hands; the man only turns his sketch toward her.

RC.q: Which action most clearly shows Mara avoiding practice at the beginning?
c: She chose a window seat before the train left.
She watched the sketcher's pencil move quickly.
She reorganized her pencils instead of reading.
She kept her story inside an envelope in her pocket.
RC.e: [¶1] lists pencil organizing among distractions from the view and story. The window seat, the watching and the envelope in her pocket may all go with being nervous, but none of them replaces practice as clearly.

y.A: Choosing the seat happens before the train leaves and avoids nothing.
y.B: Watching the sketcher is what leads to the conversation that helps her.
y.D: The envelope in her pocket is where the story lives; checking it twice is the avoidance, not keeping it there.

RC.q: What does Mara learn from watching the scenery in [¶4]?
c: The festival town is surrounded mostly by open farmland.
Separate moments can still form a complete experience.
Train travel moves too fast for careful observation.
Reading aloud is easier outdoors than on a train.
RC.e: The changing views “held together,” paralleling how selected moments can make a drawing or story. The open farmland is incidental, and neither the claim that train travel is too fast for careful observation nor the one about reading aloud outdoors is supported.

y.A: Farmhouses do flash past, but the passage uses them to make a point about the trip holding together.
y.C: She does observe, and what she notices is that no single view lasts long and the trip still holds.
y.D: She reads under her breath on the train, and nothing outdoors is compared with it.

RC.q: In [¶2], “escape” suggests that Mara was holding the envelope:
RC.e: If the envelope looked as though it might escape, Mara must have been gripping it tightly. Loosely and carelessly are the opposite, and secretly concerns visibility rather than grip.

y.A: Loosely is the opposite; an envelope held loosely would not look as though it might get away.
y.B: Carelessly would suggest she did not mind losing it, and she checks it twice.
y.C: Secretly is about who can see it, whereas the word here is about her grip.

RC.q: The mood at the end of the passage is best described as:
RC.e: Mara practices, reaches the town, and stops shaking in [¶4], showing calm improvement rather than gloom, mystery, or extreme excitement.

y.A: The paper no longer shook by the end, which is an improvement rather than a gloom.
y.B: Nothing is left unexplained: a man sketches and Mara practises.
y.D: She reads under her breath, which is quiet rather than wild.

RC.q: Which statement best summarizes Suri's solution and its result?
c: Outdoor courts are better than halls for every dance rehearsal.
A chalk diagram helped a choreographer plan movement before rehearsal.
Rain forced the dance group to cancel its Saturday performance.
The dancers invented a new game using colored chalk arrows.
RC.e: The chalk diagram covers Suri's planning method and its result in [¶1–¶4]. Saying outdoor courts are better for every rehearsal overstates the method, and the cancelled performance and the invented chalk game contradict the events.

y.A: [¶4] says the chalk did not replace rehearsal, so the court is not better for everything.
y.C: Rain erased the drawing, but Suri had photographed it and Saturday's rehearsal went ahead.
y.D: No game is invented; the arrows are a plan.

RC.q: Which question could the chalk plan NOT answer?
c: Where should each dancer begin the piece?
Do two paths cross on the same count?
Which routes show dancers moving backward?
Does a lift feel safe to the dancers?
RC.e: [¶4] explicitly says the drawing could not show whether a lift felt safe. Where each dancer begins, whether two paths cross on the same count, and which routes run backward are exactly the spatial facts the circles, intersecting arrows and dotted lines represent.

y.A: The circles drawn on the pavement are the starting positions.
y.B: The plan caught exactly that — two arrows meeting at the same place on the same count.
y.C: White dotted lines showed the moments when dancers moved backward.

RC.q: Why was saving hall time especially important?
c: The hall was available only once a week.
The box of sidewalk chalk was expensive.
The dancers disliked rehearsing in the hall.
The final performance had already taken place.
RC.e: [¶1] says the hall was available only on Saturdays, so solving spatial problems beforehand protected limited rehearsal time. Nothing is said about the chalk being expensive or the dancers disliking the hall, and the performance is still ahead of them.

y.B: A box of sidewalk chalk is mentioned without any price.
y.C: Nothing is said about how the dancers felt about the hall.
y.D: Saturday's rehearsal is still ahead when Suri draws the plan.

RC.q: In [¶4], “making invisible movement visible” means the chalk drawing:
c: allowed dancers to move without being seen
glowed when the hall lights were turned off
represented planned motion on the ground
RC.e: The circles and arrows represented motion before it happened. Moving without being seen and glowing in the dark interpret “invisible” literally, and recording a finished performance confuses planning with recording.

y.A: That reads invisible literally; it is the movement, not the dancers, that had nowhere to be seen.
y.B: No glowing chalk appears, and the drawing was outdoors on pavement.
y.D: The drawing came before the dancers arrived, so there was no performance to record.

RC.q: How does the author organize the middle of the passage?
c: By comparing four different choreographers and their styles
By describing the plan, the problem, and Suri's revision
By listing the rules for using a public basketball court
By arguing that dancers should always rehearse alone
RC.e: [¶2–¶3] moves from drawing the map to discovering a collision and revising a path. The other structures are absent.

y.A: Only Suri appears in the passage.
y.C: The court is where she works, and no rules for using it are given.
y.D: [¶4] saves hall time for the problems only dancers can answer, which is the opposite of rehearsing alone.

RC.q: Which choice best connects the roof's function with the students' investigation?
c: Students discover that every school bus shelter should be built of wood.
A leaking shelter roof creates a safety problem for waiting students.
A planted roof manages rainwater and teaches students about starting conditions.
The environmental club replaces the school's bus shelter after three storms.
RC.e: The planted-roof summary combines the roof's function [¶2] with the students' learning [¶3–¶4]. Building every shelter of wood and replacing the shelter are unsupported—the club measured rather than rebuilt—and the leaking roof mistakes delayed release for a leak.

y.A: Wood never comes up; the roof is covered with shallow trays of low-growing plants.
y.B: [¶2] says it was working as designed, so the dripping was not a leak.
y.D: The club measures and then plans a comparison; it rebuilds nothing.

RC.q: Why did the largest storm not fill the barrel the most?
c: Dry soil absorbed much of its rain.
Students emptied the barrel during the storm.
The plants blocked every drainage channel.
Strong wind blew the barrel onto its side.
RC.e: [¶3] states that dry conditions let the soil absorb much of the largest storm. Nobody empties the barrel, no drainage channel is blocked, and the barrel never falls over.

y.B: Nobody empties the barrel; the students measure what is in it after each storm.
y.C: The channels released water slowly, which is how the roof is meant to work.
y.D: Windy days are mentioned as what dried the soil, not as something that moved the barrel.

RC.q: Why will the club compare two shelters in spring?
c: To determine which shelter has more students waiting beneath it
To find out whether a bare metal roof can collect any rain
To prove that the planted shelter never becomes warm in spring
To isolate whether the planted roof is related to temperature
RC.e: Comparing planted and unplanted shelters provides a reference for the temperature question in [¶4]. Counting students and testing whether bare metal collects any rain ask different questions, and proving the planted shelter never becomes warm claims proof before evidence.

y.A: How many students wait under each shelter has nothing to do with temperature.
y.B: [¶2] already says a bare metal roof sends most water rushing off at once.
y.C: The club predicts the planted roof may be cooler, and a prediction is not a proof.

RC.q: In [¶3], “runoff” most nearly means:
c: soil carried away by strong wind
water that flows off a surface
a test that ends too early
RC.e: The passage discusses rain leaving the roof through channels, so runoff is water flowing from a surface. Wind-blown soil, spreading plants and a test that ends early all miss the water-management context.

y.A: Wind appears only as what dried the soil; this word is about water leaving a surface.
y.C: The plants stay in their shallow trays throughout.
y.D: Nothing ends early; three storms were measured.

RC.q: Why does the author include the students' future temperature study in [¶4]?
c: To show that recording conditions can guide a new investigation
To prove that the school's rain barrel was installed incorrectly
To introduce a disagreement between two student science clubs
To explain why spring storms are heavier than winter storms
RC.e: [¶4] transfers the students' lesson about starting conditions to a new test.

y.B: The barrel worked. What surprised the students was which storm filled it most.
y.C: Only one club appears in the passage.
y.D: Nothing compares spring storms with winter ones.

MA.q: A reading drive collected 4,608 books in spring and 2,795 in fall. How many books were collected altogether?
MA.e: 4,608 + 2,795 = 7,403; 7,393 and 7,503 reflect carrying errors, and 6,403 drops one thousand.

y.B: 7,393 is 10 short: the units make 8 + 5 = 13, so a ten carries into 0 + 9 and that column reaches 10.
y.C: 6,403 is 1,000 short; the hundreds make 6 + 7 + 1 = 14, which carries a thousand into 4 + 2.
y.D: 7,503 is 100 over; the hundreds column comes to 14, leaving a 4.

MA.q: What is 7/8 − 1/3?
MA.e: With denominator 24, 21/24 − 8/24 = 13/24.

y.A: 6/5 subtracts the denominators as well as the numerators, (7 − 1)/(8 − 3); once the denominators match, only the numerators are subtracted.
y.B: 5/8 keeps eighths and takes something other than 1/3 away from them; over 24, 1/3 is 8/24, not 2/24.
y.D: 4/5 uses a denominator that 8 and 3 do not share; the smallest they do share is 24.

MA.q: Six identical notebooks cost $4.75 each. What is the total cost?

y.A: 24.75 multiplies only the dollars, 4 × 6 = 24, and then puts the 75 cents back once instead of six times.
y.C: 28.05 has the dollars right and the cents digits swapped; 0.75 × 6 = 4.50, so the cents end in .50.
y.D: 30.75 rounds $4.75 up to $5 for $30 and then adds the 75 cents back — but rounding up had already added 25 cents six times.

MA.q: A printer places 945 cards equally into 15 boxes. How many cards are in each box?
MA.e: 945 ÷ 15 = 63 because 15 × 63 = 945; the other choices come from incomplete division or rounding.

y.A: 53 is ten too few: 15 × 53 = 795, a full 150 short of 945.
y.B: 60 gives 15 × 60 = 900, leaving 45 still to share — three more per box.
y.C: 65 overshoots: 15 × 65 = 975.

MA.q: A 240-page book has illustrations on 35% of its pages. How many pages have illustrations?

y.A: 72 is 30% of 240 and stops there; the other 5% is 12 more.
y.B: 80 is a third of 240, and 35% is a little more than a third.
y.D: 96 is 40% of 240, one step too far.

MA.q: What is the greatest common factor of 36 and 54?
MA.e: Common factors include 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, and 18; 18 is greatest. 9 and 6 are common but not greatest, and 108 is a multiple.

y.B: 9 is a common factor but not the greatest; 18 divides both numbers as well.
y.C: 6 is common and smaller still; 18 goes into 36 and 54 too.
y.D: 108 is a common multiple of 36 and 54, not a factor of either.

MA.e: 1/4 + 2/3 = 3/12 + 8/12 = 11/12, and whole parts total 5. The distractors add denominators or regroup incorrectly.

y.A: 5 3/7 adds the tops and the bottoms of the fractions; quarters and thirds both go over 12 first.
y.B: 6 1/12 carries a whole that is not there: 3/12 + 8/12 = 11/12, still under 1.
y.C: 5 5/7 also adds denominators; over twelfths the fractions make 11/12.

MA.q: Which fraction is equal to 0.625?
MA.e: 0.625 = 625/1000 = 5/8; 3/5 and 5/6 are nearby values, and 625/10 places the decimal incorrectly.

y.A: 3/5 is 0.6 — close, but 0.625 is 625/1000, which reduces to 5/8.
y.C: 5/6 is about 0.833, well above 0.625.
y.D: 625/10 is 62.5; three decimal places make 0.625 into 625/1000.

MA.q: Solve 5x + 7 = 42.
MA.e: Subtract 7 from both sides to get 5x = 35, then divide by 5 for x = 7.

y.A: 5 divides 35 by the 7 rather than by the 5; the 5 is what multiplies x.
y.C: 9 follows from taking 42 − 7 as 45; it is 35, and 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
y.D: 49/5 adds the 7 to 42 instead of subtracting it; a + 7 moves across as − 7.

MA.q: What is the value of 3x² − 5 when x = 4?
MA.e: 4² = 16, then 3 × 16 − 5 = 43. 19 squares after multiplying incorrectly, and 31 and 37 reflect arithmetic errors.

y.A: 19 comes from taking 4² as 8 — doubling instead of squaring. 4² is 16, so 3 × 16 − 5 = 43.
y.B: 31 is not 3 × 16 − 5; squaring the 4 first gives 16, and 48 − 5 = 43.
y.C: 37 falls six short: 3 × 16 = 48, then take away 5.

MA.q: Which expression is equivalent to 6(y + 3)?
MA.e: Multiply both terms by 6: 6y + 18. 6y + 3 fails to distribute to the 3, and 9y and 18y combine unlike terms.

y.B: 6y + 3 multiplies the y by 6 but leaves the 3 alone, and 6 × 3 = 18.
y.C: 9y adds the 6 and the 3 and hangs a y on the result; the terms inside the bracket stay separate.
y.D: 18y multiplies both terms by 6 and then merges them, but 6y and 18 are unlike terms.

MA.q: Which inequality is equivalent to n/4 < 6?
MA.e: Multiplying both sides by positive 4 gives n < 24; n > 24 reverses the sign, and n < 2 and n > 10 use wrong operations.

y.A: n < 2 divides where it should multiply; n/4 < 6 means n is under 4 × 6.
y.B: n > 24 reverses the sign; multiplying both sides by a positive 4 leaves the direction alone.
y.D: n > 10 reverses the sign and uses 4 + 6 rather than 4 × 6.

MA.q: Two angles of a triangle measure 48° and 67°. What is the third angle?
MA.e: Triangle angles total 180°; 180 − (48 + 67) = 65°. The distractors reflect addition or subtraction errors.

y.A: 55 subtracts 125 from 180; 48 + 67 is 115.
y.B: 61 falls four short: 180 − 115 = 65.
y.C: 63 is two short; the two known angles total 115, not 117.

MA.q: A parallelogram has a base of 13 cm and a perpendicular height of 8 cm. What is its area?
MA.e: Area = base × perpendicular height = 13 × 8 = 104 cm².

y.A: 42 is 2 × (13 + 8), a perimeter; area multiplies the base by the height.
y.C: 84 is not 13 × 8; multiplying those out gives 104.
y.D: 208 is 13 × 8 × 2, the area counted twice; a parallelogram needs no doubling or halving.

MA.q: A circular table has a diameter of 18 feet. What is its radius?
MA.e: Radius is half the diameter, so 18 ÷ 2 = 9 feet.

y.A: 36 is 18 × 2, doubling the diameter instead of halving it.
y.B: 18 is the diameter itself; a radius reaches only from the centre to the edge.
y.D: 6 is 18 ÷ 3; a radius is half the diameter, not a third.

MA.q: A storage box is 7 feet long, 4 feet wide, and 3 feet high. What is its volume?
MA.e: Volume = 7 × 4 × 3 = 84 cubic feet. 28 ft³ multiplies only length and width (7 × 4), while 42 ft³ and 98 ft³ first add all three dimensions (7 + 4 + 3 = 14) and then multiply by the height (14 × 3 = 42) or the length (14 × 7 = 98) instead of multiplying all three dimensions.

y.B: 28 is 7 × 4, the floor of the box; volume multiplies that by the height of 3.
y.C: 42 is 14 × 3, adding the three dimensions (7 + 4 + 3) and then multiplying by the height.
y.D: 98 is 14 × 7, adding the three dimensions and then multiplying by the length.

MA.q: A ribbon is 2.35 meters long. How many centimeters long is it?
MA.e: One meter is 100 centimeters, so 2.35 × 100 = 235 cm.

y.A: 23.5 multiplies by 10; a meter holds 100 centimeters.
y.B: 2.35 leaves the number alone; centimeters are smaller than meters, so the count goes up.

MA.q: A workshop begins at 3:40 p.m. and lasts 2 hours 35 minutes. When does it end?
MA.e: 3:40 + 2 hours = 5:40, plus 35 minutes = 6:15. The distractors omit time or fail to regroup 60 minutes.

y.A: 5:15 adds 1 hour 35 rather than 2 hours 35.
y.B: 5:55 adds only 15 minutes past 5:40; there are 35 to add.
y.C: 6:05 adds 25 minutes past 5:40 rather than 35.

MA.q: What is the mean of 12, 15, 17, 20, and 21?
MA.e: The sum is 85, and 85 ÷ 5 = 17. The other choices result from choosing a middle or dividing incorrectly.

y.A: 16 would need a total of 80; 12 + 15 + 17 + 20 + 21 is 85.
y.C: 18 would need a total of 90.
y.D: 19 would need a total of 95, ten more than there is.

MA.q: A fair spinner is numbered 1 through 8. What is the probability of spinning an even number?
MA.e: Four of eight outcomes—2, 4, 6, 8—are even, so 4/8 = 1/2. The distractors miscount favorable outcomes.

y.B: 1/4 counts two even numbers; from 1 to 8 there are four — 2, 4, 6 and 8.
y.C: 3/8 counts three; 8 itself is even, which makes four.
y.D: 5/8 counts five, one more than there are.

MA.q: The number of minutes spent practicing over seven days was 18, 24, 18, 30, 21, 18, and 27. What is the mode?
MA.e: Eighteen appears three times, more than any other value. 21, 24 and 30 each appear once — the mode is the value that turns up most often, not the largest or the last.

y.A: 21 appears once, and the mode is the value that appears most often.
y.B: 24 also appears just once.
y.C: 30 is the largest value and appears once; the mode is about frequency, not size.

MA.q: In which quadrant is the point (−5, −2)?
MA.e: A negative x-coordinate and negative y-coordinate place the point in Quadrant III. The others correspond to different sign pairs.

y.A: Quadrant I has both coordinates positive.
y.B: Quadrant II has a negative x and a positive y, and here y is −2.
y.D: Quadrant IV has a positive x and a negative y, and here x is −5.

MA.q: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have?
MA.e: Each vertex-to-opposite-side-midpoint axis gives one line, for 5 total.

y.A: 1 counts a single axis; a regular pentagon has one through each of its five vertices.
y.C: 10 counts every axis twice, once from the vertex and once from the midpoint, but it is the same line both ways.
y.D: 0 would be right for an irregular pentagon; a regular one has five equal sides and five axes.

MA.q: A 10-by-8-meter rectangular patio has a 3-by-2-meter rectangular garden removed from one corner. What is the remaining patio area?
MA.e: Full area is 80 m² and removed area is 6 m², leaving 74 m². 80 m² ignores the removal, and 68 m² and 70 m² subtract dimensions or the wrong area.

y.A: 68 takes 12 away rather than 6; the garden is 3 × 2 = 6 square meters.
y.B: 70 takes 10 away, and the removed piece is 6 square meters.
y.D: 80 is the whole patio with nothing removed.

MA.e: Multiply and divide first: 18 − 12 + 4 = 10. 13 and 19 change the operation order, and 64 combines the numbers without precedence.

y.B: 13 is not 18 − 12 + 4, which comes to 10.
y.C: 19 is what working strictly left to right gives — (18 − 3) × 4 = 60, then + 16 = 76, then ÷ 4 — instead of multiplying and dividing first.
y.D: 64 is 16 × 4; that term is divided, not multiplied.

MA.q: Which is the prime factorization of 180?
MA.e: 180 = 4 × 45 = 2² × 3² × 5, and all factors are prime. 2 × 3 × 30, 2² × 45 and 3² × 20 each still leave a composite factor — 30, 45 and 20 — so none of them is a full prime factorization.

y.A: 2 × 3 × 30 does make 180, but 30 is not prime — it is 2 × 3 × 5.
y.C: 2² × 45 leaves 45, which is 3 × 3 × 5.
y.D: 3² × 20 leaves 20, which is 2 × 2 × 5.

MA.sk: fractions—fraction of a fraction in context
MA.q: A class uses 3/5 of 45 sheets of paper. Of the sheets used, 2/3 are blue. How many blue sheets are used?
MA.e: 3/5 of 45 is 27, and 2/3 of 27 is 18. 27 stops after the first fraction, and 12 and 15 apply the fractions incorrectly.

y.A: 12 is neither step; 3/5 of 45 is 27, and 2/3 of 27 is 18.
y.B: 15 is not 2/3 of 27, which comes to 18.
y.D: 27 comes from taking 3/5 of 45 and stopping there; two thirds of those 27 are blue.

MA.q: On a drawing, 1 centimeter represents 250 centimeters. A hallway measures 6 centimeters on the drawing. How long is the actual hallway in meters?

y.A: 1.5 is out by a factor of ten; 1,500 centimeters is 15 meters.
y.C: 150 divides 1,500 by 10; a meter is 100 centimeters.
y.B: 6.25 is not 1,500 centimeters in meters; 6 × 250 = 1,500, and 1,500 ÷ 100 = 15.

MA.q: Twelve of 30 survey responses chose option A. What percent chose option A?

y.A: 30% is the number of responses, not a percentage of them; 12 out of 30 is 40%.
y.C: 60% is the 18 who chose something else; the question asks about the 12.
y.D: 75% is not 12 out of 30, which comes to 40%.

MA.q: A train travels 156 miles in 3 hours at a constant speed. What is its speed?
MA.e: Speed = 156 ÷ 3 = 52 mph.

y.B: 53 is one too many — 53 × 3 = 159, not 156.
y.C: 78 is 156 ÷ 2; the journey took 3 hours.
y.D: 468 is 156 × 3, multiplying the hours in instead of dividing them out.

VR.q: ADAPTABLE most nearly means:
VR.e: Adaptable means able to adjust, so flexible is precise; the distractors describe privacy, age, or accuracy.

y.A: Secretive means keeping things hidden.
y.C: Exact means precise, which is close to the opposite of bending to fit.
y.D: Ancient means very old.

VR.q: BARREN most nearly means:
VR.e: Barren land produces little or nothing; the other choices concern location, population, or worth.

y.A: Crowded means full of people or things, and barren land is nearly empty.
y.B: Valuable means worth a lot.
y.C: Distant means far away, which is about position.

VR.q: COMMENCE most nearly means:
VR.e: Commence means to begin; compare and gather are different actions, while delay opposes beginning.

y.A: Compare means to set side by side.
y.C: Gather means to collect together, which may happen before something begins.
y.D: Delay means to put off — the opposite of starting.

VR.q: METICULOUS most nearly means:
VR.e: Meticulous describes extremely careful attention to detail; the distractors describe luck, sound, or mood.

y.A: Cheerful means in good spirits.
y.C: Quiet means making little sound, and careful work can be noisy.
y.D: Fortunate means lucky, the opposite sort of explanation for getting something exactly right.

VR.q: ELATED most nearly means:
VR.e: Elated means extremely joyful; exhaustion, confusion, and readiness do not express happiness.

y.B: Puzzled means confused.
y.C: Prepared means ready in advance.
y.D: Exhausted means worn out — nearly the opposite of being lifted up with joy.

VR.q: FRUGAL most nearly means:
VR.e: Frugal means careful about spending, closest to thrifty; wealth and elegance are unrelated, and wasteful is the opposite.

y.A: Wealthy means having a lot of money, and a frugal person may be rich or poor.
y.B: Elegant means graceful or stylish.
y.C: Wasteful is the opposite: using more than is needed.

VR.q: AMIABLE most nearly means:
VR.e: An amiable person is friendly and pleasant; the other choices describe size, commonness, or speed.

y.A: Ordinary means usual or unremarkable.
y.B: Enormous means very large.
y.C: Hurried means rushed.

VR.q: HOSTILE most nearly means:
VR.e: Hostile means unfriendly or opposing; harmless weakens the meaning, while uncertain and distant are unrelated.

y.A: Distant means far away, or reserved in manner; hostile goes further than merely cool.
y.C: Uncertain means unsure.
y.D: Harmless means unable to do damage, which is the opposite.

VR.q: LOFTY most nearly means:
VR.e: Lofty means very high or elevated; height does not require hollowness, heaviness, or completeness.

y.A: Heavy means weighing a lot.
y.B: Complete means whole, with nothing missing.
y.C: Hollow means empty inside.

VR.q: JAGGED most nearly means:
VR.e: Jagged describes a rough, sharply uneven edge; polish, width, and strength are separate qualities.

y.B: Polished means smooth — the opposite of a jagged edge.
y.C: Fragile means easily broken, and a jagged rock can be very hard.
y.D: Narrow is about width.

VR.q: OMIT most nearly means:
VR.e: To omit something is to leave it out; complaining, hurrying, and wandering are unrelated actions.

y.A: Complain means to express dissatisfaction.
y.B: Wander means to move about without a fixed course.
y.C: Hurry means to move fast.

VR.q: MEAGER most nearly means:
VR.e: Meager means too small in amount, so small is closest; balanced, fresh, and useful do not indicate a lack.

y.A: Useful means serving a purpose, and a meagre amount can still be useful.
y.B: Balanced means evenly arranged.
y.D: Fresh means new or recently made.

VR.q: TRANQUIL most nearly means:
VR.e: Tranquil means calm and peaceful; hidden, uncertain, and ordinary describe different qualities.

y.A: Hidden means out of sight.
y.B: Uncertain means unsure, which is nearer to unsettled than to calm.
y.C: Ordinary means usual or unremarkable.

VR.q: PERIL most nearly means:
VR.e: Peril is serious danger; shelter may protect from peril, while journey and argument are not synonyms.

y.A: Shelter is protection from danger — the opposite.
y.B: Journey means a trip; a journey may hold peril without being peril.
y.D: Argument means a disagreement in words.

VR.q: RESTORE most nearly means:
VR.e: To restore is to return something to a good condition, often by repairing it; the other verbs do not express renewal.

y.B: Borrow means to take for a while and give back.
y.C: Divide means to split into parts.
y.D: Announce means to make public.

VR.q: SINCERE most nearly means:
VR.e: Sincere words or feelings are genuine; skill, caution, and formality do not guarantee honesty.

y.A: Cautious means careful of danger.
y.C: Formal is about style and manners; a formal note can be insincere and a rough one sincere.
y.D: Skillful means good at something.

VR.q: VANISH most nearly means:
VR.e: To vanish is to disappear from sight; shrinking and traveling may change appearance or location, while arrive is unrelated.

y.A: Shrink means to get smaller, and a thing can shrink and still be there.
y.B: Arrive means to reach a place — the opposite.
y.D: Travel means to move from place to place.

VR.q: The mystery's first chapter was ____, but the ending explained everything.
VR.e: But signals contrast with an ending that explained everything, so confusing fits; brief, complete, and familiar do not create that contrast.

y.A: Complete does not contrast with an ending that explains everything.
y.B: Brief means short, and shortness is not what an explanation puts right.
y.D: Familiar means already known, which needs no explaining.

VR.q: The sidewalk was still wet, so Milo stepped ____ around the puddles.
VR.e: Wet pavement and puddles call for cautious movement; the distractors do not address the risk.

y.A: Noisily is about sound, not about care around puddles.
y.C: Proudly describes how he felt about himself.
y.D: Randomly would be the opposite of choosing where to step.

VR.q: The two recipes called for exactly the same ingredients and steps; there was no ____ between them.
VR.e: Calling for exactly the same ingredients and steps means no difference; promise, distance, and purpose are not defined by the clue.

y.B: Distance would be about how far apart the recipes sat, not how alike they were.
y.C: Promise does not fit; nothing here was promised.
y.D: Purpose is what a recipe is for, and the sentence is about the two being identical in what they contain.

VR.q: Grandpa keeps his childhood drawings in a sealed box to ____ them for the family.
VR.e: A sealed box helps preserve, or protect, the drawings for the future; measuring, releasing, or coloring them does not explain keeping them safe.

y.A: Colouring the drawings would change them rather than keep them.
y.C: Measure means to find the size of, which a sealed box does not do.
y.D: Release means to let go — the opposite of keeping them safe.

VR.q: Mei returned each borrowed tool clean and on time, proving she was ____.
VR.e: Consistently caring for and returning borrowed items shows dependability; the other traits are unsupported.

y.A: Talkative is about how much she says.
y.B: Inventive is about coming up with new ideas, not about keeping to an arrangement.
y.D: Adventurous is about taking risks.

VR.q: From the hilltop, the distant lighthouse looked so ____ that it seemed no larger than a pencil.
VR.e: Appearing pencil-sized supplies a size clue for tiny; brightness, strength, and loneliness are not established.

y.B: Bright is about light, and the clue is that it seemed no larger than a pencil.
y.C: Lonely is a feeling about the lighthouse, not a description of its size from far off.
y.D: Sturdy means strongly built, which distance does not change.

VR.q: Before signing the form, Luis paused to ____ every line.
VR.e: Reviewing a form logically comes before signing; folding, copying, or skipping lines does not check it.

y.A: Skip means to pass over — the opposite of pausing at every line.
y.B: Fold is something done to paper, not to what it says.
y.D: Copy means to reproduce, and he is about to sign rather than duplicate it.

VR.q: The critic's comments were firm but ____, offering clear ways to improve the play.
VR.e: Suggestions for improvement make criticism constructive; the distractors do not explain its usefulness.

y.B: Amusing means funny, which is not what offering ways to improve amounts to.
y.C: Hesitant means unsure, and the comments were firm.
y.D: Secretive means keeping things hidden, and these were given plainly.

VR.q: The detective tried to ____ the owner of the unlabeled suitcase by checking its contents.
VR.e: Examining contents can identify the owner; imitation, invitation, and warning do not solve the ownership question.

y.A: Inviting someone requires knowing who they are already.
y.B: Warn means to tell of a danger, and the detective does not yet know whom to tell.
y.C: Imitate means to copy.

VR.q: The room looked plain at noon, yet candlelight made it appear warm and ____.
VR.e: Yet contrasts plainness with a positive atmosphere, so inviting fits; the other choices continue or add negative traits.

y.B: Empty goes with plain rather than against it, and the sentence turns on a contrast.
y.C: Unfinished also fits the plain look, not the warm one.
y.D: Narrow is about width, which candlelight does not change.

VR.q: The small nation wanted to write its own laws rather than follow another country's, so it declared itself ____.
VR.e: Wanting to make its own laws leads a nation to declare itself independent; official, distant, and cheerful do not follow from that goal.

y.B: Distant is about how far away it is.
y.C: Official means formally recognized, which a country under another's laws can still be.
y.D: Cheerful describes a mood.

VR.q: The fallen branch ____ the narrow trail, forcing hikers to climb around it.
VR.e: Having to climb around the branch shows that it blocked the trail; the other verbs do not cause the detour.

y.A: Decorated would not force anyone to climb around.
y.C: A branch does not follow a trail, and following would not be in the way.
y.D: Measured means found the size of, which a fallen branch cannot do.

VR.q: Helmets are required at the bike park, but knee pads are ____; each rider chooses whether to wear them.
VR.e: Since each rider chooses, the knee pads are optional, in contrast with required helmets; costly, modern, and popular do not describe something left to choice.

y.A: Modern is about how new they are.
y.B: Popular is about how many riders like them, not about whether they must be worn.
y.D: Costly is about price, and the sentence is about the choice each rider makes.

VR.q: The path was ____: it curved so often that travelers could not see far ahead.
VR.e: Frequent curves define a winding path; slope, shade, and mud are not mentioned.

y.A: Muddy is about the surface, not about curves.
y.B: Shaded is about light, and shade does not stop you seeing along a straight path.
y.C: Steep is about slope, and a steep straight path lets you see a long way.

VR.q: At the end of the meeting, the secretary read the decisions aloud to ____ the group's agreement.
VR.e: Reading decisions aloud can confirm shared agreement; the other verbs oppose or delay that purpose.

y.A: Postpone means to put off, and the meeting is ending.
y.B: Confuse is the opposite of what reading the decisions aloud achieves.
y.D: Challenge means to dispute, and the secretary is recording what was agreed.

VR.q: When the first plan failed, the team had to ____ a different approach.
VR.e: To adopt an approach is to choose and begin using it; the distractors mean dismantle, miss, or forecast.

y.B: Predict means to say what will happen, and the team needs to act rather than forecast.
y.C: Take apart is something you would do to the failed plan, not to the new approach.
y.D: Overlook means to miss or ignore — the opposite of taking one up.

VR.q: The model was imperfect; ____, it revealed where the bridge needed extra support.
VR.e: Nevertheless shows that the model was useful despite its flaw; the other transitions express comparison, alternative, or simultaneous time.

y.A: Otherwise means in other circumstances, and the sentence needs a phrase for in spite of that.
y.C: Similarly signals agreement between two things, and here the two halves pull against each other.
y.D: Meanwhile is about time running alongside, not about a contrast.

QR.q: Red and blue flags are hung in a ratio of 3:5. If 64 flags are hung, how many are red?
QR.e: Eight ratio parts make 64, so each is 8 and red is 3×8=24; 40 is blue, while 32 and 48 misuse the ratio.

y.B: 32 is half of 64; the ratio is 3 to 5, not 1 to 1.
y.C: 40 is 5 × 8, the blue flags.
y.D: 48 is 6 × 8, twice the red share; red is 3 parts.

QR.q: Six identical jars of paint cost $16.50. At the same rate, what do ten jars cost?
QR.e: One jar costs $2.75, so ten cost $27.50; the distractors add quantities or scale the price incorrectly.

y.A: 26.50 would make one jar $2.65; $16.50 ÷ 6 is $2.75.
y.C: 30.00 is $2.50 over; ten jars at $2.75 come to $27.50.
y.D: 33.00 is 2 × $16.50, which buys twelve jars rather than ten.

QR.q: A tank is 7/10 full. Water equal to 2/5 of the tank's total capacity is used. What fraction of the tank remains filled?
QR.e: 2/5 of the tank = 4/10, so 7/10 − 4/10 = 3/10 remains.

y.B: 1/5 is 2/10, from taking the 5 in 2/5 away from the 7 in 7/10; 2/5 has to become 4/10 first.
y.C: 1/2 is 5/10, from subtracting 2/10 rather than 4/10.
y.D: 9/10 adds the water instead of taking it away; it was used, so less is left.

QR.q: In a class of 40 students, 35% ride a bicycle to school. How many students is that?
QR.e: 35% of 40 is 0.35×40=14; the other values reflect nearby percentages or rounding.

y.A: 12 is 30% of 40, and the remaining 5% is 2 more.
y.B: 13 would be 32.5% of 40; 35% is 14.
y.D: 16 is 40% of 40, one step too far.

QR.q: A display doubles the number of lights and adds one each round: 4, 9, 19, 39, .... How many lights appear next?
QR.e: 39×2+1=79; 78 omits the added one, while 59 and 80 use inconsistent rules.

y.A: 59 is 39 + 20; the rule doubles first and then adds one.
y.C: 78 is 39 × 2 and leaves off the added one.
y.D: 80 is 39 × 2 + 2, adding two instead of one.

QR.q: A librarian shelves an average of 28 books per day for five days. She shelves 103 books during the first four days. How many does she shelve on day five?
QR.e: The five-day total is 5×28=140, and 140−103=37; 28 repeats the mean and 140 is the total.

y.A: 28 is the average itself, not the fifth day's count.
y.B: 32 leaves the five days totalling 135; five days averaging 28 total 140.
y.D: 140 is the five-day total, from which the first four days' 103 comes off.

QR.q: A rectangular garden has perimeter 54 meters and length 16 meters. What is its width?
QR.e: Half the perimeter is 54 ÷ 2 = 27, so the width is 27 − 16 = 11.

y.A: 5 is how much longer the length is than the width, 16 − 11, not the width.
y.B: 19 takes one length off the whole perimeter and halves the rest, (54 − 16) ÷ 2; halve first, then subtract the length.
y.C: 22 subtracts both lengths, 54 − 32, and forgets that what is left is two widths.

QR.q: A bag holds 5 yellow, 7 green, and 8 blue tiles. What is the probability of drawing a tile that is not blue?
QR.e: Twelve of 20 tiles are not blue, so 12/20=3/5; 2/5 is the blue probability and the others miscount colors.

y.A: 2/5 is 8/20, the blue tiles; the question asks about the other twelve.
y.C: 7/20 is the green tiles alone, and the five yellow count too.
y.D: 4/5 is 16/20, four more tiles than are not blue.

QR.q: A theater charges a $6 service fee plus $4 per student. A group pays $50. How many students are in the group?
QR.e: 4s+6=50 gives 4s=44 and s=11; the distractors divide before removing the fee or add it.

y.A: 9 students cost 6 + 4 × 9 = $42, not $50.
y.B: 10 students come to $46.
y.C: 14 comes from adding the $6 fee before dividing, 56 ÷ 4; the fee comes off first.

QR.q: On a trail map, 2.5 centimeters represent 15 kilometers. How many kilometers do 7 centimeters represent?
QR.e: The scale is 15÷2.5=6 kilometers per centimeter, so 7×6=42; the distractors use additive or inverted scaling.

y.B: 35 is 7 × 5; the scale is 15 ÷ 2.5 = 6 kilometers per centimeter.
y.C: 45 is three over 7 × 6.
y.D: 52.5 is 7 × 7.5, and the scale is 6 kilometers per centimeter.

QR.q: Crew A packs 84 cartons in 7 hours. Crew B packs 99 cartons in 9 hours. How many more cartons per hour does Crew A pack?
QR.e: Crew A packs 12 per hour and Crew B 11, a difference of 1; other choices compare totals or partial rates.

y.A: 3 is not the gap; Crew A packs 84 ÷ 7 = 12 an hour and Crew B 99 ÷ 9 = 11.
y.B: 2 is the difference in the hours, 9 − 7, rather than in the rates.
y.D: 11 is Crew B's own rate.

QR.q: An artist triples every edge length of a cube-shaped model. How many times as great is the new volume?
QR.e: Volume scales in three dimensions, so 3×3×3=27; 3 and 9 apply linear or area scaling only.

y.A: 3 is the scale on one edge, and volume uses all three.
y.B: 6 is 3 + 3, adding the tripled directions rather than multiplying them.
y.C: 9 is 3 × 3, which is how area grows; volume has a third dimension.

QR.q: A warehouse divides about 4,086 bolts equally among 79 bins. Which is the best estimate of bolts per bin?
QR.e: 4,000÷80=50, close to the given values; the distractors contain place-value or divisor-as-answer errors.

y.B: 5 is ten times too small; 79 × 5 is only about 400.
y.C: 400 is ten times too big — 79 × 400 would be about 31,600.
y.D: 80 is the number of bins, not the count that goes in each one.

QR.q: A game token starts at (−4,−1), moves 9 units right, then 6 units up. Where does it stop?
QR.e: Add 9 to x and 6 to y to get (5,5); the distractors reverse a direction, swap a change, or misadd.

y.A: (−13,5) moves left instead of right; right adds 9 to −4, giving 5.
y.B: (5,−7) moves down instead of up; up adds 6 to −1, giving 5.
y.C: (3,5) adds 7 to x rather than 9.

QR.q: The ratio of adult volunteers to student volunteers is 2:7. If 81 people volunteer, how many are adults?
QR.e: Nine parts make 81, so each part is 9 and adults are 2×9=18; 63 is the student count.

y.A: 9 is one part, and the adults make up two of them.
y.B: 14 is 2 × 7, multiplying the two ratio numbers; each part is 81 ÷ 9 = 9.
y.D: 63 is 7 × 9, the student count.

QR.q: A backpack priced at $80 is discounted 15%. What is the sale price?
QR.e: The discount is $12, leaving $68; $12 is the discount itself and the other choices use incorrect percentages.

y.A: 12 is the discount itself, not the price after it.
y.C: 65 takes off $15 rather than 15% of $80, which is $12.
y.D: 72 takes off 10%, and the discount is 15%.

QR.q: Wren finishes before Xena, and Zane finishes after Xena. Yori's position is unknown. Which order could be correct from first to last?
QR.e: Only C preserves Wren before Xena before Zane; every distractor reverses at least one required relation.

y.A: Xena comes before Wren here, and Wren has to finish first of the two.
y.B: Zane comes before Xena here, and Zane finishes after her.
y.D: Zane is first here, and Zane finishes after Xena.

QR.q: A fair spinner numbered 1 through 8 is spun 96 times. About how many spins should land on a number greater than 6?
QR.e: Two of eight outcomes qualify, so 1/4×96=24; the distractors miscount outcomes or use the complement.

y.B: 12 counts one face out of eight; 7 and 8 are both greater than 6.
y.C: 32 is a third of the spins, and two of the eight numbers qualify — a quarter.
y.D: 72 is the other three quarters, the spins that come out 6 or less.

QR.q: A rectangular photograph is enlarged so both its length and width double. How does its area change?
QR.e: Area has two dimensions, so the scale factor is 2×2=4; the distractors use linear, additive, or volume scaling.

y.A: Doubling both sides doubles each direction, and area uses both: 2 × 2 = 4.
y.C: 6 times is neither 2 × 2 nor 2 × 2 × 2; a rectangle has two dimensions, so the area grows fourfold.
y.D: 8 times is how a volume would grow, 2 × 2 × 2; a photograph has only length and width.

QR.q: After spending 3/8 of her savings, Talia has $45 left. How much did she have before spending?
QR.e: The $45 is 5/8 of the original, so 45×8/5=$72; the distractors treat 45 as the spent part or add a fraction of 45.

y.A: 60 would leave five eighths as $37.50, not $45.
y.B: 64 would leave five eighths as $40.
y.D: 120 treats the $45 as the 3/8 spent; it is the 5/8 that is left.

QR.q: Of 30 club members, 18 play chess, 16 play table tennis, and 7 play both. How many play neither?
QR.e: At least one is 18+16−7=27, so 30−27=3 play neither; distractors double-count or omit the overlap.

y.A: 1 would need 29 members to play at least one game; 18 + 16 − 7 = 27.
y.C: 5 would need 25 to play at least one; the overlap comes off once, giving 27.
y.D: 11 is 18 − 7, the chess-only group, not those playing neither.

QR.q: At sunrise the temperature is −6°C. By noon it is 9°C. By how many degrees did it rise?
QR.e: Moving from −6 to 0 is 6 degrees and then to 9 is 9 more, totaling 15; the distractors subtract absolute values or ignore the negative start.

y.B: 3 is 9 − 6, the two numbers with the minus dropped; the rise crosses zero, so the distances add.
y.C: 9 is only the climb up from zero, and there are 6 degrees below it as well.
y.D: 54 is 6 × 9, multiplying the two temperatures instead of adding the distances.

QR.q: A costume uses one of 3 shirts, one of 4 pairs of pants, and one of 2 hats. How many different costumes are possible?
QR.e: Multiply the independent choices: 3 × 4 × 2 = 24.

y.A: 9 is 3 + 4 + 2. Choices that combine multiply rather than add.
y.B: 14 is 12 + 2, multiplying shirts by pants and then adding the hats; the hats multiply too.
y.C: 18 is 3 × 6, shirts times pants-and-hats added together; each stage multiplies.

QR.q: A printer places 1,756 labels into sheets of 15. How many labels are left after filling as many complete sheets as possible?
QR.e: 15×117=1,755, leaving 1 label; the distractors use digit sums or distance from a wrong multiple.

y.C: 10 would need 1,746 to be a multiple of 15; 1,755 is the largest one below 1,756.
y.D: 14 is the largest remainder 15 can leave, and here it is 1.

QR.q: Every dren is a vop, and no vop is a sal. Which statement must be true?
QR.e: Because all drens belong to the vop group and vops exclude sals, drens cannot be sals; the distractors reverse or invent existence claims.

y.A: The chain runs from drens to vops and says nothing about what sals are.
y.B: No vop is a sal, which rules this out rather than supporting it.
y.D: Nothing here says drens do not exist; they are only kept out of the sal group.

QR.q: A mural is painted 2/9 on Monday and 1/3 on Tuesday. What fraction remains unpainted?
QR.e: 1/3=3/9, so 5/9 is painted and 4/9 remains; distractors report the painted part or add unlike denominators.

y.B: 5/9 is the painted part — 2/9 plus 3/9 — not what is left.
y.C: 2/3 is 6/9, one ninth more than was painted.
y.D: 7/9 would leave only 2/9 painted; 1/3 is 3/9, so 5/9 is done.

QR.sk: data reasoning—median after adding a value
QR.q: The recorded times are 2, 5, 9, 11, and 14 minutes. If a 20-minute time is added, what is the new median?
QR.e: With six values, average the middle two: (9+11)/2=10; the distractors choose one middle value or average the wrong pair.

y.A: 9 is the third of six values; with an even count the middle two are averaged.
y.C: 11 is the fourth value, and it pairs with 9 for an average of 10.
y.D: 12 is not the average of 9 and 11, which is 10.

QR.q: A square plaza has area 175 square meters. Which is the closest estimate of one side length?
QR.e: Since 13²=169 and 14²=196, √175 is about 13.2; the distractors are farther from the correct interval or endpoint.

y.A: 11.5 squared is about 132, well under 175.
y.B: 12 squared is 144, still under 175.
y.C: 14 squared is 196, past 175; the side falls between 13 and 14.

QR.sk: spatial reasoning—surface area with excluded face
QR.q: A 4 m by 3 m by 2 m display box is painted on the top and four sides, but not the bottom. What area is painted?
QR.e: Top area is 12; side areas total 2(4×2)+2(3×2)=28; painted area is 40. The distractors omit the top, include the bottom, or find volume.

y.A: 28 is the four sides only and leaves the top out.
y.C: 52 counts the bottom as well, and the bottom is not painted.
y.D: 24 is 4 × 3 × 2, the volume of the box.

QR.q: A culture begins with 200 cells, grows 20%, and then grows 25% from the new amount. How many cells are there?
QR.e: 200×1.20=240 and 240×1.25=300; the distractors add percentages to the original or apply one increase only.

y.B: 290 adds 45% of 200 to 200; the second increase works on 240, not on the original.
y.C: 250 is 200 × 1.25, applying only the second increase.
y.D: 320 would need the second increase to be about 33%; 25% of 240 is 60, giving 300.

QR.q: Two angles together form a straight line. One angle is 4 times as large as the other. What is the measure of the larger angle?
QR.e: The two angles total 180° and make 5 equal parts, so the smaller is 180 ÷ 5 = 36° and the larger is 4 × 36 = 144°.

y.A: 36 is the smaller angle; the larger is 4 × 36.
y.B: 45 is 180 ÷ 4; the two angles make five parts together, not four.
y.C: 72 is 4 × 18, taking 90° as the total; two angles on a straight line total 180°.

QR.q: Three workers assemble 72 kits in 4 hours at equal steady rates. How many kits can five workers assemble in 6 hours?
QR.e: Each worker makes 72÷3÷4=6 kits per hour; 5×6×6=180. The distractors scale only workers, only time, or both incorrectly.

y.A: 120 is not 5 × 6 × 6; each worker makes 72 ÷ 3 ÷ 4 = 6 kits an hour.
y.B: 150 is 5 × 5 × 6, five hours rather than six.
y.D: 240 is more than 5 × 6 × 6, which comes to 180.

QR.q: Set A is 6, 10, 12, 18. Set B is 4, 9, 15, 23. How much greater is Set B's range than Set A's range?
QR.e: Set A's range is 18 − 6 = 12 and Set B's is 23 − 4 = 19, so the difference is 7.

y.A: 5 is neither range nor their difference; Set A's range is 12 and Set B's is 19.
y.B: 6 is Set A's smallest value, not a range.
y.C: 12 is Set A's own range, 18 − 6; the question asks how much greater Set B's is.

QR.q: A group buys 6 tickets at $(x+2) each and uses a $5 coupon. Which expression gives the final cost?
QR.e: 6(x+2)−5=6x+12−5=6x+7; the distractors fail to distribute, omit the coupon, or multiply only part of the price.

y.B: 6x − 3 takes the coupon off the 2 inside the bracket; the 6 multiplies that 2 first.
y.C: 6x + 12 distributes correctly and then forgets the $5 coupon.
y.D: x + 7 never multiplies by 6, and there are six tickets.

QR.q: A court is 30 m by 18 m. A runner completes 1 3/4 laps around it. How far does the runner travel?

y.A: 96 is one lap; the runner does one and three-quarters.
y.B: 126 is 96 + 30, adding a single long side for the extra part of a lap; three-quarters of a lap is 72 m.
y.C: 144 is 1.5 × 96, one and a half laps rather than one and three-quarters.

QR.q: A box holds cards numbered 1 through 15. One card is drawn at random. What is the probability that the number drawn is greater than 9?
QR.e: The favorable cards are 10 through 15 — six of the 15 — so the probability is 6/15 = 2/5.

y.A: 3/5 is 9/15, the cards that are 9 or less; the question asks for greater than 9.
y.B: 7/15 includes the 9 itself; greater than 9 starts at 10.
y.D: 1/3 is 5/15, one favorable card short; 10 through 15 is six cards.

QR.q: After a 30% discount, a lamp costs $63. What was its original price?
QR.e: The sale price is 70% of the original, so 63÷0.70=90; the distractors add 30% of the sale price or use incorrect bases.

y.A: 81 would leave a sale price of $56.70 after 30% off.
y.B: 84 would leave $58.80.
y.C: 88 would leave $61.60.

QR.q: Parcel P is heavier than parcel Q. Parcel R is lighter than parcel Q. Which statement must be true?
c: P and R have equal weight.
QR.e: The chain P>Q>R guarantees P>R; every distractor reverses or contradicts that chain.

y.A: The chain runs P heavier than Q heavier than R, which puts R lightest.
y.C: P is heavier than Q, not the other way round.
y.D: Nothing in the chain allows two parcels to weigh the same.

RC.q: Which summary best captures the ferry-signal passage?
c: Simple signals made ferry trips more efficient.
The bending river became impossible to cross.
The shop owner built the first permanent bridge.
Freight mattered more to the ferry than passengers.
RC.e: The problem, signal system, and reduced unnecessary crossings support A; the other choices exaggerate, invent construction, or make an unsupported comparison.

y.B: Ferries crossed it all along and a bridge came later; the bend only meant one landing could not see the other.
y.C: The shop owner helped invent the signal. The bridge arrives later, with no builder named.
y.D: Both signals existed — red for passengers, white for freight — so neither is ranked above the other.

RC.q: What did a white square signal?
c: The river was too foggy for boats.
The new bridge was open at last.
RC.e: S3 directly assigns white to freight; waiting passengers are the red signal, and fog on the river and the bridge opening are not flag meanings.

y.A: Fog broke the flag system entirely, so a bell was rung instead; no square stood for fog.
y.B: When the bridge opened the flags disappeared, so there was no signal for it.
y.C: Passengers waiting is what the red square meant.

RC.q: Why was a bell useful during fog?
c: It counted every crate waiting on the landing.
It frightened the animals waiting on the bank.
Sound could carry when the flags could not be seen.
It announced that the bridge was finally done.
RC.e: S5 contrasts invisible flags with bell patterns, supporting C; the distractors assign functions the passage never gives.

y.A: [S4] says the flags never gave exact numbers, and a bell rung in patterns gives no more.
y.B: Animals were carried on the ferry, and nothing says the bell frightened them.
y.D: The bell was used during fog, long before the bridge.

RC.q: In S6, “unnecessary” most nearly means:
RC.e: Better information prevented trips that were not needed; danger, cost, and completion are not the stated issue.

y.A: Danger is never mentioned; the account books record crossings that did not need to happen.
y.C: Cost is not discussed, though fewer wasted trips would have saved some.
y.D: An unfinished crossing would be one that stopped halfway, which is not what the books show.

RC.q: Which sequence best describes the author's organization of the Silverbend passage?
c: A long debate followed by a final vote
Two rival ferrymen compared in careful detail
A numbered list of rules for crossing the river
A problem, a solution, a limit, and a result
RC.e: The bend creates a problem, flags solve it, fog limits them, and records show a result; the other structures do not match the sequence.

y.A: Nobody debates and no vote is taken; two people invent a signal.
y.B: There is one ferry keeper, and no rival.
y.C: The sentences are numbered for reference, but they are not a list of rules.

RC.q: Which summary best captures the fog-collector passage?
c: Fog collectors work everywhere without maintenance.
Mesh panels can collect useful water in suitable places.
Covered tanks create the fog that drifts over hills.
Strong winds always improve the water collected.
RC.e: The mesh-panel summary includes both the method and its conditions; working everywhere without maintenance and strong winds always improving collection ignore the limitations, and covered tanks creating the fog reverses the process.

y.A: [S6] and [S7] give the limits: salt and dust block the mesh, and a site has to be chosen with care.
y.C: The tank is where the water ends up; the fog drifts in off the coast.
y.D: Strong winds can tear the mesh, which is one of the named problems.

RC.q: What happens after droplets join into larger drops?
c: They turn into salt and dust.
They rise upward through the pipe.
They tear holes in the mesh.
RC.e: S3 states that larger drops slide into a channel; the other choices reverse motion or confuse problems with steps.

y.B: Salt and dust are what block the mesh, not what the droplets turn into.
y.C: The pipe carries water on to the tank; the drops slide down into a channel first.
y.D: Strong wind tears the mesh, and water sliding off it does not.

RC.q: Why do designers study local wind direction?
c: To leave the water tank uncovered outdoors
To stop salt and dust from ever forming
To be sure moving fog blows through the mesh
To change salty seawater into fresh drinking water
RC.e: Collection depends on wind pushing fog through mesh, so site direction matters; the distractors invent unrelated effects.

y.A: [S4] says the tank is covered.
y.B: Salt and dust cannot be prevented; mesh spacing and the site are chosen with them in mind.
y.D: No seawater is treated here; the water comes out of fog.

RC.q: Why does the author mention torn or blocked mesh?
c: To show practical limits that require planning
To argue that fog never contains any water
To explain how the covered storage tanks are built
To prove that rain falls more often than fog
RC.e: Those examples qualify the method and motivate site study; the other choices contradict or leave the passage.

y.B: The whole method depends on fog carrying droplets.
y.C: The tank is mentioned once, and how it is built is never described.
y.D: [S1] says rain is rare in these regions even when fog is common, which is the reverse.

RC.q: In S8, “suitable” most nearly means:
RC.e: Suitable places have appropriate wind, weather, and conditions; the other adjectives are not supported.

y.A: [S8] contrasts these places with a large city, so crowding is not what makes them fit.
y.B: Distance is not the point; wind and weather are.
y.C: Cost is never discussed.

RC.q: What does Inez learn by the end?
c: Every window box should look perfectly neat.
Clubs work best when they avoid making plans.
A plan can guide people without rigid divisions.
Feeding birds matters more than any other goal.
RC.e: S9 states the flexible-plan insight. Perfectly neat window boxes, clubs that avoid planning altogether, and birds above every other goal each turn a balanced lesson into an extreme claim.

y.A: [S8] says their box looked less orderly than the chess club's, and birds came to it.
y.B: Inez brings a plan — three paper squares — and that is what gets them started.
y.D: Food is one of three sections, alongside color and bare ground.

RC.q: What did Inez place in the empty box?
RC.e: S5 directly names three paper squares; the distractors name planting-day objects the passage never places in the box or ideas that come later.

y.A: The squares mark out sections; no seeds are placed in [S5].
y.B: The berry plant comes later, when the members notice one plant can serve two purposes.
y.C: The chess club planted purple flowers, and no chess pieces appear.

RC.q: Why had the club's box remained empty?
c: Members waited for a plan that satisfied competing goals.
The spring festival had been canceled before planting day.
Inez had lost all of the club's flower seeds.
The community center forbade berries and blossoms.
RC.e: The disagreement and desire for a complete plan delayed action; the distractors invent events or rules.

y.B: The festival opens at the end, and birds visit before it does.
y.C: Nothing is lost; the members simply cannot agree on a plan.
y.D: The disagreement is among the members themselves, and no rule is mentioned.

RC.q: What lesson does the window-box episode best support?
c: The neatest window box is always the most useful.
Combining purposes helps a group move past disagreement.
A successful group must agree on one single goal.
A nature project should never use written labels.
RC.e: The group succeeds by combining food, color, and habitat; the other choices reverse or overstate the lesson.

y.A: The less orderly box is the one the birds visited.
y.C: [S9] says a plan can guide cooperation without forcing everything into a single category.
y.D: The cooking club's tiny signs are described without any criticism.

RC.q: What does “sharp borders” in S7 suggest?
c: Dangerous edges on the wooden box
Brightly painted lines on the soil
Small fences around the whole center
RC.e: The sections represent purposes, and one plant can cross categories; the other choices interpret borders physically without support.

y.A: Nothing about the wooden box is dangerous; the phrase is about the sections inside it.
y.B: No lines are painted; the sections were marked with paper squares.
y.C: The borders in question are inside one window box.

RC.q: What central idea does the passage develop?
c: Every faded mural should be completely repainted in bright color.
Careful restoration balances clarity with honesty about gaps.
Infrared light permanently changes the mural's pigments.
The new paint is weaker than the wall's old plaster.
RC.e: The team's limited, distinguishable repairs support B; the other choices contradict or focus on an unsupported technical claim.

y.A: [S2] warns that repainting every missing shape would replace evidence with guesswork.
y.C: Infrared light revealed hidden outlines; it changed nothing.
y.D: Strength is never compared; the repairs are removable and meant to be told apart.

RC.q: What did the team do before adding repairs?
c: Covered the whole mural with fresh plaster
Asked viewers to guess the missing scene
Photographed the wall and cleaned a test area
Repainted every missing shape in new color
RC.e: S3-S5 give photography and test cleaning before repair; fresh plaster over the whole mural and repainting every missing shape reverse the work, and no one is ever asked to guess the missing scene.

y.A: Plaster is what had hidden the mural, and the team uncovered it.
y.B: Guesswork is exactly what [S2] warns against.
y.D: Repainting every shape is the tempting mistake the team avoided.

RC.q: Why were the new marks kept visible when viewed up close?
c: So viewers could tell repairs from original paint
Because the team ran out of matching paint
So infrared cameras could find the buried mural
Because people standing close cannot see faded color
RC.e: Distinguishability avoids pretending uncertain repairs are original; the distractors invent material limits or misuse infrared.

y.B: The repairs were chosen to be removable and lightly colored, not limited by what paint was left.
y.C: The photography came first and had already revealed the outlines.
y.D: Up close is precisely where the new marks can be told from the old paint.

RC.q: In S5, “supported” most nearly means:
RC.e: Hidden outlines provide evidence for a pattern, so supported means backed by evidence; the other choices use literal or unrelated senses.

y.A: Nothing here is holding the wall up; the question is whether the pattern is known.
y.C: Visitors see the result from across the room, but their liking it is not what decided where to paint.
y.D: The plaster had hidden the mural rather than protecting its pattern.

RC.q: Which statement would the author most likely agree with?
c: A beautiful guess is worth as much as real historical evidence.
Every missing detail should be left impossible for anyone to see.
Restoration should aid understanding without hiding uncertainty.
Modern tools such as infrared make careful judgment unnecessary.
RC.e: The final choice combines understanding and honesty; the distractors reject evidence, usefulness, or expert judgment.

y.A: [S2] sets guesswork against evidence and comes down on the side of evidence.
y.B: The repairs help viewers understand the scene from across the room, so the gaps are not left blank.
y.D: The photography only revealed outlines; the team still judged where the pattern was well supported.

RC.q: Which summary best captures the library's new lending project?
c: A library should stop lending books and recordings.
Every household should buy its own drill and telescope.
Shared objects never break and never need new parts.
A library adapted its rules so objects could be shared safely.
RC.e: Adapting the rules so objects could be shared safely carries both the expansion and the safeguards; the other three contradict the passage or make absolute claims.

y.A: The library added the objects to what it already lent.
y.B: [S9] says careful sharing makes rarely used items available to more people.
y.C: [S7] says a few parts had been replaced.

RC.q: Why did staff photograph each kit before checkout?
c: To advertise the new kits to residents
To teach borrowers how to take photographs
To record the kit's parts and condition
To shorten the waiting list for popular kits
RC.e: Photographs and labels support inspection and complete returns; the distractors give unrelated purposes.

y.A: The photographs were taken before each checkout, one kit at a time.
y.B: The demonstrations were about using the tools safely.
y.D: The waiting list guided what to buy next; photographs did not shorten it.

RC.q: What did the waiting list help the staff infer?
c: Which library books should be removed
Which residents already owned their own tools
RC.e: A long wait signals demand and helps guide purchases; the distractors concern information the list does not contain.

y.A: The list was for the objects, and no books are removed.
y.C: A waiting list shows what people want to borrow, not what they already have.
y.D: The demonstrations were given to keep returns safe, and the list says nothing about them.

RC.q: Why did the library allow extra time between object loans?
c: The objects were less popular than the library's books.
Borrowers needed extra time to buy replacements.
Staff needed to inspect the objects and parts.
The library building closed between every loan.
RC.e: Different objects and labeled parts required inspection; the distractors invent low demand, borrower duties, or closures.

y.A: The waiting list suggests the opposite.
y.B: Staff replaced a few parts; borrowers were never asked to buy anything.
y.D: Nothing closes; the gap between loans is for inspection.

RC.q: What lesson does the library-of-things project best support?
c: Sharing succeeds when the rules match what is shared.
Careful rules always prevent shared objects from breaking.
People should borrow everything they use at home.
Predictions about new library projects are never useful.
RC.e: The library adapts rules and succeeds with manageable repairs; the other choices use absolutes that the passage does not support.

y.B: [S7] says a few parts had been replaced even so.
y.C: [S8] says the project did not remove the need to own everyday objects.
y.D: The gloomy prediction in [S6] is reported and then tested, which is what makes it worth mentioning.

MA.e: Place-value addition gives 9,803; the distractors reflect regrouping or place-value slips.

y.B: 9,793 is 10 short: the units make 7 + 6 = 13, so a ten carries into 4 + 5 and that column reaches 10.
y.C: 8,803 is 1,000 short; the hundreds make 8 + 9 + 1 = 18, which carries a thousand into 6 + 2.
y.D: 9,903 is 100 over; the tens column comes to 10, carrying one hundred, and the hundreds then leave 8.

MA.e: Regrouping across zeros gives 4,416; the distractors reverse digits or subtract without regrouping.

y.A: 5,416 is 1,000 too many; after the regrouping the thousands column is 11 − 7 = 4, not 12 − 7.
y.B: 4,516 is 100 over; after regrouping the hundreds column is 9 − 5 = 4.
y.D: 5,584 puts 12 − 7 in front and then copies 584 down instead of subtracting it.

MA.q: What is 74×36?
MA.e: 74×(30+6)=2,220+444=2,664; the distractors contain partial-product errors.

y.C: 2,724 is 60 over 74 × 36; check the two partial products, 2,220 and 444.
y.D: 3,164 is 500 over, from taking 74 × 30 as 2,720 instead of 2,220.

MA.q: What is 2,916÷27?
MA.e: 27×108=2,916; the distractors reflect quotient-estimation or place-value errors.

y.B: 98 is ten too few: 27 × 98 = 2,646, a full 270 short of 2,916.

MA.e: Using denominator 36 gives 10/36+21/36=31/36; the distractors add denominators or convert only one fraction.

y.A: 12/30 adds the tops and the bottoms; both fractions go over 36 first.
y.C: 17/36 converts only one of the two: 5/18 is 10/36 and 7/12 is 21/36.
y.D: 2/3 is 24/36, well under the 31/36 the two make.

MA.q: What is 5/6−7/20?
MA.e: 5/6=50/60 and 7/20=21/60, so the difference is 29/60; the distractors subtract denominators or use a wrong common denominator.

y.A: 2/14 subtracts the numerators and the denominators separately; both fractions go over 60 first.
y.B: 43/60 takes 7/60 away rather than 21/60, and 7/20 is 21/60.
y.C: 3/10 is 18/60, eleven sixtieths under the difference.

MA.e: Cancel 8/32 to 1/4 and 25/15 to 5/3, giving 5/12; the distractors add, over-cancel, or combine denominators incorrectly.

y.B: 1/3 over-cancels: 8/15 × 25/32 is 200/480, which reduces to 5/12.
y.C: 10/15 is 2/3, far above the product, which is under a half.
y.D: 200/47 multiplies the tops and adds the bottoms; 15 × 32 = 480, not 47.

MA.q: What is 3 1/3÷5/6?
MA.e: 10/3×6/5=4; the distractors fail to invert the divisor or mishandle the mixed number.

y.A: 2 7/9 multiplies instead of dividing, 10/3 × 5/6; dividing by 5/6 means multiplying by 6/5.
y.D: 5 overshoots; 10/3 × 6/5 = 60/15, which is exactly 4.

MA.e: Align decimals: 18.709+6.840=25.549; the distractors misalign places or regroup incorrectly.

y.A: 24.549 is a whole 1 short; 0.709 + 0.840 = 1.549, so a one carries into 18 + 6.
y.B: 25.459 has the tenths and hundredths swapped; lined up, the tenths make 7 + 8 = 15.

MA.q: What is 4.8×2.35?
MA.e: 235×48=11,280, then place three decimal digits to get 11.28; the distractors misplace the decimal or add.

y.A: 10.28 is a whole 1 short; 235 × 48 = 11,280, and three decimal places make 11.28.
y.B: 112.8 has the point one place out; 11,280 with three decimals is 11.280.
y.D: 7.15 is 4.8 + 2.35, adding instead of multiplying.

MA.e: Scale to 277.2÷42=6.6; the distractors move the decimal the wrong number of places or estimate poorly.

y.B: 0.66 is a tenth of the quotient; 277.2 ÷ 42 = 6.6.
y.C: 66 is ten times too big — 4.2 × 66 would be 277.2, not 27.72.
y.D: 7.2 is not the quotient; 4.2 × 6.6 = 27.72.

MA.q: What is 22% of 450?
MA.e: 20% of 450 is 90 and 2% is 9, totaling 99; the distractors omit a part or misplace the decimal.

y.A: 90 is 20% of 450 and stops there; the other 2% is 9 more.
y.B: 95 is four short; 20% gives 90 and 2% gives 9.
y.D: 110 would be about 24% of 450, and 22% is 99.

MA.e: Parentheses first: 42÷7=6 and 5×2=10, then 6+10=16; distractors ignore grouping or multiplication priority.

y.A: 11 is 6 + 5, leaving the × 2 off the end.
y.C: 60 is 42 ÷ 7 × 5 × 2, multiplying straight through instead of adding the two parts.

MA.q: What is 5^3?
MA.e: 5^3=5×5×5=125; the distractors multiply base by exponent, square, or use the fourth power.

y.B: 15 is 5 × 3, multiplying the base by the exponent.
y.C: 25 is 5², one factor of 5 short.
y.D: 625 is 5⁴, one factor too many.

MA.q: Which is the prime factorization of 126?
MA.e: 126=2×3×3×7, all prime; every distractor leaves composite factors.

y.A: 6 × 21 does make 126, but neither 6 nor 21 is prime.
y.C: 2 × 63 leaves 63, which is 3 × 3 × 7.
y.D: 3 × 42 leaves 42, which is 2 × 3 × 7.

MA.q: What is the greatest common factor of 48 and 72?
MA.e: 24 divides both and no larger common factor does; 12 and 8 are common but not greatest, while 144 is a multiple.

y.B: 12 is a common factor but not the greatest; 24 divides both numbers as well.
y.C: 8 is common to both and smaller still; 24 divides 48 and 72 too.
y.D: 144 is a common multiple of 48 and 72, not a factor of either.

MA.q: Solve 6x−11=43.
MA.e: Add 11 to get 6x=54, then divide by 6 to get x=9; the distractors stop early or undo operations incorrectly.

y.A: 7 does not check: 6 × 7 − 11 = 31, not 43.
y.D: 54 is 43 + 11 and stops there; that 54 still has to be divided by 6.

MA.q: What is 2c²+3c when c=4?
MA.e: 2(4²)+3(4)=32+12=44; the distractors square the coefficient or apply the exponent to the whole expression.

y.C: 56 is not 2 × 4² + 3 × 4; squaring only the c gives 32, and 3 × 4 adds 12.
y.D: 80 is 64 + 16, squaring the 2c together as (2 × 4)²; only the c is squared.

MA.q: Which value of n satisfies 3n−5≥16?
MA.e: For n=7, 3n−5=16, which satisfies ≥; the smaller choices produce values below 16.

y.B: 6 gives 3 × 6 − 5 = 13, which is below 16.
y.C: 5 gives 10, further below still.
y.D: 4 gives 7.

MA.q: What is the reflection of (−3,8) across the y-axis?
