MA.e: A y-axis reflection changes the sign of x only; the distractors reflect across x, swap coordinates, or change both signs.

y.A: (−3,−8) changes the sign of y; reflecting across the y-axis changes x.
y.B: (8,−3) swaps the two coordinates and changes a sign as well.
y.C: (3,−8) changes both signs, and only x changes.

MA.q: A parallelogram has base 14 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm. What is its area?
MA.e: Area is base×height=14×9=126 cm²; the distractors find perimeter-like totals, halve, or double the product.

y.A: 46 is 2 × (14 + 9), a perimeter; area multiplies base by height.
y.B: 63 is half of 126; a parallelogram is not halved the way a triangle is.
y.D: 252 is 14 × 9 × 2, the area doubled.

MA.q: A triangle has angles of 52° and 61°. What is the third angle?
MA.e: Triangle angles total 180°, so 180 − (52 + 61) = 180 − 113 = 67°. 113° stops at the sum of the two given angles, while 57° and 77° come from misadding 52 + 61 (as 123 or 103) before subtracting from 180°.

y.A: 57 comes from adding 52 + 61 as 123 before subtracting from 180.
y.C: 77 comes from adding 52 + 61 as 103; the sum is 113.
y.D: 113 is 52 + 61, the two given angles; that total still has to come off 180.

MA.q: Using 22/7 for π, what is the circumference of a circle with radius 7 cm?
MA.e: Circumference=2πr=2×(22/7)×7=44 cm; the distractors use half the formula or compute area.

y.A: 22 is (22/7) × 7, which is πr — half the circumference.
y.B: 38.5 is neither 2πr nor πr²; 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 44.
y.D: 154 is (22/7) × 7², the area of the circle; circumference is 2πr.

MA.q: What is the volume of a rectangular prism measuring 8 cm by 6 cm by 5 cm?
MA.e: Volume = 8 × 6 × 5 = 240 cm³. 96 cm³ finds only the top and bottom faces (2 × 48), and 190 cm³ and 220 cm³ are slips in the final step 48 × 5: misreading 48 as 38 gives 190, and taking 200 + 4 × 5 instead of 200 + 8 × 5 gives 220.

y.A: 96 is 2 × 48, the top and bottom faces; volume multiplies all three edges.
y.B: 190 comes from misreading 48 as 38 in the last step; 48 × 5 = 240.
y.C: 220 comes from taking 200 + 4 × 5 in the last step instead of 200 + 8 × 5.

MA.q: How many milliliters are in 4.25 liters?
MA.e: One liter is 1,000 milliliters, so 4.25×1,000=4,250; the distractors move the decimal the wrong number of places.

y.A: 425 multiplies by 100; a liter holds 1,000 millilitres.
y.C: 42.5 multiplies by 10 only.
y.D: 42,500 multiplies by 10,000.

MA.q: How much time passes from 1:47 p.m. to 4:15 p.m.?
MA.e: From 1:47 to 2:00 is 13 minutes, to 4:00 is 2 hours, and to 4:15 is 15 minutes: 2 h 28 min. Distractors subtract minute digits directly.

y.A: 2 hours 18 minutes falls ten short; 1:47 to 4:15 is 2 hours and 28 minutes.
y.B: 2 hours 22 minutes is six short of the gap.
y.C: 3 hours 28 minutes counts an extra hour; 1:47 to 4:15 never reaches three full hours.

MA.q: On a drawing, 1.5 cm represents 6 m. What actual distance does 8 cm represent?
MA.e: The scale is 6÷1.5=4 m per cm, so 8×4=32 m; the distractors use additive or inverted scaling.

y.B: 24 is 8 × 3; the scale is 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4 meters per centimeter.
y.C: 36 is 6 × 6, using the meters twice.
y.D: 48 is 8 × 6, multiplying by the meters instead of by the 4 meters each centimeter stands for.

MA.q: What is the mean of 18, 23, 27, 32, and 40?
MA.e: The sum is 140, and 140÷5=28; the distractors choose a middle value or divide incorrectly.

y.A: 25 would need a total of 125; 18 + 23 + 27 + 32 + 40 is 140.
y.B: 27 is the middle value of the five, which is the median rather than the mean.
y.D: 30 would need a total of 150, ten more than there is.

MA.q: A card numbered 1 through 20 is chosen at random. What is the probability that its number is a factor of 18?
MA.e: Factors within the set are 1,2,3,6,9,18: 6/20=3/10; the distractors omit factors or count multiples.

y.A: 1/4 is 5/20, one factor short; 18 has six inside the set — 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18.
y.C: 2/5 is 8/20, two more than there are.
y.D: 1/2 is 10/20, which would be the even numbers rather than the factors of 18.

MA.q: How far apart are points (−4,2) and (−4,−7)?
MA.e: The x-coordinates match, and vertical distance is |2−(−7)|=9; the distractors subtract absolute values or add coordinates incorrectly.

y.A: 5 is 7 − 2, the two numbers with their signs dropped; the points sit either side of zero, so the distances add.
y.B: 7 is only the drop from 0 down to −7; there are 2 more up to the other point.
y.C: 11 is wider than the gap: 2 down to 0, then 7 more, makes 9.

catcare._note: What a cat actually needs, for the Den (docs/world.md). Every item carries a named source, because this is real advice about a real animal and the content rule applies: never invent a fact. Keyed by the ledger id in site/src/lib/base.js — those ids are permanent, so a thing can be renamed but never re-keyed. `check` is a real question drawn from the note above it; getting it wrong costs nothing and can be answered again. None of it is ISEE content and none of it is recorded as practice.
catcare._disclaimer: General guidance from animal-welfare charities and veterinary bodies, not veterinary advice. A vet decides what is right for a particular cat.

word-lab.need: A collar with an ID tag is the fastest way home, because anyone who finds the cat can read it. A microchip cannot fall off — but it holds only a number, so it works only if the number is registered and the phone number on it is kept up to date. Even a cat who never goes outside should wear a tag.

check.q: What is actually stored inside a microchip?
c: Your name, address and phone number
Just a number, which has to be registered to you
A tracker that shows where the cat is
check.e: Only a unique number. If nobody registers it — or the phone number goes out of date — a scanner finds the number and it leads nowhere. A microchip is not a tracker either.

source.name: ASPCA — Position Statement on Pet Identification

reading-den.thing: A high shelf by the window
reading-den.need: Cats feel safest high up. Somewhere solid to climb to and watch from gives them exercise, privacy, and a way out of trouble. They also need somewhere to hide when something frightens them — a cat with nowhere to hide has nowhere to feel safe.

check.q: Why does a cat want somewhere high to sit?
c: Cats feel safest high up and like to watch from above
Cats cannot see well at floor level
To be closer to the light
check.e: High places are about safety and watching, not warmth. Being able to get up and away is also how a cat avoids a fight instead of having one.

source.name: International Cat Care — Making your home cat friendly

number-works.need: Fresh, clean water every day, in bowls washed and refilled daily. Put the water away from the food — given the choice a cat drinks well away from where it eats — and put both a long way from the litter tray. Where several cats live together the rule is one of everything per cat, plus one spare, in different places.

check.q: Where should the water bowl go?
c: Right next to the food bowl
Next to the litter tray so it is all in one place
Away from the food, and a long way from the litter tray
Anywhere, as long as it is filled
check.e: Given the choice, a cat drinks well away from where it eats, and will not eat or drink near where it goes to the toilet.

source.name: International Cat Care — Making your home cat friendly

math-shop.need: Scratching is not naughtiness. It is stretching, marking territory, and pulling the worn outer layer off the claws so the sharp new ones show. The post has to be sturdy enough not to wobble when leaned on, and tall enough for the cat to stretch right out — at least 60 cm.

check.q: How tall does a scratching post need to be?
c: About the height of the cat sitting down
At least 60 cm, so the cat can stretch right out
As short as possible so it does not tip
It does not matter as long as it is rough
check.e: The stretch is half the point, so the cat has to be able to reach full length up it — and the base has to be heavy enough that it does not wobble, or the cat will use your sofa instead.

writing-studio.need: Register with a vet as soon as the cat arrives. Kittens usually start their vaccinations at about eight or nine weeks old, with a second set three to four weeks later and a booster a year on; Cats Protection advises neutering from four months or younger. Your vet decides the real schedule for your cat. Write down what was given and when — that record is the cat's story as much as its name is.

check.q: About how old is a kitten when it usually has its first vaccinations?
check.e: Around eight or nine weeks, then a second set three to four weeks after that. The exact plan is the vet's call, not the internet's.

source.name: Cats Protection — Neutering, vaccinations and microchipping

library.thing: A warm bed of their own
library.need: Somewhere quiet, warm and theirs, where nobody will disturb them — and somewhere to hide as well as somewhere to sleep. A new cat should have a room set up with everything in it before it arrives, and be allowed to come out in its own time.

check.q: A cat needs somewhere to sleep. What does it need just as much?
c: A clock so it knows when meals are
check.e: Hiding is how a cat handles being frightened. Take away the hiding place and the fear does not go away — only the way of coping with it does.

source.name: RSPCA — Creating a good home for cats

rehearsal-hall.need: Leave the carrier out all the time, so it becomes part of the furniture — somewhere the cat chooses to sleep, rather than a box that only ever appears on the way to the vet. Putting their own unwashed bedding inside makes it smell like them, which is what makes it feel safe.

check.q: When should the carrier be out where the cat can see it?
c: Only on the morning of a vet trip
The night before, so it is not a surprise
All the time, so it is just part of the furniture
Never — keep it hidden so the cat does not worry
check.e: If the carrier only ever appears before something frightening, the carrier becomes frightening. Out all the time, with their own bedding in it, it turns into just another good place to sleep.

source.name: Cats Protection — How to choose and use a cat carrier

help.note: Every cat in this world is invented — its coat and its voice come out of the letters of a word. Real cats are not invented, and there are far more of them than there are homes. This is what the same organisations say actually helps.

ways.how: Looking after a shelter cat at home for a while — waiting for adoption, recovering from surgery, or just growing big enough. It is free to do: the shelter provides the food, the bowls and the medicine, and you provide the room and the company. It also empties a shelter pen for the next cat, so one foster home helps twice.

source.name: ASPCA — What does it mean to be an animal foster caregiver?

ways.how: Kittens under eight weeks are the most fragile animals a shelter takes in, and the youngest need feeding round the clock. A trained foster carer with the right supplies is often the difference between a kitten surviving and not.

source.name: ASPCA — Different types of animal foster caregivers

ways.how: Street cats are trapped, neutered and returned to where they live, which stops the number growing without harming the cats already there. It needs people to feed, to trap, to drive cats to the vet and back, and to keep them somewhere warm for a night after surgery.

source.name: International Cat Care — What can I do to help unowned cats?

ways.how: Cats Protection advises neutering from four months old or younger. One unneutered cat is where a whole street of unowned cats starts.

source.name: Cats Protection — Neutering, vaccinations and microchipping

ways.how: Small charities have almost no paid staff. Cleaning pens, feeding, driving, fundraising and socialising kittens are all jobs that need doing and all of them are done by people who volunteered.

source.name: International Cat Care — What can I do to help unowned cats?

learn.note: Our own explainer for a skill, shown the moment she gets one wrong. First-party and bundled, so it costs nothing, needs no account and works offline — the AoPS chapter is the paid-or-free extra beside it, not the only way back in. Written to a ten-year-old: short sentences, one method, and the trap named out loud. Every `links` entry carries a `url` to a page somebody has opened. There is no search-only entry, because a badge naming a site is indistinguishable from a badge opening that site's lesson, and two of them were searches wearing a lesson's clothes. A skill with no on-topic page on a given site simply does not list that site; the card's own Search the web badge is the search, and it says so. The old rule here was that a deep link which 404s two years from now is worse than a search that always lands, and it is still the right worry — it is answered by keeping the search badge on the card beside the deep links rather than by refusing to link, and by checking the urls against the sites' own indexes when they are added or changed. Every url here was checked that way on 2026-09-16. A url with no course path in it, of the bare /a/<slug> form, is the shape that failed: it is what a search engine hands you when it has the slug and not the page. What the index cannot be replaced by, for Khan specifically, is fetching the page: Khan answers a script with a bot-challenge page and answers it 200, and it does that for a url invented on the spot just as readily as for a real one. So a status code proves nothing there and must never be mistaken for a check — the khanacademy.org urls stand on the index having returned them as canonical, and the bbc.co.uk and mathsisfun.com ones on their pages having actually been read. Anyone adding a link later: verifying a Khan url needs a real browser session or the search index, not curl.
learn.links_note: free: true means no account and no payment. Anything marked false costs money to use properly.

Synonyms.what: The choice that means most nearly the same thing — not the one that belongs to the same story.
how: Say what the word means in your own words first, before you read a single choice.
Try each choice in the word's place in a sentence you make up.
If two still fit, ask which is closer in strength: warm and scorching are both hot, but not the same.
Stuck? Use the parts you know. Sub- is under, -script is written, bi- is two.
Synonyms.trap: A choice about the same subject as the word but not its meaning. SANCTUARY is about safety, not about churches.

example.work: Your own words first: to hold something back. Now look — reveal, encourage, expand, suppress. Only suppress holds back.

links.name: Khan Academy
links.q: Latin and Greek roots and affixes

Sentence completion.what: The word the sentence is asking for. The sentence always tells you — the clue is inside it.
how: Read all the way to the full stop before you look at any choice.
Say your own word for the gap, in your head, before reading the four.
Find the signpost: but, although, because, however, and every member agreed. It says whether the gap carries on with the sentence or turns against it.
Put your pick back in and read the whole sentence again.
Sentence completion.trap: A clever-sounding word that would fit some other sentence. If the sentence says but, the gap has to turn — a word that agrees is wrong however good it sounds.

example.q: The committee reached a ______ decision; every member agreed.
example.work: The clue is every member agreed. Your own words: agreed by all. That is unanimous — and you had it before you read the choices.

links.name: Khan Academy
links.q: using context clues to figure out new words

Main idea.what: What the whole passage is about — not one interesting thing in it.
how: Say the passage back in one sentence, in your head, before looking at the choices.
A right answer covers the beginning, middle AND end. A wrong one covers only a bit.
Cross out any choice that is true but small.
Main idea.trap: The most tempting wrong answer is usually a real detail from the passage. True is not the same as main.

Supporting detail/evidence.what: Something the passage actually says — findable, word for word.
how: Find the line. Do not answer from memory.
Put your finger on the sentence that proves it before you pick.
If you cannot find a line for it, it is not the answer.
Supporting detail/evidence.trap: A choice that sounds sensible and is true about the world, but is never said in the passage.

Inference.what: Something the passage makes almost certain without saying it outright.
how: Ask: what must be true, given what it does say?
Stay close. An inference is one small step, not a big guess.
You should still be able to point at the lines that force it.
Inference.trap: Going too far. If you need to invent anything at all, it is a guess, not an inference.

Organization/logic.what: How the parts of the passage fit together — why this paragraph comes after that one.
how: Give each paragraph a job in three words: sets it up, gives an example, argues back, sums up.
Then ask what the question is asking about: one paragraph, or how two relate?
Words like but, however, for example and so are the joins. Circle them.
Organization/logic.trap: Answering about what a paragraph SAYS when the question asked what it DOES.

Vocabulary in context.what: What a word means in THIS sentence — which may not be its usual meaning.
how: Cover the word. Read the sentence and say your own word in the gap.
Now find the choice closest to your word.
Put each choice back into the sentence and read it aloud.
Vocabulary in context.trap: Picking the word's most common meaning. The question exists because the passage is using a less common one.

Tone/style/figurative language.what: How the writer feels about it, and the tricks they use to show you.
how: Look at the adjectives and the verbs — that is where feeling hides.
Decide first whether it is warm, cold, or neutral. Then pick the closest word.
A comparison with like or as is a simile; without them it is a metaphor.
Tone/style/figurative language.trap: Choosing a very strong word — furious, terrified — when the passage is only mildly anything. Most writing is mild.

Perimeter.what: The distance all the way round the outside of a shape.
how: Walk the edge in your head and add every side you step along.
A rectangle has four: length + width + length + width, which is 2 x (length + width).
Going backwards? Take off the two sides you know, then halve what is left.
Perimeter.trap: Multiplying. Length x width is the area — the space inside — not the walk around the edge.

example.q: A banner is 10 cm by 3 cm. What is its perimeter?
example.work: 10 + 3 + 10 + 3 = 26 cm. (10 x 3 = 30 would be the area.)

Area.what: How much flat space is inside a shape.
how: Rectangle: length x width — think of the squares that would fill it.
Triangle: half of base x height, because a triangle is half a rectangle.
Given the area and one side, divide to get the other side back.
Area.trap: Forgetting the half on a triangle, and adding sides instead of multiplying.

example.q: A triangular flag has base 10 cm and height 6 cm.
example.work: Half of 10 x 6 = half of 60 = 30 cm2. (60 is the whole rectangle.)

Angles.what: How far something turns, measured in degrees.
how: The three angles of any triangle add to 180.
Angles on a straight line add to 180; all the way round a point is 360.
Given two angles of a triangle, subtract both from 180.
Angles.trap: Using 360 for a triangle. A triangle is 180 — a four-sided shape is 360.

example.q: A triangle has angles 45 and 60. What is the third?

Percent.what: A number out of a hundred. 25% means 25 for every 100.
how: Percent of a number: turn the percent into a fraction over 100, then multiply.
Learn the easy ones by heart: 50% is half, 25% is a quarter, 10% is divide by ten.
Build harder ones from those: 30% is three lots of 10%.
Percent.trap: Finding the percent when the question asked what the whole was, or the other way round. Say out loud which number is the whole.

Fractions.what: Part of a whole. The bottom says how many pieces; the top says how many you have.
how: Adding or subtracting: make the bottoms match first, then only the tops change.
Multiplying: tops together, bottoms together. No matching needed.
Dividing by a fraction: flip it over and multiply.
Fractions.trap: Adding the bottoms. A half plus a quarter is not two sixths.

Decimals.what: Another way of writing fractions, using place value after a dot.
how: Line up the dots before adding or subtracting — always.
Multiplying: ignore the dots, multiply, then count how many digits came after dots altogether.
0.5 is a half, 0.25 a quarter, 0.1 a tenth.
Decimals.trap: Thinking 0.35 is bigger than 0.5 because it has more digits. Compare place by place.

Whole-number operations.what: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing ordinary numbers, carefully.
how: Line up the columns by place value before you start.
Estimate first: 2,400 + 1,750 is about 4,000, so an answer near 400 or 40,000 is wrong.
Check the answer against your estimate before moving on.
Whole-number operations.trap: A single place-value slip. Estimating first catches almost all of them.

Order of operations.what: Which part of a long sum to do first.
how: Brackets first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.
Multiply and divide are equal — do them left to right.
So are add and subtract. Left to right again.
Order of operations.trap: Working strictly left to right through everything, which gets 2 + 3 x 4 wrong.

Parity.what: Whether a number is odd or even, and what happens when you combine them.
how: Even + even = even. Odd + odd = even. Odd + even = odd.
Anything multiplied by an even number is even.
Odd x odd is the only way to keep a product odd.
Parity.trap: Assuming odd + odd is odd. Two odds always make an even.

Number sense.what: Knowing roughly what the answer should be before you work it out.
how: Round each number to something easy and do the easy sum first.
Ask whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than what you started with.
Then compare your real answer to that. If they disagree, one of them is wrong.
Number sense.trap: Trusting a worked answer that is wildly the wrong size. The estimate is the check.

Geometry.what: Shapes, their sides and angles, and what stays true about them.
how: Draw it, even roughly. Most geometry mistakes are picture mistakes.
Label every length and angle you are given, on the drawing.
Then ask which rule connects what you have to what you want.
Geometry.trap: Answering from the picture looking about right instead of from the numbers given.

Algebraic reasoning.what: Working with a number you do not know yet, usually called a letter.
how: Write the sentence as a sum, with a letter where the unknown goes.
Do the same thing to both sides until the letter is alone.
Put your answer back into the original sentence and check it works.
Algebraic reasoning.trap: Changing one side and not the other. Whatever you do, do it to both.

Mean.what: The average: share everything out equally.
how: Add every number together.
Divide by how many numbers there were.
Check: the mean must land between the smallest and the largest.
Mean.trap: Dividing by the wrong count. Count the numbers, not the total.

links.name: Khan Academy
links.q: mean average of a data set

Median.what: The middle number once they are in order.
how: Put them in order first. Always.
Odd count: the one in the middle. Even count: the mean of the middle two.
Cross off from both ends together until you meet.
Median.trap: Taking the middle of the list as written, without sorting it.

example.work: Already in order, five numbers, so the third: 59.

Mode.what: The value that appears most often.
how: Count how many times each value appears.
The one with the highest count is the mode.
There can be two modes, or none at all.
Mode.trap: Giving how many times it appeared instead of the value itself.

Range.what: How spread out the numbers are: largest minus smallest.
how: Find the biggest and the smallest.
Subtract.
The range is one number, not a pair.
Range.trap: Writing it as "5 to 20". The range of that is 15.

how: Add them all, divide by how many.
If the average and the count are given, multiply to get the total back.
Check the answer sits between the smallest and largest.
Average.trap: Forgetting that a missing value can be found by working backwards from the total.

Volume.what: How much space is inside a solid.
how: A box: length × width × height.
Think of it as the area of the bottom, stacked up as many layers as it is tall.
Units are cubed.
Volume.trap: Adding the three numbers, or multiplying only two of them.

Volume reasoning.what: Working backwards from a volume, or comparing two solids.
how: Volume = length × width × height, so divide by the two you know to find the third.
Doubling one side doubles the volume; doubling all three makes it eight times.
Same volume does not mean same shape.
Volume reasoning.trap: Assuming two boxes with the same volume must have the same surface area.

Probability.what: How likely something is, written as a fraction.
how: Top: how many ways it can happen. Bottom: how many ways anything can happen.
Count the total carefully — it is every item, not just the ones you want.
Always between 0 and 1.
Probability.trap: Putting the wrong number on the bottom. 4 red and 6 blue means 10 on the bottom, not 6.

how: Divide the total by how many there were.
Say the units out loud: dollars per item, miles per hour.
To compare two deals, get both down to one.
Unit rate.trap: Dividing the wrong way round. The thing you want "per" goes on the bottom.

Ratio.what: How two amounts compare, part to part.
how: 3 : 2 means for every 3 of the first there are 2 of the second.
Total parts = 3 + 2 = 5. Divide the whole by 5 to find one part.
Scale both sides by the same number to keep the ratio.
Ratio.trap: Treating 3 : 2 as 3 out of 2. It is 3 out of 5.

Scale.what: A drawing or model where every length is multiplied by the same number.
how: Find the scale factor: real length ÷ drawing length.
Multiply to go from drawing to real; divide to come back.
Every length uses the same factor.
Scale.trap: Applying the factor to some measurements but not others.

Scale reasoning.what: What happens to area and volume when you scale a shape.
how: Double every length and the area goes up four times.
Double every length and the volume goes up eight times.
Lengths × k, areas × k², volumes × k³.
Scale reasoning.trap: Assuming doubling the sides doubles the area. It quadruples it.

Measurement.what: Converting between units without losing track.
how: Write the conversion you know: 1 foot = 12 inches.
Going to smaller units, multiply. Going to bigger units, divide.
Check the size: inches should be a bigger number than feet.
Measurement.trap: Multiplying when you should divide. Ask first whether the answer should get bigger or smaller.

Coordinates.what: Finding a point on a grid using two numbers.
how: (x, y): along the corridor first, then up the stairs.
Distance along a flat line is just the difference of the numbers.
Plot the points before answering — always draw it.
Coordinates.trap: Swapping x and y. The first number is sideways.

Algebra.what: Using a letter for a number you do not know yet.
how: Turn the sentence into a sum with a letter in it.
Do the same thing to both sides until the letter stands alone.
Substitute your answer back in and check.
Algebra.trap: Doing something to one side and forgetting the other.

Expression.what: A sum with a letter in it, which you evaluate rather than solve.
how: Replace the letter with the number given.
Then follow the order of operations: brackets, multiply/divide, add/subtract.
There is no equals sign to balance — just work it out.
Expression.trap: Trying to solve for the letter when the question only asked you to put a number in.

Exponents.what: A small raised number saying how many times to multiply.
how: 4³ means 4 × 4 × 4, not 4 × 3.
Anything to the power 1 is itself; to the power 0 is 1.
Work out the power before multiplying or adding.
Exponents.trap: Multiplying the base by the exponent. 4³ is 64, not 12.

how: Learn 1 to 15 by heart — they come up constantly.
A square number is the area of a square with whole sides.

Square roots.what: The number that was multiplied by itself to get this one.
how: √49 asks: what times itself makes 49? 7.
If it is not a perfect square, find the two whole numbers it sits between.
Squaring and square-rooting undo each other.
Square roots.trap: Halving instead of rooting. √36 is 6, not 18.

Factors.what: Numbers that divide into it exactly, with nothing left over.
how: Go up in pairs from 1: 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4.
Stop when the pair meets in the middle.
Every number has 1 and itself as factors.
Factors.trap: Mixing up factors with multiples. Factors are smaller; multiples are bigger.

Multiples.what: What you get counting up in steps of that number.
how: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, and on forever.
A common multiple appears in both lists.
The lowest common multiple is the first one they share.
Multiples.trap: Calling a factor a multiple. Multiples are the bigger ones.

Divisibility.what: Quick tests for whether one number divides another.
how: 2: ends even. 5: ends 0 or 5. 10: ends 0.
3: the digits add to a multiple of 3. 9: they add to a multiple of 9.
4: the last two digits make a multiple of 4.
Divisibility.trap: Doing the whole division when a digit test would have answered it in two seconds.

Prime factors.what: Breaking a number into the primes that multiply to make it.
how: Split it into any two factors, then keep splitting.
Stop when every branch is prime.
Every number has exactly one prime factorisation.
Prime factors.trap: Stopping too early and leaving a number that can still be split.

Remainders.what: What is left over when a division does not come out exactly.
how: Divide as far as whole numbers go, then see what is left.
The remainder is always smaller than what you divided by.
Check: divisor × answer + remainder = the number you started with.
Remainders.trap: Giving a remainder bigger than the divisor — that means the answer was too small.

Division.what: Sharing into equal groups, or asking how many fit.
how: Ask which it is: how many each, or how many groups?
Estimate first so you know roughly what to expect.
Multiply back to check.
Division.trap: Dividing the wrong way round. The whole goes inside the bracket.

Number properties.what: Facts that stay true about numbers whatever the numbers are.
how: Try it with small numbers first — 2, 3, 10.
If you can find one case where it fails, it is false.
Odd and even, positive and negative, zero and one behave in fixed ways.
Number properties.trap: Testing only one example and assuming it always holds.

how: Call the first one n; the next are n+1, n+2.
Their total is the middle one times how many there are, when the count is odd.
Consecutive even or odd numbers go up in twos.
Consecutive integers.trap: Writing n, n+1, n+2 for consecutive EVEN numbers. Those go n, n+2, n+4.

Pattern.what: A sequence built by the same rule each step.
how: Find the difference between one term and the next.
Same difference each time? Keep adding it. Doubling? It is multiplying.
Write the rule in words before using it.
Pattern.trap: Guessing from the first two terms. Check the rule against a third.

Estimation.what: A rough answer, quickly, to check the real one.
how: Round each number to something easy.
Do the easy sum in your head.
Compare it with your worked answer — they should be close.
Estimation.trap: Rounding both numbers the same way and forgetting the estimate is now always high or always low.

Data.what: Reading a table, chart or graph without misreading it.
how: Read the title and both axis labels before anything else.
Check what one square or one step on the scale is worth.
Find the number the question asks for; do not eyeball it.
Data.trap: Assuming each gridline is 1 when the scale says 5.

Data reasoning.what: Drawing a conclusion from a chart or a set of numbers.
how: Say what the data shows in one plain sentence first.
Only then look at the choices.
A conclusion must follow from the numbers, not from what seems likely.
Data reasoning.trap: Choosing an answer that is probably true in real life but is not shown by this data.

Symmetry.what: A shape that folds onto itself exactly.
how: Imagine folding along a line — do the halves match?
A square has four lines of symmetry; a rectangle has two.
Rotational symmetry is turning, not folding.
Symmetry.trap: Counting a diagonal as a line of symmetry on a rectangle. It is not.

Mixed reasoning.what: A question that needs more than one idea joined together.
how: Work out what you are actually being asked for, in words.
List what you were given, and what each piece lets you find.
Do it one step at a time, writing each result down.
Mixed reasoning.trap: Trying to leap straight to the answer. Two small steps beat one guess.

rule.zh: 先听，再用笔在格子里写——点"写好了"会显示标准写法，按笔顺判；也可以在纸上写，显示对照，自己或家长打分。
rule.en: Listen, then write it with the Pencil in the box — the standard form appears when you tap Done and the strokes are judged by rule; or write it on paper, show it, and rate it yourself or with a parent.

zh-char.q: 「你一定要照顾好自己。」中，"一定"的读音是？
zh-char.e: 一 changes tone depending on what comes after it. In front of a fourth-tone syllable like 定 (dìng), 一 is said in the second tone, so 一定 is yídìng.
zh-char.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期一，练习4（printed p.32）
zh-char.qe: How is 一定 pronounced in 「你一定要照顾好自己。」?
zh-char.ez: "一"的声调会随后面的字变化：后面是第四声（定 dìng）时，"一"读第二声，所以"一定"读 yídìng。

y.A: yīdìng keeps 一 in the first tone, which is how it sounds when you count — 一, 二, 三 — but not when it sits in front of a fourth-tone syllable.
y.B: yīdīng puts 定 in the first tone, but 定 is always a fourth tone, dìng, falling at the end of the word.
y.D: yìdīng has both tones the wrong way round: 一 is not a fourth tone here, and 定 is not a first tone.

yz.A: yīdìng 是"一"单独数数时的第一声（一、二、三），可是在第四声的字前面要变成第二声。
yz.B: yīdīng 把"定"读成了第一声，可"定"一直是第四声 dìng。
yz.D: yìdīng 两个声调都反了："一"在这里不读第四声，"定"也不读第一声。

zh-char.e: 突 is built from 穴 on top and 犬 underneath. 穴 takes five strokes and 犬 takes four, so 突 has nine in all, and the radical is the part on top, 穴 — the textbook prints 穴 → 突 beside the character list.
zh-char.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期一，练习4（printed p.32）
zh-char.qe: How many strokes does 突 have, and what is its radical?
zh-char.ez: "突"上面是"穴"，下面是"犬"。"穴"五画，"犬"四画，一共九画；部首是上面的"穴"——课本第50页写着"穴→突"。

y.B: 十；穴 picks the radical correctly but adds a stroke that is not there — 穴 is five strokes and 犬 is four, which comes to nine.
y.C: 九；犬 counts the strokes correctly, but 犬 is the part underneath; the radical of 突 is the 穴 above it.
y.D: 十；犬 misses twice over: the stroke count is nine, and the radical is 穴 rather than 犬.

yz.B: 十；穴 部首对了，但多数了一画："穴"五画加"犬"四画是九画。
yz.C: 九；犬 笔画数对了，可"犬"在下面，"突"的部首是上面的"穴"。
yz.D: 十；犬 两处都不对：九画，部首是"穴"。

zh-word.q: 选词填空：明天开会，你______不要迟到。
zh-word.e: 最好 is how you give someone friendly advice — you had best not be late. A reminder about tomorrow's meeting is a suggestion, not a command.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期一，练习4（printed p.32）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 明天开会，你______不要迟到。
zh-word.ez: "最好"用来给人提建议——你最好别迟到。提醒明天开会，是建议，不是命令。

y.A: 只好 means there is nothing else you can do, the way 小马只好回家问妈妈 — it describes being left with no choice, not being advised.
y.C: 原来 means it turns out, and it looks back at something just discovered rather than forward to tomorrow.
y.D: 都要 means all must, which needs a group of things to be about; only one person is being reminded here.

yz.A: "只好"是没有别的办法，像"小马只好回家问妈妈"，说的是没得选，不是提建议。
yz.C: "原来"是"原来如此"的意思，说的是刚弄明白的事，不是明天的事。
yz.D: "都要"是"全都必须"，要有一群人或一堆事才说得通；这里只提醒一个人。

zh-word.q: 选词填空：天快黑了，你______不要出去了。
zh-word.e: 最好 offers gentle advice — it is getting dark, so you had best stay in. The sentence suggests rather than orders.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期二，练习4（printed p.34）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 天快黑了，你______不要出去了。
zh-word.ez: "最好"是温和的建议——天快黑了，你还是别出去。这句话是劝，不是命令。

y.A: 只好 means no other option is left, but going out is still a choice here; she is being advised against it, not prevented.
y.B: 一定 would turn this into an order — you definitely must not go out — and the sentence is softer than that.
y.C: 突然 means something happened all at once, so it describes an event rather than what somebody should do.

yz.A: "只好"是没有别的办法，可这里出不出去还可以选，只是劝你别去。
yz.B: "一定"就成了命令——你绝对不能出去——这句话没那么重。
yz.C: "突然"说的是事情一下子发生，不是该做什么。

zh-word.q: 选词填空：老师进来了，教室______安静了。
zh-word.e: 突然 marks a change that happens all at once — the teacher walks in and the room goes quiet in that very moment.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期二，练习4（printed p.34）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 老师进来了，教室______安静了。
zh-word.ez: "突然"说一下子变了——老师一进来，教室一下就安静了。

y.B: 只好 means being left with no other option, but a classroom does not choose to go quiet; it simply does.
y.C: 最好 offers advice, and nobody is being advised — the sentence reports what happened when the teacher came in.
y.D: 一定 means certainly, which would say the room was bound to go quiet rather than describing the moment it did.

yz.B: "只好"是没有办法只能这样，可教室不会"选择"安静，它就是一下子安静了。
yz.C: "最好"是提建议，这句话没有在劝谁，只是说发生了什么。
yz.D: "一定"是"肯定会"，说的是必然，不是那一刻的变化。

zh-word.q: 选词填空：我没带雨伞，______等雨停之后再走。
zh-word.e: 只好 is for when every other option has gone. With no umbrella, waiting for the rain to stop is all that is left.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期二，练习4（printed p.34）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 我没带雨伞，______等雨停之后再走。
zh-word.ez: "只好"是别的办法都没有了。没带雨伞，只能等雨停。

y.A: 一定 means certainly, which would promise that she will wait rather than explain that she has no choice but to wait.
y.C: 突然 describes something happening all at once, and waiting for rain to stop is the opposite — it takes a while.
y.D: 最好 would make waiting the best idea among several, but with no umbrella it is the only idea.

yz.A: "一定"是"肯定会"，像在保证会等，而不是说没办法只能等。
yz.C: "突然"是一下子发生的事，等雨停正好相反——要等好一会儿。
yz.D: "最好"是几个办法里挑最好的，可没带伞，等雨停是唯一的办法。

zh-word.q: 选词填空：我______要早睡早起，这样才能身体好。
zh-word.e: 一定 is a firm promise to yourself — I will certainly keep early hours. The second half gives the reason, which makes the first half a resolution.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期二，练习4（printed p.34）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 我______要早睡早起，这样才能身体好。
zh-word.ez: "一定"是对自己下的决心——我肯定要早睡早起。后半句说了原因，所以前半句是决心。

y.A: 最好 would soften it into advice for somebody else, while this sentence is a promise the speaker makes about herself.
y.B: 突然 means all at once, which cannot describe a habit kept night after night.
y.D: 只好 means having no choice, but nobody is forcing these early nights — they are being chosen.

yz.A: "最好"变成在劝别人，可这句话是说话的人在给自己下决心。
yz.B: "突然"是一下子，不能用来说天天坚持的习惯。
yz.D: "只好"是没办法，可早睡早起是自己决定的，没人逼。

zh-word.q: 选词填空：小马不知道______怎么做。
zh-word.e: 应该 is for what someone ought to do. The pony has been given two opposite answers and cannot work out what he ought to do next.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期三，练习2（printed p.35）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 小马不知道______怎么做。
zh-word.ez: "应该"说的是该做什么。小马听了两种相反的话，不知道该怎么办。

y.A: 原来 means it turns out, and it introduces something just discovered rather than something one ought to do.
y.B: 既……也…… joins two things that are both true, so it needs two halves to join; this sentence has only one.
y.C: 小心 means careful, and the pony is not being careless — he simply does not know whose advice to follow.

yz.A: "原来"是刚弄明白的事，不是该做什么。
yz.B: "既……也……"把两件都对的事连起来，要两半才能用；这句话只有一半。
yz.C: "小心"是当心、仔细，小马不是不小心，是不知道该听谁的。

zh-word.q: 选词填空：下雨的时候走路要______一点儿。
zh-word.e: 小心 means careful. Wet ground is slippery, so walking in the rain asks for a little more care.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期三，练习2（printed p.35）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 下雨的时候走路要______一点儿。
zh-word.ez: "小心"是当心。下雨路滑，走路要更当心一点儿。

y.B: 应该 means ought to, and the 要 already in the sentence says that; what is missing is the word for being careful.
y.C: 原来 means it turns out, which looks back at a discovery rather than telling you how to walk.
y.D: 既……也…… links two things that are both true, and this sentence names only one thing to do.

yz.B: "应该"是"该"，句子里的"要"已经是这个意思了，缺的是"当心"这个词。
yz.C: "原来"说的是刚发现的事，不是教你怎么走路。
yz.D: "既……也……"连两件都对的事，这句话只说了一件要做的事。

zh-word.q: 选词填空：他______喜欢吃中国菜，______喜欢吃美国菜。
zh-word.e: 既……也…… joins two things that are both true at once. Notice that the sentence has two blanks and two halves — that is the shape this pattern is built to fill.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期三，练习2（printed p.35）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blanks: 他______喜欢吃中国菜，______喜欢吃美国菜。
zh-word.ez: "既……也……"把两件同时都对的事连起来。看，句子有两个空、两个半句——正是这个句式。

y.A: 小心 means careful, which has nothing to do with liking two kinds of food.
y.C: 应该 means ought to, but nobody is being told what to do — the sentence reports what he enjoys.
y.D: 原来 means it turns out, and it goes at the front of a single statement; it cannot stretch across two halves.

yz.A: "小心"是当心，和喜欢吃什么菜没关系。
yz.C: "应该"是该做什么，可这句话没人在要求谁，只是说他喜欢什么。
yz.D: "原来"放在一句话开头，说刚发现的事；它跨不了两个半句。

zh-word.q: 选词填空：亮亮长得很像你，______他是你的弟弟啊。
zh-word.e: 原来 marks the moment something clicks — he looks so much like you, and it turns out he is your younger brother. The 啊 at the end is the sound of working it out.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期三，练习2（printed p.35）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 亮亮长得很像你，______他是你的弟弟啊。
zh-word.ez: "原来"是忽然明白的那一下——他长得这么像你，原来是你弟弟。句尾的"啊"就是明白过来的语气。

y.A: 应该 means ought to, which would make the sentence tell him to be your brother — something nobody can be told.
y.B: 小心 means careful, and nothing here is risky.
y.D: 既……也…… joins two things that are both true, and this sentence is one discovery rather than two facts side by side.

yz.A: "应该"是该做什么，总不能要求他"该"当你的弟弟。
yz.B: "小心"是当心，这里没有什么要当心的。
yz.D: "既……也……"连两件都对的事，这句话是一个发现，不是两件事。

zh-word.q: 选择正确的答案填空：小马听了老牛的话，______要过河，小松鼠来了。
zh-word.e: 正 in front of a verb means right at that moment — he was just about to cross when the squirrel arrived. The story puts it the same way: 小马听了老牛的话，正要过河。
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期四，练习1（printed p.38）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 小马听了老牛的话，______要过河，小松鼠来了。
zh-word.ez: "正"放在动词前面，是"正要、刚要"——小马刚要过河，小松鼠就来了。课文里也是这么写的：小马听了老牛的话，正要过河。

y.A: 从 means from, and it needs a starting place after it, the way 从树上跳下来 does; it cannot sit in front of 要.
y.B: 到 means to or arrive, so it would need somewhere to arrive at — and the pony has not crossed yet.
y.D: 也 means too, which would say the pony crossed as well, as though somebody else had already crossed.

yz.A: "从"后面要跟一个地方，像"从树上跳下来"，不能直接放在"要"前面。
yz.B: "到"是到达，后面要有到的地方——小马还没过河呢。
yz.D: "也"是"也一样"，好像别人已经过了河，小马也过。

zh-word.q: 选择正确的答案填空：奶奶画了一张画儿，我______画了一张。
zh-word.e: 也 means too. Grandma drew one and I drew one too — two different people doing the same thing is exactly the job 也 does.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期四，练习1（printed p.38）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 奶奶画了一张画儿，我______画了一张。
zh-word.ez: "也"是"也一样"。奶奶画了一张，我也画了一张——两个人做同一件事，正是"也"。

y.B: 又 means doing something again, which needs the same person to draw twice; here the second drawing is by somebody else.
y.C: 既 does not stand on its own — it waits for 也 or 又 later in the sentence, as in 既……也…….
y.D: 才 means only then or not until, which would say the drawing came later than expected rather than as well.

yz.B: "又"是同一个人再做一次，可第二张画是另一个人画的。
yz.C: "既"不能单独用，它要等后面的"也"或"又"，像"既……也……"。
yz.D: "才"是"这才、直到……才"，说的是晚了才做，不是"也"。

zh-word.q: 选择正确的答案填空：水很浅，小马过______去。
zh-word.e: 得 links a verb to what is said about it: 过得去 means able to get across. The ox says it this way in the story — 水很浅，你过得去。
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期四，练习1（printed p.38）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 水很浅，小马过______去。
zh-word.ez: "得"接在动词后面，说能不能——"过得去"就是能过去。课文里老牛就是这么说的：水很浅，你过得去。

y.A: 的 joins a describing word to a noun, the way 美丽的花朵 does, so it needs a noun after it rather than 去.
y.B: 地 comes before a verb to say how it is done, like 小心地过河, but here the blank falls after 过.
y.D: 了 marks something finished, and the pony has not crossed yet — he is being told that he is able to.

yz.A: "的"连接形容词和名词，像"美丽的花朵"，后面要跟名词，不是"去"。
yz.B: "地"放在动词前面，说怎样做，像"小心地过河"；这里的空在"过"后面。
yz.D: "了"说事情做完了，可小马还没过河——是在说他能过去。

zh-word.q: 选择正确的答案填空：公园里有很多美丽______花朵。
zh-word.e: 的 ties a describing word to the noun it describes: 美丽的花朵, beautiful flowers.
zh-word.src: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》 星期四，练习1（printed p.38）
zh-word.qe: Fill the blank: 公园里有很多美丽______花朵。
zh-word.ez: "的"把形容词和它形容的名词连起来：美丽的花朵。

y.B: 地 goes in front of a verb to say how something is done, like 慢慢地走, but 花朵 is a thing rather than an action.
y.C: 得 follows a verb to say how it turned out, as in 过得去, and 美丽 is not a verb.
y.D: 了 marks something completed, and nothing is being completed here — the flowers are simply there.

yz.B: "地"放在动词前面说怎样做，像"慢慢地走"，可"花朵"是东西，不是动作。
yz.C: "得"接在动词后面说结果，像"过得去"，"美丽"不是动词。
yz.D: "了"说做完了，这里没有什么做完的事——花朵就在那里。

L05.source: 中文（小学）第四册（2023年第三版） 练习册A 第五课《小马过河》

explanation.en: 亻 on the left, 白 on the right: left–right.

explanation.en: 氵 on the left, 罙 on the right: left–right.

explanation.en: 穴 above, 犬 below: top–bottom.

explanation.zh: 木在左、公在右：左右结构。
explanation.en: 木 on the left, 公 on the right: left–right.

explanation.en: 突 + 然 = 突然, suddenly.
最 + 好 = 最好, had best.
只 + 好 = 只好, had no choice but.
那 + 么 = 那么, so / that.
一 + 定 = 一定, certainly.

items.text: 他______出现在我面前，让我很惊喜。

explanation.zh: "突然"：一下子出现，所以我很惊喜。
explanation.en: 突然 — suddenly: he appeared all at once, which is why I was surprised.

items.text: 他想不出别的办法，______请人帮忙。

explanation.zh: 想不出别的办法，只好请人帮忙。
explanation.en: No other way, so he had to ask for help — 只好.

items.text: 他跑得______快，我都追不上他。

explanation.en: 那么快 — that fast.
一定要来 — you must come.

given.en: Sentence (2) is filled in by the book: 最好.

exercises.title: 连词成句
exercises.title_en: Write the words in the correct order to make sentences

explanation.zh: 正确的顺序：老牛一定会觉得河水很浅。
explanation.en: In order: 老牛一定会觉得河水很浅 — the ox would surely think the river is shallow.

explanation.zh: 正确的顺序：我一定会努力学习中文。
explanation.en: In order: 我一定会努力学习中文 — I will surely study Chinese hard.

explanation.zh: 正确的顺序：亮亮一定会帮妈妈做家务。
explanation.en: In order: 亮亮一定会帮妈妈做家务 — Liangliang will surely help Mother with the housework.

explanation.zh: 正确的顺序：妹妹一定会喜欢爸爸买的玩具。
explanation.en: In order: 妹妹一定会喜欢爸爸买的玩具 — Little sister will surely like the toy Father bought.

exercises.title: 根据课文判断正误
exercises.title_en: Decide whether the statements are true or false according to the text

explanation.zh: 课文第一句就是：小马要过河。
explanation.en: The first line of the text: 小马要过河 — the pony wants to cross the river.

items.text: 老牛说水很浅，因为他又高又大。

explanation.zh: 老牛说"水很浅"；妈妈解释了原因：老牛又高又大，他会觉得水很浅。
explanation.en: The ox says the water is shallow, and Mother explains why: the ox is tall and big, so to him it feels shallow.

items.text: 小松鼠也认为很容易过河。

explanation.zh: 小松鼠说的正相反：别过河！水深得很，你会淹死的。
explanation.en: The squirrel says the opposite: don't cross — the water is very deep, you will drown.

items.text: 小马没有回家问妈妈的建议。

explanation.zh: 小马不知道该怎么办，只好回家问妈妈。
explanation.en: The pony did not know what to do, so he went home and asked his mother.

explanation.zh: 小马又跑到河边，小心地过了河。
explanation.en: The pony went back to the river and crossed it carefully.

exercises.title: 根据课文和图片给句子排序
exercises.title_en: Sequence the sentences according to the text and the pictures

note.zh: 图在练习册第37页；句子按故事先后排。
note.en: The pictures are on workbook p.37; put the sentences in the story's order.

pieces: 小松鼠从树上跳下来，告诉小马水很深，他会淹死的。
小马跑回家问妈妈，妈妈告诉他最好自己试一试。
小马又跑到河边，小心地过了河。
小马想要过河，牛伯伯告诉他水很浅，过得去。

explanation.zh: 故事的顺序：先问牛伯伯（①），松鼠跳下来（②），回家问妈妈（③），最后小心地过了河（④）。
explanation.en: The story's order: ask the ox first (①), the squirrel jumps down (②), home to ask Mother (③), then across the river carefully (④).
